messages.body_plain:
On Friday, July 31, 2015 at 10:33:10 PM UTC-4, MT wrote:
>
> However, As Ben pointed out, the lagrange multiplier is really a function of the original model parameters declared in the stan parameters {} Block.

Yes, that is the key point.

>
> To find the lagrange multiplier, It seems like there are 2 useful pursuits:
>
> 1) In C++ - Find the lagrange multiplier using built optimizers, say from boost.

This is the better route, and one could even use Stan's LBFGS optimization and / or autodiff. I suspect if integrate_ode() were used as a template, adding an optimize() function would take 1 day to implement, test, and document. There would need to be an implicit differentiation too. But I don't know how to get the parser to generate the C++ code like it does for ODEs.

>
> 2) Remain in STAN: Doing some further reading, we can actually solve for lambda a brute force way involving control loops and a singular value decomposition. From my understanding, although a default 'optimizer' isn't accessible within stan, control loops and svd are.

Only singular values but in any event, this is much less promising than 1)

>
> For both these approaches, it seems crucial to tell stan NOT to rely on autodiff, so the user computed log empirical likelihood and it's gradient can update the log posterior and it's gradient correctly. (Which basically gets at the original post of this thread)

The likelihood would mostly be a log_sum_exp(), which is already pretty-well optimized. But being able to write

w ~ empirical_likelihood();

in Stan programs wouldn't hurt.

Ben

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Question about Wiener Diffusion Model Distribution in rstan_2.7.0-2
messages.body_plain:
I think the problem here was that Andrew looked at the documentation in
wiener_log.hpp file which wrongly describes the possibility of lower
boundary by negating y (random variable) which was originally what the
patch of Joachim Vandekerckhove did.

I changed this (thus forcing y to be strictly positive) because there
was no computational advantage in doing so and thought it would be
potentially dangerous for users. I realize I should have discussed such
change with stan-dev at the time.

The Stan manual, however, correctly describes the current behavior
(although it does deserves a better explanation), and I didn't put it
there that y must positive because it is already in the category
"Non-negative Continuous Distributions".

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: ESS confusion
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: ESS confusion
messages.body_plain:
No, the name's not misleading.  The ESS is an estimate of the
statistical power of the sample you have scaled to the number of
i.i.d. draws to which it would be equivalent.

What happens is that a sequence of autocorrelated draws have more
power than thinning because there's information in the thinned draws
that gets lost when you thin them.

There's a very nice overview in Geyer's chapter for the MCMC
Handbook, which is one of the free samples:

  http://www.mcmchandbook.net/HandbookChapter1.pdf

Just don't listen to his advice on convergence monitoring!  His
comments are right in theory, but not in practice if you want
answers in finite amounts of time.

And we do our calculations a little differently, as described in
BDA3 and in the manual --- we basically take cross-chain information
into account, which makes our ESS calculations more conservative than
the typical approach of estimating each chain separately (they give
you the same answer in the stationary limit).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Memory Allocation issue with STAN running in Google Cloud?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Memory Allocation issue with STAN running in Google Cloud?
messages.body_plain:
RStan allocates memory to store the draws ahead of time.  You
can either try running CmdStan, which streams out the output,
or you can try running fewer draws, thinning more, or saving fewer
parameters.  If there's no problem with mc.cores=1 then you are
probably just exhausting memory when you try two.  Two runs should
use twice as much memory --- there's no sharing (yet, anyway).

- Bob

>

When I enabled mc.cores = 2 (my "trail" VM can only have 2 cores max), my R script would get stuck and when I press Ctrl-C, I can see R is complaining "memory allocation problem". Thought such problem does not seem to have arise when I run with mc.cores=1.

>
> The Google VM is running Debian Jessie and R 3.2.1 (from CRAN).

Will changing the value of eta, which I currently have set to 1, in the lkj_corr_cholesky(eta) distribution constrain closer to the initial value? If so, would increasing or decreasing be better?

Only if your initial value is the identity matrix. The LKJ density does not have a location parameter, but its mode is the identity matrix for any eta > 1 and is more peaked for larger values of eta.

Ben

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] ESS confusion
messages.body_plain:
I can see why "power" is bad, but why "information"?
I tend to think of information content as being measured
by things like entropy.  Is it by analogy to the expected
information about the mean contained in N i.i.d. draws?

I never quantify any units or other generic nouns in the manual.

Geyer uses "statistical accuracy", in the context "statistical accuracy
is inversely proportional to the square root of the sample size",
which also seems sub-optimal terminologically.

- Bob

> On Aug 1, 2015, at 10:21 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>
> Fine, but just to be careful with jargon, replace “power” by “information” in Bob’s response below.
>
>> On Aug 1, 2015, at 2:56 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>>
>> No, the name's not misleading.  The ESS is an estimate of the
>> statistical power of the sample you have scaled to the number of
>> i.i.d. draws to which it would be equivalent.
>>
>> What happens is that a sequence of autocorrelated draws have more
>> power than thinning because there's information in the thinned draws
>> that gets lost when you thin them.
>>
>> There's a very nice overview in Geyer's chapter for the MCMC
>> Handbook, which is one of the free samples:
>>
>> http://www.mcmchandbook.net/HandbookChapter1.pdf
>>
>> Just don't listen to his advice on convergence monitoring!  His
>> comments are right in theory, but not in practice if you want
>> answers in finite amounts of time.
>>
>> And we do our calculations a little differently, as described in
>> BDA3 and in the manual --- we basically take cross-chain information
>> into account, which makes our ESS calculations more conservative than
>> the typical approach of estimating each chain separately (they give
>> you the same answer in the stationary limit).
>>
>> - Bob
>>
>>

>>>

>>>
>>> thanks a lot. I guess I have to look at the definitions to see what makes most sense in my application. messages.subject: Any reason that Optimize may fail when NUTS doesn't?
messages.subject_clean: Any reason that Optimize may fail when NUTS doesn't?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have a model which generates (at least seemingly) good samples when running NUTS, but generates very poor estimates (all parameters at boundaries) when using L-BFGS. Are there any known conditions that would make this happen?

The model is a truncated generalised gamma distribution, with uncertain variates (lognormal uncertainty, they are dark matter halo masses, intrinsically between 10^12 and 10^15 ish). At the moment, all uncertainties are the same (though this will have to change in future versions). Other than the masses, there are four parameters:
alpha encoding the power-law slope,
logHs encodes the (log) cut-off mass
beta encodes the steepness of the cutoff.
log_mmin encodes the minimum mass.

The 3 first parameters are all highly covariant, which may be causing problems, not sure (I thought NUTS was fairly good at navigating high covariance?). I'm at a bit of a loss as to what information to to post here. Perhaps I'll just go for as much as I think might help (though it might be a bit to wade through).

So the explicit model: (I'm not posting the functions block here for clarity, but it defines the truncated_GGD_log function which calculates the log of the truncated generalised gamma -- for negative values of the shape parameter)

data {
    int<lower=0> N; // number of halos
    vector<lower=0>[N] log_m_meas; // observed mass of halos
    vector<lower=0>[N] err; //uncertainty in halo masses

    // CONTROLS FOR PARAMETER BOUNDS
    real<lower=0> hs_min; //The lower bound of loghs
    real<lower=0,upper=20> hs_max; //Upper bound of loghs
    real<lower=-2,upper=0> alpha_min; //Lower bound of alpha
    real<lower=-2,upper=0> alpha_max; //Upper bound of alpha
    real<lower=0> beta_min; //Lower bound of beta
    real<lower=0> beta_max; //Upper bound of beta
    real<lower=0,upper=20>mtrue_max; // Upper bound of true masses
    real<lower=0> mmin_min;
    real<lower=0> mmin_max;
}

parameters {
    real<lower=beta_min,upper=beta_max> beta;
    real<lower=hs_min,upper=hs_max> logHs;
    real<lower=alpha_min,upper=alpha_max> alpha;
    real<lower=mmin_min,upper=mmin_max> log_mmin;
    vector<lower=log_mmin,upper=mtrue_max>[N] log_mtrue; //True mass estimates
}

transformed parameters {
   real xmin;
   xmin <- pow(10,beta*(log_mmin-logHs));
}

model {
    vector[N] log10y;
    vector[N] x;

    log10y <- log_mtrue-logHs;
    for (i in 1:N) x[i] <- pow(10,beta*log10y[i]);

    //truncated GGD is beta*10^(alpha*log10y)*exp(-x)/(10^logHs*Gamma((alpha+1)/beta,x)
    log10y ~ truncated_GGD(x, logHs,alpha, beta, xmin);
    log_mtrue ~ normal(log_m_meas,err);
}

I want to use about 25,000 halos for my true run, but have tested with fewer, and wouldn't mind running it with more as well.

I produce my mock halos in the following manner:

library(gsl)

dtggd = function(logm,logmmin,logh,a,b){
  # GSL required!
  return = b*10^(a*(logm-logh))*exp(-10^((logm-logh)*b))/(10^logh * gamma_inc((a+1)/b,10^(b*(logmmin-logh))))
}

qtggd = function(logm,logmmin,logh,a,b){
  return = 1 - gamma_inc((a+1)/b,10^(b*(logm-logh)))/gamma_inc((a+1)/b,10^(b*(logmmin-logh)))
}

rtggd = function(N,logmmin,logh,a,b){
  mmax = logh + 2.5/b

  logm = seq(logmmin, mmax, 0.0001)
  cdf = qtggd(logm,logmmin,logh,a,b)

  icdf = approxfun(cdf, logm)

  x = runif(N)
  return = icdf(x)
}

############## GET MOCK DATA ###################################
N = 5000
err = 0.1
logmmin = 12
logh = 14
alpha = -1.8
beta = 0.7
seed = 1111

set.seed(seed)
intrinsic = rtggd(N,logmmin,logh,alpha,beta)
mock.masses = rnorm(N,intrinsic,std)

To be certain, with this, ie. N=5000, I get the following density plot:

Then I run the following to run stan, and also two optimization runs

############## SETUP RSTAN DATA ################################
data = list(N=N,log_m_meas=mock.masses,err=rep(err,N),
            hs_min=12,hs_max=15,alpha_min=-2.0,
            alpha_max=-1.6,beta_min=0.05,beta_max=1.5,
            mtrue_max=16.5,mmin_min=11,mmin_max=13)

init = list(list(logHs=12.1,alpha=-1.95,beta=1.2,log_mmin=11.1,log_mtrue=mock.masses),   # Far away but reasonable masses
            list(logHs=14.9,alpha=-1.61,beta=0.2,log_mmin=12.5),                         # Opposite side, random masses
            list(logHs=13.5,alpha=-1.61,beta=1.2,log_mmin=11.5,log_mtrue=mock.masses),   # Swap alpha/beta relationship
            list(logHs=logh,alpha=alpha,beta=beta,log_mmin=logmmin,log_mtrue=intrinsic)) # Exact answer if perfect sample

opt.init.exact = init[[4]]
opt.init.bad = init[[2]]

model = stan_model(file="model_NO_S.stan")

############# RUN MCMC #########################################
result <- sampling(model, data=data, pars = c('logHs','alpha','beta',"log_mmin"), chains=4,
                   iter=2000, warmup=1000,cores=4,init=init)

opt.res.exact <- optimizing(model,data=data,init=opt.init.exact,as_vector=FALSE)
opt.res.bad <- optimizing(model,data=data,init=opt.init.bad,as_vector=FALSE)

The results look good for the MCMC: In fact, in this particular case it seems that logHs and alpha are reproduced perfectly (as the median) though beta is estimated as 0.83 rather than 0.7 (it makes sense that beta isn't estimated very well, since it mostly comes from the cut-off where there are basically no objects.

In terms of diagnostics, using the amazing shinyStan, I have:

Chain     accept_stat    stepsize    treedepth    n_leapfrog    n_divergent
All ch    0.8142    0.1093    5.4253    81.8334    0.0119
chain1    0.8282    0.1038    5.691     91.5345    0.012
chain2    0.8056    0.1159    5.2375    59.803     0.0095
chain3    0.8056    0.1089    5.3905    85.8465    0.0135
chain4    0.8176    0.1087    5.382     90.1495    0.0125

Everything looks good I think, as far as I understand. The only things perhaps worth mentioning are the correlation plot:

Where chain 2 is obviously worse than the rest -- this is probably because it starts with random masses. Also the large amount of covariance can be seen in the pairs plot:

Finally, the run took a fair while, especially in the warmup -- not sure if that's normal?:

          warmup   sample
chain:1 767.6131 213.1524
chain:2 539.0624 188.2982
chain:3 798.0353 136.3628
chain:4 852.1482 121.8508

So everything seems pretty much fine. BUT, when I check the results of the optimization runs, it returns this:

> opt.res.exact$par[1:4]
$beta
[1] 0.1685809

$logHs
[1] 12

$alpha
[1] -1.999999

$log_mmin
[1] 12.09832

> opt.res.bad$par[1:4]
$beta
[1] 0.05

$logHs
[1] 14.99999

$alpha
[1] -1.6

$log_mmin
[1] 11

I'm not really sure what else would be useful -- it would be nice if the optimization worked so that I could get quick estimates for testing purposes.

Sorry I feel like I've been spamming you guys lately -- thanks very much for all the work you do. I certainly have not been disappointed.

Cheers.

messages.subject: estimating the variability of the Colorado growth model
messages.subject_clean: estimating the variability of the Colorado growth model
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm working on a project to estimate the variability of "growth" measures in education, specifically the Colorado model, which uses quantile regression to estimate the conditional distribution of the most current test results for a student given between 1 and 4 years of prior test scores.  The growth score is presented as a point estimate with no indication of its variability.

I want to use a Bayesian model with an IRT model with known parameters as the data generating process to estimate the conditional distribution of the most recent score given the scores from previous years, and using it to compute the "growth" score and its variability, where the "growth" score is defined as 100 times the sum of the conditional probabilities of all possible scores that are lower than the student's actual score.

I have a STAN model that seems to work pretty well with two years of data and I'm interested in any suggestions on how to go about incorporating more than two years of data.  Each year will have a different IRT model, and I'd like to tie them together to get a single posterior predictive distribution for the most current year.

In the two year case, I did this by providing only a single ability parameter value for each student that applies to both years (I'm using a 1PL model and the difficulty values vary from year to year).  I'm wondering if there is a better way to do this.

Best regards,

Gene Quinn

code is on github https://github.com/equinn1/STAN.   growth.pdf contains background information on the project.

messages.subject: (dark matter halo model) Re: [stan-users] Any reason that Optimize may fail when NUTS doesn't?
messages.subject_clean: (dark matter halo model) Re: [stan-users] Any reason that Optimize may fail when NUTS doesn't?
messages.body_plain:
> On Aug 2, 2015, at 3:44 AM, Steven and Jeanette Murray <steven.j...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi,
>

Thanks for the detailed model dump.

> I have a model which generates (at least seemingly) good samples when running NUTS, but generates very poor estimates (all  parameters at boundaries) when using L-BFGS. Are there any known conditions that would make this happen?

Yes.  Any hierarchical model, for instance, will not have
posterior modes (i.e., max a posteriori or penalized
maximum likelihood estimates are not defined).   Nor will
a simple model like

parameters {
  real<lower=0, upper=1> theta;
}
model {
 theta ~ beta(0.5, 0.5)
}

The thing to do is explore the log density.  You can do that
with our diagnose mode in all the interfaces.  It lets you
plug in parameters and evaluate the log density.  Compare ones
near boundaries to ones that you get with NUTS.

I'll leave the physics model to others --- I tried to highlight
the subject to get the attention of people who may be able to help.

- Bob

> The model is a truncated generalised gamma distribution, with uncertain variates (lognormal uncertainty, they are dark matter halo masses, intrinsically between 10^12 and 10^15 ish). At the moment, all uncertainties are the same (though this will have to change in future versions). Other than the masses, there are four parameters:
> 	• alpha encoding the power-law slope,
> 	• logHs encodes the (log) cut-off mass
> 	• beta encodes the steepness of the cutoff.
> 	• log_mmin encodes the minimum mass.
> The 3 first parameters are all highly covariant, which may be causing problems, not sure (I thought NUTS was fairly good at navigating high covariance?). I'm at a bit of a loss as to what information to to post here. Perhaps I'll just go for as much as I think might help (though it might be a bit to wade through).
>
>
>
> So the explicit model: (I'm not posting the functions block here for clarity, but it defines the truncated_GGD_log function which calculates the log of the truncated generalised gamma -- for negative values of the shape parameter)
>
>
> data {
>     int<lower=0> N; // number of halos
>     vector<lower=0>[N] log_m_meas; // observed mass of halos
>     vector<lower=0>[N] err; //uncertainty in halo masses
>
>     // CONTROLS FOR PARAMETER BOUNDS
>     real<lower=0> hs_min; //The lower bound of loghs
>     real<lower=0,upper=20> hs_max; //Upper bound of loghs
>     real<lower=-2,upper=0> alpha_min; //Lower bound of alpha
>     real<lower=-2,upper=0> alpha_max; //Upper bound of alpha
>     real<lower=0> beta_min; //Lower bound of beta
>     real<lower=0> beta_max; //Upper bound of beta
>     real<lower=0,upper=20>mtrue_max; // Upper bound of true masses
>     real<lower=0> mmin_min;
>     real<lower=0> mmin_max;
> }
>
> parameters {
>     real<lower=beta_min,upper=beta_max> beta;
>     real<lower=hs_min,upper=hs_max> logHs;
>     real<lower=alpha_min,upper=alpha_max> alpha;
>     real<lower=mmin_min,upper=mmin_max> log_mmin;
>     vector<lower=log_mmin,upper=mtrue_max>[N] log_mtrue; //True mass estimates
> }
>
> transformed parameters {
>    real xmin;
>    xmin <- pow(10,beta*(log_mmin-logHs));
> }
>
> model {
>     vector[N] log10y;
>     vector[N] x;
>
>     log10y <- log_mtrue-logHs;
>     for (i in 1:N) x[i] <- pow(10,beta*log10y[i]);
>
>     //truncated GGD is beta*10^(alpha*log10y)*exp(-x)/(10^logHs*Gamma((alpha+1)/beta,x)
>     log10y ~ truncated_GGD(x, logHs,alpha, beta, xmin);
>     log_mtrue ~ normal(log_m_meas,err);
> }
>
>
> I want to use about 25,000 halos for my true run, but have tested with fewer, and wouldn't mind running it with more as well.
>
>
>
> I produce my mock halos in the following manner:
>
>
> library(gsl)
>
> dtggd = function(logm,logmmin,logh,a,b){
>   # GSL required!
>   return = b*10^(a*(logm-logh))*exp(-10^((logm-logh)*b))/(10^logh * gamma_inc((a+1)/b,10^(b*(logmmin-logh))))
> }
>
> qtggd = function(logm,logmmin,logh,a,b){
>   return = 1 - gamma_inc((a+1)/b,10^(b*(logm-logh)))/gamma_inc((a+1)/b,10^(b*(logmmin-logh)))
> }
>
> rtggd = function(N,logmmin,logh,a,b){
>   mmax = logh + 2.5/b
>
>   logm = seq(logmmin, mmax, 0.0001)
>   cdf = qtggd(logm,logmmin,logh,a,b)
>
>   icdf = approxfun(cdf, logm)
>
>   x = runif(N)
>   return = icdf(x)
> }
>
> ############## GET MOCK DATA ###################################
> N = 5000
> err = 0.1
> logmmin = 12
> logh = 14
> alpha = -1.8
> beta = 0.7
> seed = 1111
>
> set.seed(seed)
> intrinsic = rtggd(N,logmmin,logh,alpha,beta)
> mock.masses = rnorm(N,intrinsic,std)
>
> To be certain, with this, ie. N=5000, I get the following density plot:
>
>
>
>

> <Auto Generated Inline Image 1.png>

>
>
>
> Then I run the following to run stan, and also two optimization runs
>
>
> ############## SETUP RSTAN DATA ################################
> data = list(N=N,log_m_meas=mock.masses,err=rep(err,N),
>             hs_min=12,hs_max=15,alpha_min=-2.0,
>             alpha_max=-1.6,beta_min=0.05,beta_max=1.5,
>             mtrue_max=16.5,mmin_min=11,mmin_max=13)
>
> init = list(list(logHs=12.1,alpha=-1.95,beta=1.2,log_mmin=11.1,log_mtrue=mock.masses),   # Far away but reasonable masses
>             list(logHs=14.9,alpha=-1.61,beta=0.2,log_mmin=12.5),                         # Opposite side, random masses
>             list(logHs=13.5,alpha=-1.61,beta=1.2,log_mmin=11.5,log_mtrue=mock.masses),   # Swap alpha/beta relationship
>             list(logHs=logh,alpha=alpha,beta=beta,log_mmin=logmmin,log_mtrue=intrinsic)) # Exact answer if perfect sample
>
> opt.init.exact = init[[4]]
> opt.init.bad = init[[2]]
>
> model = stan_model(file="model_NO_S.stan")
>
> ############# RUN MCMC #########################################
> result <- sampling(model, data=data, pars = c('logHs','alpha','beta',"log_mmin"), chains=4,
>                    iter=2000, warmup=1000,cores=4,init=init)
>
> opt.res.exact <- optimizing(model,data=data,init=opt.init.exact,as_vector=FALSE)
> opt.res.bad <- optimizing(model,data=data,init=opt.init.bad,as_vector=FALSE)
>
>
>
> The results look good for the MCMC: In fact, in this particular case it seems that logHs and alpha are reproduced perfectly (as the median) though beta is estimated as 0.83 rather than 0.7 (it makes sense that beta isn't estimated very well, since it mostly comes from the cut-off where there are basically no objects.
>
>
>
> In terms of diagnostics, using the amazing shinyStan, I have:
>
>
> Chain     accept_stat    stepsize    treedepth    n_leapfrog    n_divergent
> All ch    0.8142    0.1093    5.4253    81.8334    0.0119
> chain1    0.8282    0.1038    5.691     91.5345    0.012
> chain2    0.8056    0.1159    5.2375    59.803     0.0095
> chain3    0.8056    0.1089    5.3905    85.8465    0.0135
> chain4    0.8176    0.1087    5.382     90.1495    0.0125
>
>
>
>
>
> Everything looks good I think, as far as I understand. The only things perhaps worth mentioning are the correlation plot:
>
>
>

> <Auto Generated Inline Image 2.png>

>
> Where chain 2 is obviously worse than the rest -- this is probably because it starts with random masses. Also the large amount of covariance can be seen in the pairs plot:
>
>
>

> <Auto Generated Inline Image 3.png>

>
> Finally, the run took a fair while, especially in the warmup -- not sure if that's normal?:
>
>
>           warmup   sample
> chain:1 767.6131 213.1524
> chain:2 539.0624 188.2982
> chain:3 798.0353 136.3628
> chain:4 852.1482 121.8508
>
>
>
> So everything seems pretty much fine. BUT, when I check the results of the optimization runs, it returns this:
>
>
> > opt.res.exact$par[1:4]
> $beta
> [1] 0.1685809
>
> $logHs
> [1] 12
>
> $alpha
> [1] -1.999999
>
> $log_mmin
> [1] 12.09832
>
> > opt.res.bad$par[1:4]
> $beta
> [1] 0.05
>
> $logHs
> [1] 14.99999
>
> $alpha
> [1] -1.6
>
> $log_mmin
> [1] 11
>
>
>
> I'm not really sure what else would be useful -- it would be nice if the optimization worked so that I could get quick estimates for testing purposes.
>
>
>
> Sorry I feel like I've been spamming you guys lately -- thanks very much for all the work you do. I certainly have not been disappointed.
>
>
>
> Cheers.
>
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] estimating the variability of the Colorado growth model
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] estimating the variability of the Colorado growth model
messages.body_plain:
What we'd probably do is treat the student abilities in the IRT
model as a time series then give everything a multilevel prior.

So something like for your model, generalize theta to allow
it to vary by year,

  vector[N_year] theta[N_stu];

then take a multivariate prior (as described in the manual
regression chapter), so that

  for (n in 1:N_stu)
    theta[n] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(...);

That is, there's a multivariate normal prior on a student's abilities
across years.

- Bob

> On Aug 2, 2015, at 10:05 AM, Eugene Quinn <epqu...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hello,
>
> I'm working on a project to estimate the variability of "growth" measures in education, specifically the Colorado model, which uses quantile regression to estimate the conditional distribution of the most current test results for a student given between 1 and 4 years of prior test scores.  The growth score is presented as a point estimate with no indication of its variability.
>
> I want to use a Bayesian model with an IRT model with known parameters as the data generating process to estimate the conditional distribution of the most recent score given the scores from previous years, and using it to compute the "growth" score and its variability, where the "growth" score is defined as 100 times the sum of the conditional probabilities of all possible scores that are lower than the student's actual score.
>
> I have a STAN model that seems to work pretty well with two years of data and I'm interested in any suggestions on how to go about incorporating more than two years of data.  Each year will have a different IRT model, and I'd like to tie them together to get a single posterior predictive distribution for the most current year.
>
> In the two year case, I did this by providing only a single ability parameter value for each student that applies to both years (I'm using a 1PL model and the difficulty values vary from year to year).  I'm wondering if there is a better way to do this.
>
> Best regards,
>
> Gene Quinn

generated quantities {

    for (n in 2:N_tilde)

}

messages.body_plain:
Sorry this question has languished for so long.  I still
don't quite understand the intent, so I haven't answered.

> we run HMM recursively through the time series, and use
> ARCH(1) model to optimize parameters in the two latent states?...

I wrote the examples for the manual, but am hardly a time-series
expert.  Usually if you can write the model's likelihood down, it's
down to some programming.  Which can be a pain for something like
HMMs because the unobserved discrete states need to be marginalized
out.

- Bob

> On Jul 17, 2015, at 1:42 AM, Wad Wan <cphni...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>
> Yo-yo, check my rhyme!..

>
> So, guys to be more specific, I mean the following. Suppose that we have a financial or economic time series, where we have a prior subjective belief that
> there are two different latent states (i.e., bull and bear markets). Now, we want to use a hidden Markov models (i.e., Markov Regime State Switching) that is
> somewhat similar to SWARCH model by Hamilton and Susmel. But to keep it simple and stupid, we begin to look at ARCH(1) model and Markov Regime State Switching Model. Now, what I have a great difficulty to figure out how to use Stan to combine these two models together. When I read Stan's user manual, they
> write very well the explanation for how to solve ARCH(1) model, and the explanation for how to solve HMM, but there is that missing link that how do you combine these two models in Stan, such that, we run HMM recursively through the time series, and use ARCH(1) model to optimize parameters in the two latent states?...
>
> So, to keep it simple and stupid we begin with the first order ARCH(1) stochastic process estimation of paramters in the model. The definition of ARCH(1) looks something like that:
>
> \begin{eqnarray}
>      a_t = \sigma_t \epsilon_t, \text{ } \sigma_t = \sqrt[]{\alpha_0 + \alpha_1 a^2_{t-1}},  \text{ }  \sigma_t^2 = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 a^2_{t-1},
>  \end{eqnarray}
>
> where $\alpha_0 > 0$, $\alpha_1 \geq 0$, $\epsilon_t$ is independent of the past, and $\sigma_t$ is known function value of the prior information
> at time $t-1$.
>
> We begin our implementation in R and Stan, which looks like that:
>

> # 1st we simulate ARCH(1) stochastic process, with known user-defined-true-parameters
>

>   library(rstan)   # we load in the Stan package
>   library(tseries)
>

> # In first step, we generate ARCH(1) process
> #

> alpha0 <- 0.06321  # user defined subjective constant
> alpha1 <- 0.03548  # user defined subjective constant
> T <- 10000         # number of replications
>
> r_t <- rep(0,T)
>
> sigma2_t <- 0.1    # initial guess; user defined parameter
> r_t[1] <- sqrt(sigma2_t)*rnorm(1,0,1)
>
> for (i in 2:T) {
>     eps <- rnorm(1,0,1)
>     sigma2_t <- alpha0 + alpha1*r_t[i-1]^2
>     r_t[i] <- sqrt(sigma2_t)*eps
> }
>
> plot.ts(r_t)

> hist(r_t)

>
> ## Stan modelling in R
> #

> modelString = "
>
>     data {
>         int<lower=0> T; // number of time points
>         real r_t[T]; // return at time t
>     }
>
>     parameters {
>         real mu;
>         real<lower=0> alpha0; // noise intercept
>         real<lower=0,upper=1> alpha1; // noise slope
>     }
>
>     model {
>
>         for (t in 2:T)
>             r_t[t] ~ normal(mu, sqrt(alpha0 + alpha1 * pow(r_t[t-1] - mu,2)));
>     }
> "
>
> sm <- stan_model(model_code = modelString) # Stan model
>
> fit <- sampling(sm, data=list(r_t=r_t, T=T), iter=1000, chains=4, warmup=250, thin=5); fit
>
> print(fit, digits_summary = 5)
> plot(fit)
>
> fit_sim <- extract(fit)
> hist(fit_sim$alpha0)
> hist(fit_sim$alpha1)

> # Done!..

>

> on page 61 and Semisupervised Estimation on p. 81.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] ESS confusion
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] ESS confusion
messages.body_plain:
Hi, yes, information is sometimes defined as inverse variance, so it’s pretty close to what we’re talking about here.  “Power” would be fine except that that term is already taken.

> On Aug 2, 2015, at 12:23 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> I can see why "power" is bad, but why "information"?
> I tend to think of information content as being measured
> by things like entropy.  Is it by analogy to the expected
> information about the mean contained in N i.i.d. draws?
>
> I never quantify any units or other generic nouns in the manual.
>
> Geyer uses "statistical accuracy", in the context "statistical accuracy
> is inversely proportional to the square root of the sample size",
> which also seems sub-optimal terminologically.
>
> - Bob
>
>> On Aug 1, 2015, at 10:21 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>>
>> Fine, but just to be careful with jargon, replace “power” by “information” in Bob’s response below.
>>
>>> On Aug 1, 2015, at 2:56 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>>>
>>> No, the name's not misleading.  The ESS is an estimate of the
>>> statistical power of the sample you have scaled to the number of
>>> i.i.d. draws to which it would be equivalent.
>>>
>>> What happens is that a sequence of autocorrelated draws have more
>>> power than thinning because there's information in the thinned draws
>>> that gets lost when you thin them.
>>>
>>> There's a very nice overview in Geyer's chapter for the MCMC
>>> Handbook, which is one of the free samples:
>>>
>>> http://www.mcmchandbook.net/HandbookChapter1.pdf
>>>
>>> Just don't listen to his advice on convergence monitoring!  His
>>> comments are right in theory, but not in practice if you want
>>> answers in finite amounts of time.
>>>
>>> And we do our calculations a little differently, as described in
>>> BDA3 and in the manual --- we basically take cross-chain information
>>> into account, which makes our ESS calculations more conservative than
>>> the typical approach of estimating each chain separately (they give
>>> you the same answer in the stationary limit).
>>>
>>> - Bob
>>>
>>>
>>>> On Aug 1, 2015, at 6:27 AM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>>
>>>> Hi all,
>>>>
>>>> thanks a lot. I guess I have to look at the definitions to see what makes most sense in my application. What Aki points out seems to be closest to what I am looking for, i.e. a sample which has no autocorrelations. I thought this is about what ESS would tell me (but the naming here may be misleading).
>>>>
>>>> Sebastian
>>>>
>>>> BTW, throwing away a bit of information is not an issue - Stan is so efficient and generates huge ESS in no time for my problem, I rather have a memory and speed problem in follow up analyses if I were to keep all samples.
>>>>
>>>> On Friday, July 31, 2015 at 10:50:06 PM UTC+2, Aki Vehtari wrote:
>>>>
>>>> For follow up analyses (of the prediction) I thin down the sample to it's effective sample size.
>>>>
>>>> In addition to others comments, even if you are examining one quantity, note that if you were going to select ESS number of draws from the whole sample, then the effective sample size for the thinned set is likely to be smaller than the original ESS as the thinning throws away information. If you want to thin to get almost independent draws to simplify the follow up analysis, you need to look at the autocorrelations and not ESS.
>>>>
>>>> Aki

messages.subject: detectCores under Windows
messages.subject_clean: detectCores under Windows
messages.body_plain:
RSTan Version 2.7.0.1 Windows 64 bit on I7 Processor with 4 logical and a total of 8 cores:

Under the above configuration, using parallel::detectCores() is not recommended, it gives 8 and a performance worse than 4
because of overhead. Note that this is not an effect of setup, with 32 seconds setup is negligible.

> options(mc.cores = 4)
> system.time(fit6 <- stan("horseshoe6.stan", data = d, iter = 30000, thin = 10,
+             pars = c("beta","lambda")))
   user  system elapsed
   0.17    0.24   28.28
> options(mc.cores = 8)
> system.time(fit6 <- stan("horseshoe6.stan", data = d, iter = 30000, thin = 10,
+             pars = c("beta","lambda")))
   user  system elapsed
   0.30    0.59   32.92

The problem is in documentation: while it says that logical = FALSE is the default, in fact it is not:

> parallel::detectCores()
[1] 8
> parallel::detectCores(logical=FALSE)
[1] 4

Recommended setting under my configuration is:

options(mc.cores= parallel::detectCores(logical=FALSE))

Dieter

messages.body_plain:
On Monday, August 3, 2015 at 5:01:21 AM UTC-4, Dieter Menne wrote:
> RSTan Version 2.7.0.1 Windows 64 bit on I7 Processor with 4 logical and a total of 8 cores:
>
>
> Under the above configuration, using parallel::detectCores() is not recommended, it gives 8 and a performance worse than 4
> because of overhead. Note that this is not an effect of setup, with 32 seconds setup is negligible.

That is possible, but test it passing the arguments chains = 8 and seed = something both times you call stan(). By default, stan() only does 4 chains, so using 8 logical cores in that case is not going to help more than just using 4 physical cores. But also, wall times are highly variable for Stan programs, so you need to call it with the same seed to ensure that it is taking the same number of leapfrog steps over the course of the run.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] detectCores under Windows
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] detectCores under Windows
messages.body_plain:
What Ben said about evaluation.  Plus...

I think it's worth detecting the physical cores if possible.  In every
experiment I've ever done, concurrency exceeding the physical
cores slows things down in scientific computing (when each thread
or process is banging away hammer and tongs).  My guess is that
it's too much memory contention and/or too much context switching
into the physical cores.

For reasons Ben mentioned, the killer isn't a 4-core machine running
the default 4 chains.  But I think it is a big problem for 2-core
machines (like the ubiquitous core duos on compact notebooks), where
running 4 chains will try to use the hyperthreading.  Assuming that is
that the 2-core core duos report 4 cores available.

- Bob

> On Aug 3, 2015, at 9:58 AM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> On Monday, August 3, 2015 at 5:01:21 AM UTC-4, Dieter Menne wrote:
> RSTan Version 2.7.0.1 Windows 64 bit on I7 Processor with 4 logical and a total of 8 cores:
>
>
> Under the above configuration, using parallel::detectCores() is not recommended, it gives 8 and a performance worse than 4
> because of overhead. Note that this is not an effect of setup, with 32 seconds setup is negligible.
>
> That is possible, but test it passing the arguments chains = 8 and seed = something both times you call stan(). By default, stan() only does 4 chains, so using 8 logical cores in that case is not going to help more than just using 4 physical cores. But also, wall times are highly variable for Stan programs, so you need to call it with the same seed to ensure that it is taking the same number of leapfrog steps over the course of the run.
>

messages.subject: Re: Default priors for coefficients in logistic regression models
messages.subject_clean: Default priors for coefficients in logistic regression models
messages.body_plain:
On Monday, August 3, 2015 at 11:20:41 AM UTC-4, Ben Lambert wrote:
> 1. What do we currently recommend? Is there any reading on these specifically?

A variety of things that may change from month to month. There are a lot of papers (perhaps not for the logistic regression case) that try to obtain priors that facilitate making a yes-no decision on whether the coefficient is zero, which is not particularly Bayesian and not a great goal (Rob McCullogh was going around this summer saying that "sparsity is part of your utility function not your prior density").

Outside of that, there are some papers whose goals are to prevent separation (mostly in the case of a binary outcome) and achieve regularization (for any regression model), which can be accomplished by a variety of prior distributions and don't prescribe a particular density or hyperparameter values. Approximately all of these papers specify independent priors on the coefficients that are also independent of the priors on any nuisance parameters, which doesn't make much substantive sense. We're going to go in a different direction for an R package of pre-compiled models, but we won't agree on the priors and thus have to offer different options to users that they don't want.

> 2. Is this true just for logistic regression or other more general models?

The separation thing is largely a concern for models with binary outcomes. The issues of regularization and how to specify a joint prior pertain to all regression models, but the answers depend on how the outcome is measured.

Ben

messages.subject: seeking help with reinforcement learning model
messages.subject_clean: seeking help with reinforcement learning model
messages.body_plain:
Hi Stan,

we've been trying to fit a variant of the simple reinforcement learning model on a trial-by-trial basis. The task is a social decision-making paradigm, in which on each trial the subject (1) makes a choice, (2) observes the choices of 4 other players, (3) based on this social information makes a second choice, and (4) the probabilistic outcome is reveals for all players. We encountered some problems and we wish to get some hints /feedback from the mailing list. We run our model on Stan 2.7.0 (rstan) with 16500 samples per chain, 4 chains, 4000 warming-up and 5 steps of thinning, which ends up with 10000 valid samples altogether. Problems are listed below and you might also want to check the model file attached.

(1) Does the low effective sample size (ESS) in the range of 5-50% of the nominal sample size indicate a pathology in the sampling process?
Though nearly all the R-hat of all parameters of interest are below 1.10, quite a few of them have really low ESS due to the fact that they have relatively high auto-correlation. Does increase the length of chains and increase thinning steps (perhaps even thinning=20) make sense to deal with this problem?

(2) Do parameter values near the range boundaries suggest an ill-specified model?
The model uses a learning rate (range 0-1) to weight a reward prediction error, which is then use to update expected values. These are converted into action probabilities using a softmax function parameterized by a temperature parameter (range 0-3). However, the MAP/median of the posterior distribution of learning rate is close to 0 (for another model it's close to 1) and the temperature is also super low (~ 0.3, which indicates random choice). We were wondering if the model is ill-specified but so far we haven't come up with a more sophisticated idea.

(3) Is there a standard way to implement posterior predictive check (PPC) with reinforcement learning models?
We've checked previous entries on the mailing-list about PPC but couldn’t find something that seems to fit. In practice, we want to re-run the model 100 times to simulate data in the generated quantities section to generate simulated choice data. We are planning to divide each simulation of 100 trials into 6-10 bins and then compute the predictive accuracy for, say, let choice for each bin. (Just taking the overall frequency of left choice in all 100 trials or overall number switches as the target measure for a validation is losing too much information as as the overall number of left choices between simulations and data can be identical, yet the model can be wrong on every trial.) Does this binning idea sound like a valid approach to PPC? We would be eager to hear other suggestions from the community.

statements: choice1 ~ categorical_logit(), and choice2 ~ categorical_logit(). Are both of them used for incrementing the log-probability in Stan?
As the 2nd choice is more important than the 1st one (because the 2nd choice leads to reward/punishment), is there a way to weight the importance of them? say w * sampling1 + (1-w) * sampling2 and then also fit 'w' as a free parameter?

Thanks a lot in advance for giving this some thoughts and we appreciate any input or feedback.

Best,
Lei

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Question about Wiener Diffusion Model Distribution in rstan_2.7.0-2
messages.body_plain:
A little off-topic, but possibly of interest to those wondering what this distribution is used for:

Elaborations of this model have been used extensively in the study of speeded human decisions (ex. simple perceptual decisions like "is this square black or white?" or more abstract decisions like "is this word English or French?") since the 1970s to connect the observed data of response speed and response accuracy to latent variables that can be more informative on the structure of the mind. For example, a given experimental manipulation might yield fast-but-error-prone responses in one condition and slow-but-accurate responses in another. The manipulation obviously causes a trade-off of speed and accuracy, but is there any additional changes to information processing as well? Where the diffusion model explicitly operationalizes information processing efficiency (bias of the walker; more biased=faster information processing) as independent of the speed-accuracy trade-off criterion (separation of the bounds; closer bounds = more emphasis on speed, less on accuracy), one can answer this question. Other parameters of the more elaborated models can address other interesting questions and there are also several competing models (ex. linear ballistic accumulator, log-normal race, etc) that generally seek to address similar questions. I'll actually be coding up an example of both the diffusion and log-normal race (which is easy with the distributions already in stan) in the next few days, and I'll post it to the examples for anyone interested.

>> If you check the implementation of this distribution in R (same author as this one), the function has an argument resp = "upper"/"lower"/"both", even though, internally the function uses negative/positive responses.
> I'm still confused about the function, so I'll have to wait

> Just to state the obvious, if there are constraints on variables,
> either outcomes or parameters, then they should be checked.

In this distribution, we model the probability (actually probability
density) of the an specific process reach an upper boundary (alpha) or a
lower boundary (zero) (or both) in an specific time (time is the
response variable).

Examples:

 > require(RWiener)

 > # Probability of reaching the upper boundary alpha=2 in at most 100
units of time
 > pwiener(100, alpha=2,tau=0.3, beta=0.45, delta=.4, "upper")
[1] 0.6430842

 > # Probability of reaching the lower boundary 0 in at most 100 units
of time
 > pwiener(100, alpha=2,tau=0.3,beta=0.45,delta=.4, "lower")
[1] 0.3569158

 > # Probability of reaching any of the two boundaries in at most 100
units of time
 > pwiener(100, alpha=2,tau=0.3,beta=0.45,delta=.4, "both")
[1] 1

(100 is so large for this values of the parameters that the pdf is
integrating to 1 already)

We are discussing which is the best way to select "upper"/"lower"/"both"
in Stan. I think the best way is to have an extra argument at the end
wiener_log just like the R examples above, but the author originally had
negative response variable meaning "lower", positive response variables
meaning "upper" (although the response variable of the process is in
fact time elapsed, so it's strictly positive)

messages.body_plain:
assuming your Y is normally distributed, you need a sampling statement like

Y[ny] ~normal(y[ny],sigma)

you will have to declare sigma in the parameter block. one recommendation for the variance prior used to be the half cauchy (i.e. declare sigma with a lower bound 0 and sample from a chauchy distribution in the model block).

note that in the transformed parameters block you declare y, but you fill the undeclared vector mu.

I don't think it is necessary to use the transformed parameters block here. all those mu/y will create a mess when you do print(stanfit).
you could just do the following in the model block

real mu;
...
for(ny in 1:nY){
        mu <- subject_intercept[S[ny]] + X[ny]*(subject_effect[S[ny]]/2);
        Y[ny] ~ normal(mu,sigma) ;
    }

guido

PS: note that I did not look at your R code or tried to check if you calculated mu/y correctly! But I am wondering why you are dividing by two in that expression. for a simple within effect i would simply have an intercept plus a dummy variable (0,1) to capture the difference between the two conditions.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Discrete model comparision: Bayes factor in generated parameters?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Discrete model comparision: Bayes factor in generated parameters?
messages.body_plain:
> I'm imagining using stan to approximate the integral p(y|theta)*p(theta)*dTheta by sampling p(theta) in the Model block, computing the likelihood at each sample in the generated quantities block, and taking the average of these outside of stan. Code illustrating this idea for a simple hierarchical gaussian model is below the fold.

Do not do this!  This estimator has infinite Monte Carlo variance
and is essentially worthless in practice.  Computing the evidence
is really hard and requires methods that transcend Markov chain
Monte Carlo.

> Alternatives on my mind include BIC, which I understand to constitute a minor statistical sin, and a technique called "thermodynamic integration", which I don't totally understand. I guess my questions are as much about statistics as they are about stan itself:
>
> 1) Does the approach below make sense as a way of getting estimates of p(y|M) for use in a Bayes Factor?

No; see above.  BIC is also of almost no practical utility, and
thermodynamic integration is incredibly hard to tune and ensure
accurate results.

Evidence calculations are in the next generation of problems
for Stan, and robust algorithms are currently being developed
theoretically.

> 2) More generally: What are best practices in stan for comparing models based on model evidence, rather than on predictive performance?

I’m sure Aki and Andrew will have more to say, but in general
you have to be very, very careful with Bayesian Model Comparison.
The evidence is incredibly sensitive to the choice of prior, which
makes it easy to “game” if you’re not careful.  There are some
circumstances where BMC can be useful (say, identifying the
number of modes in a mixture) but in general you have to
remember that Bayes is all about reporting uncertainty and
not making any hard choices as BMC does.  One strategy
that is becoming popular is to mix the models — i.e. don’t
try to select between models but rather make one big model
that encompasses both.  It’s easier algorithmically and much
more robust statistically (no coincidence that those two go
together).

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] seeking help with reinforcement learning model
messages.body_plain:
Hi, I’d recommend you use the default of 50% warmup and 50% post-warmup, with no thinning.  Also it’s not clear why you are doing lower=0.01 on some parameters.  I think lower=0 would be fine.

Regarding your question about point estimates being close to 0, I don’t think that’s so important.  Better to just use the entire posterior distribution.

For posterior predictive check, just simulate replicates that are the same size and shape of the original data, then you can make whatever graphs you want.
A

> On Aug 4, 2015, at 3:50 AM, Lei Zhang <bnuzhan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> Hi Stan,
>
> we've been trying to fit a variant of the simple reinforcement learning model on a trial-by-trial basis. The task is a social decision-making paradigm, in which on each trial the subject (1) makes a choice, (2) observes the choices of 4 other players, (3) based on this social information makes a second choice, and (4) the probabilistic outcome is reveals for all players. We encountered some problems and we wish to get some hints /feedback from the mailing list. We run our model on Stan 2.7.0 (rstan) with 16500 samples per chain, 4 chains, 4000 warming-up and 5 steps of thinning, which ends up with 10000 valid samples altogether. Problems are listed below and you might also want to check the model file attached.
>
> (1) Does the low effective sample size (ESS) in the range of 5-50% of the nominal sample size indicate a pathology in the sampling process?
> Though nearly all the R-hat of all parameters of interest are below 1.10, quite a few of them have really low ESS due to the fact that they have relatively high auto-correlation. Does increase the length of chains and increase thinning steps (perhaps even thinning=20) make sense to deal with this problem?
>
> (2) Do parameter values near the range boundaries suggest an ill-specified model?
> The model uses a learning rate (range 0-1) to weight a reward prediction error, which is then use to update expected values. These are converted into action probabilities using a softmax function parameterized by a temperature parameter (range 0-3). However, the MAP/median of the posterior distribution of learning rate is close to 0 (for another model it's close to 1) and the temperature is also super low (~ 0.3, which indicates random choice). We were wondering if the model is ill-specified but so far we haven't come up with a more sophisticated idea.
>
> (3) Is there a standard way to implement posterior predictive check (PPC) with reinforcement learning models?
> We've checked previous entries on the mailing-list about PPC but couldn’t find something that seems to fit. In practice, we want to re-run the model 100 times to simulate data in the generated quantities section to generate simulated choice data. We are planning to divide each simulation of 100 trials into 6-10 bins and then compute the predictive accuracy for, say, let choice for each bin. (Just taking the overall frequency of left choice in all 100 trials or overall number switches as the target measure for a validation is losing too much information as as the overall number of left choices between simulations and data can be identical, yet the model can be wrong on every trial.) Does this binning idea sound like a valid approach to PPC? We would be eager to hear other suggestions from the community.
>
> (4) If you check the attached model code you’l notice that we have 2 sampling statements involving choices in each trial:
> statements: choice1 ~ categorical_logit(), and choice2 ~ categorical_logit(). Are both of them used for incrementing the log-probability in Stan?
> As the 2nd choice is more important than the 1st one (because the 2nd choice leads to reward/punishment), is there a way to weight the importance of them? say w * sampling1 + (1-w) * sampling2 and then also fit 'w' as a free parameter?
>
> Thanks a lot in advance for giving this some thoughts and we appreciate any input or feedback.
>
> Best,
> Lei

> Elaborations of this model have been used extensively in the study of speeded human decisions (ex. simple perceptual decisions like "is this square black or white?" or more abstract decisions like "is this word English or French?") since the 1970s to connect the observed data of response speed and response accuracy to latent variables that can be more informative on the structure of the mind. For example, a given experimental manipulation might yield fast-but-error-prone responses in one condition and slow-but-accurate responses in another. The manipulation obviously causes a trade-off of speed and accuracy, but is there any additional changes to information processing as well? Where the diffusion model explicitly operationalizes information processing efficiency (bias of the walker; more biased=faster information processing) as independent of the speed-accuracy trade-off criterion (separation of the bounds; closer bounds = more emphasis on speed, less on accuracy), one can answer this question. Other parameters of the more elaborated models can address other interesting questions and there are also several competing models (ex. linear ballistic accumulator, log-normal race, etc) that generally seek to address similar questions. I'll actually be coding up an example of both the diffusion and log-normal race (which is easy with the distributions already in stan) in the next few days, and I'll post it to the examples for anyone interested.
>
>
> On Tuesday, August 4, 2015 at 12:22:04 PM UTC-3, Mike Lawrence wrote:
> Yes, it'll be strictly positive. It represents the distribution of times it takes a quasi-random walker to get from a given starting point to one of a pair of given ending points on a 1-D plane. The walker is quasi-random because it may have a slight preference for toward one boundary or the other.
>
> On Tuesday, August 4, 2015 at 12:13:57 PM UTC-3, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I don't know anything about this distribution and there's
> no definition in the manual.  Is it symmetric around 0?
>
> If so, I don't see any reason to constrain it to be positive.
> You might want to do so in a model to avoid multimodality if
> +theta and -theta have the same density.
>
> - Bob
>
>
> > On Aug 4, 2015, at 11:09 AM, Matt <mattya...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi Marco,
> >
> > On Saturday, 1 August 2015 00:17:52 UTC-4, Marco Inacio wrote:
> > I changed this (thus forcing y to be strictly positive) because there
> > was no computational advantage in doing so and thought it would be
> > potentially dangerous for users.
> >
> > I'm curious as to the potential dangers of not having y as strictly positive for the Wiener distribution?
> >
> > Matt
>
>

On Monday, 3 August 2015 02:30:38 UTC+8, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
> > On Aug 2, 2015, at 3:44 AM, Steven and Jeanette Murray <steven.j...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi,
> >
>
> Thanks for the detailed model dump.
>
> > I have a model which generates (at least seemingly) good samples when running NUTS, but generates very poor estimates (all  parameters at boundaries) when using L-BFGS. Are there any known conditions that would make this happen?
>
> Yes.  Any hierarchical model, for instance, will not have
> posterior modes (i.e., max a posteriori or penalized
> maximum likelihood estimates are not defined).   Nor will
> a simple model like
>
> parameters {
>   real<lower=0, upper=1> theta;
> }
> model {
>  theta ~ beta(0.5, 0.5)
> }
>
> The thing to do is explore the log density.  You can do that
> with our diagnose mode in all the interfaces.  It lets you
> plug in parameters and evaluate the log density.  Compare ones
> near boundaries to ones that you get with NUTS.
>
> I'll leave the physics model to others --- I tried to highlight
> the subject to get the attention of people who may be able to help.
>
> - Bob
>
> > The model is a truncated generalised gamma distribution, with uncertain variates (lognormal uncertainty, they are dark matter halo masses, intrinsically between 10^12 and 10^15 ish). At the moment, all uncertainties are the same (though this will have to change in future versions). Other than the masses, there are four parameters:
> >         • alpha encoding the power-law slope,
> >         • logHs encodes the (log) cut-off mass
> >         • beta encodes the steepness of the cutoff.
> >         • log_mmin encodes the minimum mass.
> > The 3 first parameters are all highly covariant, which may be causing problems, not sure (I thought NUTS was fairly good at navigating high covariance?). I'm at a bit of a loss as to what information to to post here. Perhaps I'll just go for as much as I think might help (though it might be a bit to wade through).
> >
> >
> >
> > So the explicit model: (I'm not posting the functions block here for clarity, but it defines the truncated_GGD_log function which calculates the log of the truncated generalised gamma -- for negative values of the shape parameter)
> >
> >
> > data {
> >     int<lower=0> N; // number of halos
> >     vector<lower=0>[N] log_m_meas; // observed mass of halos
> >     vector<lower=0>[N] err; //uncertainty in halo masses
> >
> >     // CONTROLS FOR PARAMETER BOUNDS
> >     real<lower=0> hs_min; //The lower bound of loghs
> >     real<lower=0,upper=20> hs_max; //Upper bound of loghs
> >     real<lower=-2,upper=0> alpha_min; //Lower bound of alpha
> >     real<lower=-2,upper=0> alpha_max; //Upper bound of alpha
> >     real<lower=0> beta_min; //Lower bound of beta
> >     real<lower=0> beta_max; //Upper bound of beta
> >     real<lower=0,upper=20>mtrue_max; // Upper bound of true masses
> >     real<lower=0> mmin_min;
> >     real<lower=0> mmin_max;
> > }
> >
> > parameters {
> >     real<lower=beta_min,upper=beta_max> beta;
> >     real<lower=hs_min,upper=hs_max> logHs;
> >     real<lower=alpha_min,upper=alpha_max> alpha;
> >     real<lower=mmin_min,upper=mmin_max> log_mmin;
> >     vector<lower=log_mmin,upper=mtrue_max>[N] log_mtrue; //True mass estimates
> > }
> >
> > transformed parameters {
> >    real xmin;
> >    xmin <- pow(10,beta*(log_mmin-logHs));
> > }
> >
> > model {
> >     vector[N] log10y;
> >     vector[N] x;
> >
> >     log10y <- log_mtrue-logHs;
> >     for (i in 1:N) x[i] <- pow(10,beta*log10y[i]);
> >
> >     //truncated GGD is beta*10^(alpha*log10y)*exp(-x)/(10^logHs*Gamma((alpha+1)/beta,x)
> >     log10y ~ truncated_GGD(x, logHs,alpha, beta, xmin);
> >     log_mtrue ~ normal(log_m_meas,err);
> > }
> >
> >
> > I want to use about 25,000 halos for my true run, but have tested with fewer, and wouldn't mind running it with more as well.
> >
> >
> >
> > I produce my mock halos in the following manner:
> >
> >
> > library(gsl)
> >
> > dtggd = function(logm,logmmin,logh,a,b){
> >   # GSL required!
> >   return = b*10^(a*(logm-logh))*exp(-10^((logm-logh)*b))/(10^logh * gamma_inc((a+1)/b,10^(b*(logmmin-logh))))
> > }
> >
> > qtggd = function(logm,logmmin,logh,a,b){
> >   return = 1 - gamma_inc((a+1)/b,10^(b*(logm-logh)))/gamma_inc((a+1)/b,10^(b*(logmmin-logh)))
> > }
> >
> > rtggd = function(N,logmmin,logh,a,b){
> >   mmax = logh + 2.5/b
> >
> >   logm = seq(logmmin, mmax, 0.0001)
> >   cdf = qtggd(logm,logmmin,logh,a,b)
> >
> >   icdf = approxfun(cdf, logm)
> >
> >   x = runif(N)
> >   return = icdf(x)
> > }
> >
> > ############## GET MOCK DATA ###################################
> > N = 5000
> > err = 0.1
> > logmmin = 12
> > logh = 14
> > alpha = -1.8
> > beta = 0.7
> > seed = 1111
> >
> > set.seed(seed)
> > intrinsic = rtggd(N,logmmin,logh,alpha,beta)
> > mock.masses = rnorm(N,intrinsic,std)
> >
> > To be certain, with this, ie. N=5000, I get the following density plot:
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > <Auto Generated Inline Image 1.png>
> >
> >
> >
> > Then I run the following to run stan, and also two optimization runs
> >
> >
> > ############## SETUP RSTAN DATA ################################
> > data = list(N=N,log_m_meas=mock.masses,err=rep(err,N),
> >             hs_min=12,hs_max=15,alpha_min=-2.0,
> >             alpha_max=-1.6,beta_min=0.05,beta_max=1.5,
> >             mtrue_max=16.5,mmin_min=11,mmin_max=13)
> >
> > init = list(list(logHs=12.1,alpha=-1.95,beta=1.2,log_mmin=11.1,log_mtrue=mock.masses),   # Far away but reasonable masses
> >             list(logHs=14.9,alpha=-1.61,beta=0.2,log_mmin=12.5),                         # Opposite side, random masses
> >             list(logHs=13.5,alpha=-1.61,beta=1.2,log_mmin=11.5,log_mtrue=mock.masses),   # Swap alpha/beta relationship
> >             list(logHs=logh,alpha=alpha,beta=beta,log_mmin=logmmin,log_mtrue=intrinsic)) # Exact answer if perfect sample
> >
> > opt.init.exact = init[[4]]
> > opt.init.bad = init[[2]]
> >
> > model = stan_model(file="model_NO_S.stan")
> >
> > ############# RUN MCMC #########################################
> > result <- sampling(model, data=data, pars = c('logHs','alpha','beta',"log_mmin"), chains=4,
> >                    iter=2000, warmup=1000,cores=4,init=init)
> >
> > opt.res.exact <- optimizing(model,data=data,init=opt.init.exact,as_vector=FALSE)
> > opt.res.bad <- optimizing(model,data=data,init=opt.init.bad,as_vector=FALSE)
> >
> >
> >
> > The results look good for the MCMC: In fact, in this particular case it seems that logHs and alpha are reproduced perfectly (as the median) though beta is estimated as 0.83 rather than 0.7 (it makes sense that beta isn't estimated very well, since it mostly comes from the cut-off where there are basically no objects.
> >
> >
> >
> > In terms of diagnostics, using the amazing shinyStan, I have:
> >
> >
> > Chain     accept_stat    stepsize    treedepth    n_leapfrog    n_divergent
> > All ch    0.8142    0.1093    5.4253    81.8334    0.0119
> > chain1    0.8282    0.1038    5.691     91.5345    0.012
> > chain2    0.8056    0.1159    5.2375    59.803     0.0095

> > chain4    0.8176    0.1087    5.382     90.1495    0.0125
> >
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > Everything looks good I think, as far as I understand. The only things perhaps worth mentioning are the correlation plot:
> >
> >
> >
> > <Auto Generated Inline Image 2.png>
> >
> > Where chain 2 is obviously worse than the rest -- this is probably because it starts with random masses. Also the large amount of covariance can be seen in the pairs plot:
> >
> >
> >

> > Finally, the run took a fair while, especially in the warmup -- not sure if that's normal?:

messages.subject: Re: (dark matter halo model) Re: [stan-users] Any reason that Optimize may fail when NUTS doesn't?
messages.subject_clean: (dark matter halo model) Re: [stan-users] Any reason that Optimize may fail when NUTS doesn't?
messages.body_plain:
Sure.  You can look at the "EM goes boom" section of
David McKay's info theory book (free online).

An easy way to see it is to plot the density of the
hierarchical model component highly simplified for
two parameters with fixed prior means:

  p(sigma, beta1, beta2)

  = Cauchy(sigma | 0, 1) / 2 * Normal(beta1 | 0, sigma) * Normal(beta2 | 0, sigma)

and see what happens as all of sigma, beta1, beta2 -> 0 (be sure that
sigma ->0 from above).  Or swap in something simpler for the half-Cauchy.

- Bob

> On Aug 4, 2015, at 10:47 PM, Steven and Jeanette Murray <steven.j...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks Bob,
>
> This is a heirarchical model, so that would be why it didn't work with MAP techniques. Is there an intuitive way to understand why this is? Or some reference you can point me to?
>
> In terms of the rest of the model... I'm having other issues with it now. I'll explore them a bit more before reporting back so as to not waste anyone's time.
>
> Cheers,
> Steven
>
> On Monday, 3 August 2015 02:30:38 UTC+8, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
> > On Aug 2, 2015, at 3:44 AM, Steven and Jeanette Murray <steven.j...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi,
> >
>
> Thanks for the detailed model dump.
>
> > I have a model which generates (at least seemingly) good samples when running NUTS, but generates very poor estimates (all  parameters at boundaries) when using L-BFGS. Are there any known conditions that would make this happen?
>
> Yes.  Any hierarchical model, for instance, will not have
> posterior modes (i.e., max a posteriori or penalized
> maximum likelihood estimates are not defined).   Nor will
> a simple model like
>
> parameters {
>   real<lower=0, upper=1> theta;
> }
> model {
>  theta ~ beta(0.5, 0.5)
> }
>
> The thing to do is explore the log density.  You can do that
> with our diagnose mode in all the interfaces.  It lets you
> plug in parameters and evaluate the log density.  Compare ones
> near boundaries to ones that you get with NUTS.
>
> I'll leave the physics model to others --- I tried to highlight
> the subject to get the attention of people who may be able to help.
>
> - Bob
>
> > The model is a truncated generalised gamma distribution, with uncertain variates (lognormal uncertainty, they are dark matter halo masses, intrinsically between 10^12 and 10^15 ish). At the moment, all uncertainties are the same (though this will have to change in future versions). Other than the masses, there are four parameters:
> >         • alpha encoding the power-law slope,
> >         • logHs encodes the (log) cut-off mass
> >         • beta encodes the steepness of the cutoff.
> >         • log_mmin encodes the minimum mass.
> > The 3 first parameters are all highly covariant, which may be causing problems, not sure (I thought NUTS was fairly good at navigating high covariance?). I'm at a bit of a loss as to what information to to post here. Perhaps I'll just go for as much as I think might help (though it might be a bit to wade through).
> >
> >
> >
> > So the explicit model: (I'm not posting the functions block here for clarity, but it defines the truncated_GGD_log function which calculates the log of the truncated generalised gamma -- for negative values of the shape parameter)
> >
> >
> > data {
> >     int<lower=0> N; // number of halos
> >     vector<lower=0>[N] log_m_meas; // observed mass of halos
> >     vector<lower=0>[N] err; //uncertainty in halo masses
> >
> >     // CONTROLS FOR PARAMETER BOUNDS
> >     real<lower=0> hs_min; //The lower bound of loghs
> >     real<lower=0,upper=20> hs_max; //Upper bound of loghs
> >     real<lower=-2,upper=0> alpha_min; //Lower bound of alpha
> >     real<lower=-2,upper=0> alpha_max; //Upper bound of alpha
> >     real<lower=0> beta_min; //Lower bound of beta
> >     real<lower=0> beta_max; //Upper bound of beta
> >     real<lower=0,upper=20>mtrue_max; // Upper bound of true masses
> >     real<lower=0> mmin_min;
> >     real<lower=0> mmin_max;
> > }
> >
> > parameters {
> >     real<lower=beta_min,upper=beta_max> beta;
> >     real<lower=hs_min,upper=hs_max> logHs;
> >     real<lower=alpha_min,upper=alpha_max> alpha;
> >     real<lower=mmin_min,upper=mmin_max> log_mmin;
> >     vector<lower=log_mmin,upper=mtrue_max>[N] log_mtrue; //True mass estimates
> > }
> >
> > transformed parameters {
> >    real xmin;
> >    xmin <- pow(10,beta*(log_mmin-logHs));
> > }
> >
> > model {
> >     vector[N] log10y;
> >     vector[N] x;
> >
> >     log10y <- log_mtrue-logHs;
> >     for (i in 1:N) x[i] <- pow(10,beta*log10y[i]);
> >
> >     //truncated GGD is beta*10^(alpha*log10y)*exp(-x)/(10^logHs*Gamma((alpha+1)/beta,x)
> >     log10y ~ truncated_GGD(x, logHs,alpha, beta, xmin);
> >     log_mtrue ~ normal(log_m_meas,err);
> > }
> >
> >
> > I want to use about 25,000 halos for my true run, but have tested with fewer, and wouldn't mind running it with more as well.
> >
> >
> >
> > I produce my mock halos in the following manner:
> >
> >
> > library(gsl)
> >
> > dtggd = function(logm,logmmin,logh,a,b){
> >   # GSL required!
> >   return = b*10^(a*(logm-logh))*exp(-10^((logm-logh)*b))/(10^logh * gamma_inc((a+1)/b,10^(b*(logmmin-logh))))
> > }
> >
> > qtggd = function(logm,logmmin,logh,a,b){
> >   return = 1 - gamma_inc((a+1)/b,10^(b*(logm-logh)))/gamma_inc((a+1)/b,10^(b*(logmmin-logh)))
> > }
> >
> > rtggd = function(N,logmmin,logh,a,b){
> >   mmax = logh + 2.5/b
> >
> >   logm = seq(logmmin, mmax, 0.0001)
> >   cdf = qtggd(logm,logmmin,logh,a,b)
> >
> >   icdf = approxfun(cdf, logm)
> >
> >   x = runif(N)
> >   return = icdf(x)
> > }
> >
> > ############## GET MOCK DATA ###################################
> > N = 5000
> > err = 0.1
> > logmmin = 12
> > logh = 14
> > alpha = -1.8
> > beta = 0.7
> > seed = 1111
> >
> > set.seed(seed)
> > intrinsic = rtggd(N,logmmin,logh,alpha,beta)
> > mock.masses = rnorm(N,intrinsic,std)
> >
> > To be certain, with this, ie. N=5000, I get the following density plot:
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > <Auto Generated Inline Image 1.png>
> >
> >
> >
> > Then I run the following to run stan, and also two optimization runs
> >
> >
> > ############## SETUP RSTAN DATA ################################
> > data = list(N=N,log_m_meas=mock.masses,err=rep(err,N),
> >             hs_min=12,hs_max=15,alpha_min=-2.0,
> >             alpha_max=-1.6,beta_min=0.05,beta_max=1.5,
> >             mtrue_max=16.5,mmin_min=11,mmin_max=13)
> >
> > init = list(list(logHs=12.1,alpha=-1.95,beta=1.2,log_mmin=11.1,log_mtrue=mock.masses),   # Far away but reasonable masses
> >             list(logHs=14.9,alpha=-1.61,beta=0.2,log_mmin=12.5),                         # Opposite side, random masses
> >             list(logHs=13.5,alpha=-1.61,beta=1.2,log_mmin=11.5,log_mtrue=mock.masses),   # Swap alpha/beta relationship
> >             list(logHs=logh,alpha=alpha,beta=beta,log_mmin=logmmin,log_mtrue=intrinsic)) # Exact answer if perfect sample
> >
> > opt.init.exact = init[[4]]
> > opt.init.bad = init[[2]]
> >
> > model = stan_model(file="model_NO_S.stan")
> >
> > ############# RUN MCMC #########################################
> > result <- sampling(model, data=data, pars = c('logHs','alpha','beta',"log_mmin"), chains=4,
> >                    iter=2000, warmup=1000,cores=4,init=init)
> >
> > opt.res.exact <- optimizing(model,data=data,init=opt.init.exact,as_vector=FALSE)
> > opt.res.bad <- optimizing(model,data=data,init=opt.init.bad,as_vector=FALSE)
> >
> >
> >
> > The results look good for the MCMC: In fact, in this particular case it seems that logHs and alpha are reproduced perfectly (as the median) though beta is estimated as 0.83 rather than 0.7 (it makes sense that beta isn't estimated very well, since it mostly comes from the cut-off where there are basically no objects.
> >
> >
> >
> > In terms of diagnostics, using the amazing shinyStan, I have:
> >
> >
> > Chain     accept_stat    stepsize    treedepth    n_leapfrog    n_divergent
> > All ch    0.8142    0.1093    5.4253    81.8334    0.0119
> > chain1    0.8282    0.1038    5.691     91.5345    0.012
> > chain2    0.8056    0.1159    5.2375    59.803     0.0095
> > chain3    0.8056    0.1089    5.3905    85.8465    0.0135
> > chain4    0.8176    0.1087    5.382     90.1495    0.0125
> >
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > Everything looks good I think, as far as I understand. The only things perhaps worth mentioning are the correlation plot:
> >
> >
> >
> > <Auto Generated Inline Image 2.png>
> >
> > Where chain 2 is obviously worse than the rest -- this is probably because it starts with random masses. Also the large amount of covariance can be seen in the pairs plot:
> >
> >
> >
> > <Auto Generated Inline Image 3.png>
> >
> > Finally, the run took a fair while, especially in the warmup -- not sure if that's normal?:
> >
> >
> >           warmup   sample
> > chain:1 767.6131 213.1524
> > chain:2 539.0624 188.2982
> > chain:3 798.0353 136.3628

> >
> >
> >
> > So everything seems pretty much fine. BUT, when I check the results of the optimization runs, it returns this:

> >
> > I'm not really sure what else would be useful -- it would be nice if the optimization worked so that I could get quick estimates for testing purposes.
> >
> >
> >
> > Sorry I feel like I've been spamming you guys lately -- thanks very much for all the work you do. I certainly have not been disappointed.

messages.subject: Re: Discrete model comparision: Bayes factor in generated parameters?
messages.subject_clean: Discrete model comparision: Bayes factor in generated parameters?
messages.body_plain:
Thanks, everyone, for the quick and helpful replies!  I'm seeing that model comparison is indeed a trickier topic than I believed!  I think that what I need might be advice at a higher level of abstraction. Let me explain what I'm trying to do:

The common situation in my field (psychology/neuroscience) is to have several models which instantiate hypotheses about the generative process that gave rise to a dataset, and our usual goal for model comparison is to determine the relative plausibility of the hypotheses.  It seems to many of us (though I'd love to find out that we're wrong about this) that predictive-performance-based methods like cross validation and WAIC are not ideal for this purpose, since they often favor models that are too complex to be plausible hypotheses about how the brain works, especially when datasets are large and overfitting is minimal. The typical solution is to use BIC, but I'd like to do better, especially since I'd like to use hierarchical models, where BIC seems particularly terrible.

Do you have any recommendations for hypothesis testing in situations like these? Perhaps build a mixture model (as Michael suggests), and ask whether the posterior over the mixing weight is mostly to one side or the other of 0.5? Or perhaps our reasons for avoiding cross validation, etc., are wrongheaded, and there is a way to make these methods work?
I guess it's also possible that there really is no good general quantitative solution, and we should do something like report a measure of predictive performance and report model structure, and do our "plausibility" evaluations qualitatively.

I realize I'm now outside the realm of stan and asking for general statistics help - any advice will be very much appreciated!

Thanks a ton!

Kevin

The typical solution is to use BIC, but I'd like to do better, especially since I'd like to use hierarchical models, where BIC seems particularly terrible.

In psychology and neuroscience the predictive approach is very natural as you should be able to predict the behavior of the not yet observed person or brain. If you have several observations per subject, you could use leave-one-subject-out cross-validation (which is commonly used by neuroscientist I know). If you a large number of subjects, you could use k-fold-CV such that data division is made by subjects.

messages.body_plain:
Another quick thought on the possible memory leak issue; sometimes simply looking at an OS's memory monitor isn't an accurate gauge of the memory status as the OS will often show memory being allocated even when released if no new data allocations have been requested since the release. The true test is to try to allocate a new object and see if you encounter an unexpected out of memory error or paging to disk.

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~

The ELBO is an approximation to the evidence (sometimes called
the marginal likelihood).  It tends to be a better approximation then
BIC, but even if it is very accurate you have to deal with the subtleties
of the evidence itself.  For that see the numerous relevant posts on
this list as well as the discussion in Bayesian Data Analysis.

Since my statistical knowledge is pretty basic, I would like to ask your opinion - can ELBO be considered as a model selection criterion? If so, what are the neccessary conditions?

On Wednesday, August 5, 2015 at 9:53:58 AM UTC-4, Raghu Naik wrote:
> The first approach goes well. The second  LKJ priors approach throws up Rhat NaNs on some correlations coefficients. I wanted to find out how that can be fixed.

For a Cholesky factor, L, the L[i,j] elements for j > i are fixed at 0. Moreover, for a Cholesky factor of a correlation matrix, L[1,1] is fixed at 1. Therefore, no function of their "distributions" --- including Rhat --- is well-defined.

However, this

L_Sigma <- diag_post_multiply(L_Omega, L_sigma);

is miscoded and should be

L_Sigma <- diag_pre_multiply(L_sigma, L_Omega);

so that

L_Sigma * transpose(L_Sigma) = diag(L_sigma) * L_Omega * transpose(L_Omega) * diag(L_sigma)

is a covariance matrix.

Ben

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Evidence Lower Bound as model selection criterion
messages.body_plain:
Aside from subtleties with using the marginal likelihood itself, the ELBO can indeed be used. The bigger issue to keep in mind though is the sensitivity of the variational approximation to the posterior. That is, using the ELBO as a replacement for the marginal likelihood makes the assumption that the KL divergence between the posterior and the variational distribution are the same for every model. This is rarely true, and it is easy to construct scenarios where the marginal likelihood is actually lower for model 1 but the ELBO is higher for model 2, because the variational family cannot fit model 1 very well. This is not nearly as bad as AIC or BIC in "most cases”, however, so I’m not surprised by that paper’s stance.

Dustin

It is there (or at least one of them is), is called multi_student_t.

> If not, are there any work-arounds that you might suggest?

Even though multi_student_t exists, you should only use if for a likelihood of data. For an unknown, it is better to express a multivariate t random variable as a mixture of normals as in

http://journal.r-project.org/archive/2013-2/hofert.pdf

Ben

The OS memory status is bad at detecting leaks unless
you can do the alloc/free in a loop and see OS memory
exhausted when it should be zero.

Otherwise, you need to go into a memory debugger, like
valgrind.   There are lots of them:

  https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memory_debugger

- Bob

> On Aug 5, 2015, at 9:43 AM, Mike Lawrence <mike....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Another quick thought on the possible memory leak issue; sometimes simply looking at an OS's memory monitor isn't an accurate gauge of the memory status as the OS will often show memory being allocated even when released if no new data allocations have been requested since the release. The true test is to try to allocate a new object and see if you encounter an unexpected out of memory error or paging to disk.
>
>
> --
> Mike Lawrence

> Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
> Dalhousie University
