messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Rstudio & .stan files: prevent soft-wrap?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Rstudio & .stan files: prevent soft-wrap?
messages.body_plain:
We (and Google code style, which we're primarily following),
strongly recommend a max of 80-character lines.  The main reason
for us is that diff tools like the ones in GitHub are line
based and when you try to view online with something like
GitHub file viewers, it's a huge pain if the lines are wider
than that.  Given that Stan looks a lot like C++ when written,
we recommend pretty much following this:

  http://google.github.io/styleguide/cppguide.html

for exactly the reasons they lay out.

So rather than writing:

  a <- b; // a really really long comment that's going to run over

we'd suggest

  // a really really long
  // comment that can now be wrapped
  // and won't run over
  a <- b;

And even more strongly we'd suggest renaming variables or writing
functions with meaningful names so you don't need long in-code comments.
The big problem is that (a) comments get stale, whereas code never
lies, and (b) it's hard to read the code when there are a lot of comments
and you always need to read the code because of (a).

If you have long program comments about things like algorithms or
references, we suggest putting them up top in a /* ... */ comment.

- Bob

> On Aug 5, 2015, at 10:48 AM, Mike Lawrence <mike....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Probably a query more appropriately directed to the rstudio folks, but just in case anyone on this list has encountered and solve this already: is there any way to get rstudio to *not* soft-wrap .stan files? Love the proper code highlighting for .stan files in rstudio, but I'm a glutton for long comment lines and prefer unwrapped views.
>
>

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Evidence Lower Bound as model selection criterion
messages.body_plain:
Yes, to start with I think the term “evidence” is horrible; second, the whole “lower bound” thing is pretty meaningless in that if you are comparing 2 models, you’ll use the difference so a “lower bound” is no better than an “estimate”; third, it typically depends on aspects of the prior that are assigned arbitrarily, for example if you change your prior from normal(0,10) to normal(0,100), your marginal likelihood changes by a factor of 10.  So, yeah, basically don’t do it.  If you want to do model comparison I recommend predictive criteria such as disucssed here:
http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/unpublished/loo_stan.pdf
A

messages.subject: Re: Discrete model comparision: Bayes factor in generated parameters?
messages.subject_clean: Discrete model comparision: Bayes factor in generated parameters?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Aki,

Thanks for your response! I'm enjoying your papers with Andrew on WAIC and on PSIS-LOO, and I'm excited about using these tools in some of my work.

I'm not sure, though, that predictive performance measures are ideal for all of our applications. Often in neuroscience we consider out models not as tools to make predictions about the future (as one might in e.g. weather prediction or stock picking), but rather as competing hypotheses about the generative process that gave rise to the dataset (e.g. the neural algorithm a rat is using to solve a particular task). In this case, it seems to me that the Bayes factor, with it's "automatic Occam's razor", is the natural model comparison metric.

To take an extreme example, a model which is just a lookup table giving the probability of each outcome occurring in each condition will have excellent predictive performance if constrained by enough data, but this should not make us expect to find a lookup table in the brain. A Bayes factor analysis would correctly give this model a very low score, due to the huge number of free parameters.  I guess I've learned here that Bayes factors are problematic to reliably estimate, so I'm not sure where that leaves us if we want to compare models of this type.

Thanks!

Kevin

On Wednesday, August 5, 2015 at 3:57:37 AM UTC-4, Aki Vehtari wrote:
>
> On Wednesday, August 5, 2015 at 9:41:15 AM UTC+3, Kevin Miller wrote:
> > The common situation in my field (psychology/neuroscience) is to have several models which instantiate hypotheses about the generative process that gave rise to a dataset, and our usual goal for model comparison is to determine the relative plausibility of the hypotheses.  It seems to many of us (though I'd love to find out that we're wrong about this) that predictive-performance-based methods like cross validation and WAIC are not ideal for this purpose, since they often favor models that are too complex to be plausible hypotheses about how the brain works, especially when datasets are large and overfitting is minimal. The typical solution is to use BIC, but I'd like to do better, especially since I'd like to use hierarchical models, where BIC seems particularly terrible.
>
> In psychology and neuroscience the predictive approach is very natural as you should be able to predict the behavior of the not yet observed person or brain. If you have several observations per subject, you could use leave-one-subject-out cross-validation (which is commonly used by neuroscientist I know). If you a large number of subjects, you could use k-fold-CV such that data division is made by subjects.
>
> Aki

messages.body_plain:
On Thursday, August 6, 2015 at 8:03:53 AM UTC-4, Richard McAlexander wrote:
> Does anyone have any suggestions/examples for coding the estimation of instrumental variables in stan using GLM? The only example I could find <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/instrumental$20variable/stan-users/72EDeBO-bHk/FhK410IRgK8J> uses a multivariate normal likelihood. I basically want to do the two stages using a logit model. Can I just use a multivariate normal model and then use a logit link on that output or is there a better way to do this in stan?

Use a bivariate normal likelihood (composed of a univariate normal distribution for the outcome times a conditional normal distribution for the instrumented variable) is much easier because the dependence is characterized by a correlation, which is easily understood and something one could specify a prior on. In the bivariate distributions where one margin is normal and the other is logistic, the dependence could be captured by any copula but is harder to interpret. Many ignore the fact that the instrumented variable is binary when the CACE they want to estimate is additive but it is usually better to estimate a Tobin-5 model with a bivariate normal distribution for latent utility and the outcome, whose log-likelihood is given in the vignette for the sampleSelection R package.

Ben

BIC is what it is, it can be useful, but don’t kid yourself that it is Bayesian in any real sense!

I assume that you would like that your model could predict how the other rats will perform in task solving? For me the first step is to check that model generalizes out of the observed data. If there are several models which give similar predictions then it's possible to continue examining which models are plausible given other information known or measurable in the future.

I have worked with neuroscientist, and in several cases Bayes factor has been supersensitive to priors on parameters and thus completely useless for model selection (see also Andrew's comment). So it's not just the difficulty of estimating the Bayes factors, it's also that Bayes factor can be super sensitive to priors.

Aki

messages.subject_clean: GLM & Instrumental Variables in stan?
messages.body_plain:
On Friday, August 7, 2015 at 12:02:52 PM UTC-4, Richard McAlexander wrote:
> first equation: instrument ~ thing that predicts instrument
> second equation: outcome of interest ~ thing I'm trying to instrument for + controls
> third equation: outcome of interest ~ other possible predictor + controls

It is more like

first equation: T ~ controls + things that predict treatment but not outcomes conditional on the controls
second equation: (Y | T = 1) ~ controls
third equation: (Y | T = 0) ~ controls

with a 3x3 covariance matrix among the errors with the first variance restricted to 1.

The Tobin-5 model allows the intercept and coefficients to differ depending on whether T = 1 or T = 0. The LATE can be computed by averaging differences in the posterior predictive distribution where you counterfactually use the parameters from the second equation for the observations where T = 0 and use the parameters from the third equation for the observations where T = 1 (in addition to the factual posterior predictive distributions where you use the parameters from the second equation for the observations where T = 1 and use the parameters from the third equation for the observations where T = 0).

Ben

On Sunday, August 9, 2015 at 12:24:26 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I'll have to flag this more heavily in the manual, but you almost
> always want to use Cholesky factors rather than full matrices as
> data types.
>
> There's an error in the manual example for multivariate priors in
> that you need to pre-multiply, not post-multiply.

Luc's suggestion to use quad_form_diag() was a good one, although it is not really noticeable with 3x3 matrices.

This is actually one of the rare cases where it makes sense to use a 3x3 correlation matrix rather than a Cholesky factor of a 3x3 correlation matrix. Part of the reason is that the likelihood is written in terms of scalars, so you don't get the benefit of using multi_normal_cholesky() rather than multi_normal(). But the main reason --- which is the most fascinating thing about this model from a Bayesian perspective and makes frequentists' heads asplode --- is that the [3,2] correlation does not enter the likelihood but your prior beliefs about it have a major affect on the posterior distribution of the [1,2] correlation, the [1,3] correlation, and of every other parameter.

The [3,2] correlation is the correlation between the errors for Y | T = 1 and Y | T = 0, and because no one is in both the treatment and the control group at the same time, the likelihood doesn't identify the [3,2] correlation. So, if you do MLE or a two-step estimator, you don't even optimize over the [3,2] correlation. But if you are a genuine Bayesian, then you have beliefs about the [3,2] correlation and in most situations, those beliefs are that the [3,2] correlation is really close to 1.0 (i.e. whatever is omitted from the model of the outcome when T = 1 presumably has an essentially equal effect when T = 0). Moreover, if the  [3,2] correlation is really close to 1.0, then there are relatively few values  of the [1,2] correlation (between the error in the model for T and the error in the model for Y | T = 1) and the [1,3] correlation (between the error in the model for T and the error in the model for Y | T = 0) that satisfy the positive definiteness constraint on the 3x3 correlation matrix as a whole.

So, for a Tobin-5 model I like to "omit" the prior on Lambda (implicitly putting a joint uniform prior over the space of 3x3 correlation matrices) and overlay a beta prior on (1 + Lambda[3,2]) / 2 (ignoring the Jacobian warning from the parser because this transformation only involves constants). If first shape parameter is much larger than the second shape parameter in this beta prior, that implies Lambda[3,2] is close to 1.0 and consequently affects the distribution of Lambda[1,2] and Lambda[1,3].

Ben

It's not initialization/warmup that's the issue.   There's no
major difference in memory usage for the Stan infrastructure itself
between inits in the typical set or far out into the tails.

The most likely cause is an iterative algorithm that is being
autodiffed through that takes more iteration in the tails than in
the typical set.  We see this with the ODE integrator, for example.

Do you know what values the function's being called with that eat
lots of memory?

I don't know anything about how R recovers memory, but Stan itself
recovers (or should recover) all memory after each log density
evaluation (each leapfrog step in HMC or NUTS).

- Bob

> >     for (n in 1:size(X))

> >     return log_sum_exp(temp);
> >   }
> > }
> > data {
> >   int<lower=1> N;
> >   int<lower=1> K;
> >   vector[K] X[N];
> >   int<lower=K> C;

> >   // prior on theta
> > }

messages.subject_clean: HIERARCHICAL GAUSSIAN SPATIO TEMPORAL MODELS
messages.body_plain:
Hell Stan Team,

Thanks for your previous direction, I got a lot of help with defining my covariance. The forum guys are taking a bit long.

Generally, we are trying to  model an underlying Gaussian Process with binomial sampling distribution(likelihood). Our models

are hierarchical over the parameters, Bk,which I give a joint normal prior and over hyper-parameters of the covariance matrix. We approximate the spatial dependency using the non-stationary,

anisotropic matern covariance ,whose parameters : length-scale(rho) and signal-variance(sigma-squared) are given the inverse_gamma(0.001,0.001) and uniform(0,200) priors

respectively.

Specifically my target model is: "glmm-model.png"- attached in this post.

#Now if fj is an Auto-regressive dynamics- for example, when each observation was made at a yearly time-point, which is very important for our inference- then I prefer to model it using an ar model or a random-walk ,where most appropriate.

#My Challenge

I have set up the model as given in the attached script, apparently it gives back results that are not consistent with the expected/known trend. I thought first to diagnose convergence but ended up with inconsistent volatility across the sampling chains. I suspected my initial parameterization values to be a possible cause and have since given different permutations of priors and inits, including specifying flat priors but the convergence is not clearly coming out.

I would like you to help me preview my model specification if it is indeed consistent with the literature of gaussian hierarchical models especially as specified in this mail, or even point to an unintentional failure that might have occurred. Your comments are highly regarded! I have attached an example dataset(Sl_ageCorrected*), stan model(sl_multigp.stan)  with prediction raster files: (sl_prec.asc,sl_urb.asc). You can also see the surface prediction I got initially(sl_PR_180615)

Kind Regards!

Lukio

On Sunday, August 9, 2015 at 1:42:20 PM UTC-4, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Sunday, August 9, 2015 at 12:24:26 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > I'll have to flag this more heavily in the manual, but you almost
> > always want to use Cholesky factors rather than full matrices as
> > data types.
> >
> > There's an error in the manual example for multivariate priors in
> > that you need to pre-multiply, not post-multiply.
>
> Luc's suggestion to use quad_form_diag() was a good one, although it is not really noticeable with 3x3 matrices.
>
> This is actually one of the rare cases where it makes sense to use a 3x3 correlation matrix rather than a Cholesky factor of a 3x3 correlation matrix. Part of the reason is that the likelihood is written in terms of scalars, so you don't get the benefit of using multi_normal_cholesky() rather than multi_normal(). But the main reason --- which is the most fascinating thing about this model from a Bayesian perspective and makes frequentists' heads asplode --- is that the [3,2] correlation does not enter the likelihood but your prior beliefs about it have a major affect on the posterior distribution of the [1,2] correlation, the [1,3] correlation, and of every other parameter.
>
> The [3,2] correlation is the correlation between the errors for Y | T = 1 and Y | T = 0, and because no one is in both the treatment and the control group at the same time, the likelihood doesn't identify the [3,2] correlation. So, if you do MLE or a two-step estimator, you don't even optimize over the [3,2] correlation. But if you are a genuine Bayesian, then you have beliefs about the [3,2] correlation and in most situations, those beliefs are that the [3,2] correlation is really close to 1.0 (i.e. whatever is omitted from the model of the outcome when T = 1 presumably has an essentially equal effect when T = 0). Moreover, if the  [3,2] correlation is really close to 1.0, then there are relatively few values  of the [1,2] correlation (between the error in the model for T and the error in the model for Y | T = 1) and the [1,3] correlation (between the error in the model for T and the error in the model for Y | T = 0) that satisfy the positive definiteness constraint on the 3x3 correlation matrix as a whole.
>
> So, for a Tobin-5 model I like to "omit" the prior on Lambda (implicitly putting a joint uniform prior over the space of 3x3 correlation matrices) and overlay a beta prior on (1 + Lambda[3,2]) / 2 (ignoring the Jacobian warning from the parser because this transformation only involves constants). If first shape parameter is much larger than the second shape parameter in this beta prior, that implies Lambda[3,2] is close to 1.0 and consequently affects the distribution of Lambda[1,2] and Lambda[1,3].
>
> Ben

messages.body_plain:
Here's an example that might be useful.  Suppose I know
the data y come from a normal(mu, 1) distribution so that
the true model is

  y ~ normal(mu, 1)

Now suppose I draw

  y[1], y[2], y[3] ~ normal(0, 1).

I might get -1.5, -1.8, +0.3, so that the MLE is

  mu* = -1

That's why there's no reason to expect the posterior mode
to be equal to the true value.

So what you need to do is a bunch of simulations and see
if the posterior intervals have the proper coverage.  That is,
will the true value be in the posterior 80% interval around
80% of the time?  The in-between approach if you have a lot of
parameters is to make sure 80% of the parameter estimates are
in their posterior 80% intervals.

For this case (and most others), in the limit as N -> infinity,
then the posterior mean and mode both approach the true value
(here mu = 0).  The standard error's going to shrink as 1/sqrt(N).

- Bob

First step is to choose random (put reasonable) true
values, simulate data, then fit that simulated data to
ensure that the posterior covers the “true” values
reasonable well.  Compare parameters to parameters.

If you want to look at the data then you have to sample
from the posterior predictive distribution and then compare
measured data to simulated data (i.e. posterior predictive
checks).

In general parameters and data have no relation.

Hi Lukas,

When you say that it doesn't work out anymore, I'm assuming you mean that it doesn't produce the same results. If it's not running any more, then let us know -- that's something different.

If it's what I suspect (different results), it's because the model is different. Let's look at the log_mix part of the model:
for (i in 1 : num_data) {
    increment_log_prob(log_mix(Proportion,

                                                   lognormal_log(Latent_Data[i], mu_low , sigma_low ),

                                                   lognormal_log(Latent_Data[i], mu_high, sigma_high)));
}

vs.

increment_log_prob(log_mix(Proportion,

                                               lognormal_log(Latent_Data[i], mu_low , sigma_low ),
                                               lognormal_log(Latent_Data[i], mu_high, sigma_high)));

In the first section, the Proportion parameter is the mixture between individual components -- on the probability scale:
(Proportion * lognormal(Latent_Data[1], mu_low, sigma_low) + (1 - Proportion) * lognormal(Latent_Data[1], mu_high, sigma_high)) * (Proportion * lognormal(Latent_Data[2], mu_low, sigma_low) + (1 - Proportion) * lognormal(Latent_Data[2], mu_high, sigma_high)) + ...

In the second, the Proportion parameter is the mixture between two models. On the probability scale:
Proportion * lognormal(Latent_Data, mu_low, sigma_low) + (1 - Proportion) * lognormal(Latent_Data, mu_high, sigma_high)

where lognormal(Latent_Data, mu, sigma) = \sum_{i = 1}^num_data lognormal(Latent_Data[i], mu, sigma)

These are just different models. Let me know if that wasn't clear and I'll try again, or you can try to work out the math.

Daniel

The eight schools example is good for illustrating sampling pathologies, but it is sort of weird substantively and depending on how you do it, you may find that the group-level variance is near zero.

I just do a flat probit model. Gibbs with data-augmentation will perform well and Stan will perform almost equally well. One-parameter-at-a-time Gibbs or M-H will perform worse than Stan. Then, you can do an ordinal probit model where Gibbs with data-augmentation will perform worse than Stan because of the cutpoints update.

Ben

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] seeking help with reinforcement learning model
messages.body_plain:
Suppose you have a function f(theta), that takes a parameter vector
theta and returns something like your correlation vs. imaging data.

The fully Bayesian approach is to treat theta like a random variable,
condition on the observed data y, and compute the posterior f(theta).

In practice, all that means is that you take M draws theta(1), ..., theta(M)
from the posterior p(theta | y), and then f(theta(1)), ..., f(theta(M)) is
a sequence of M draws from the posterior on f(theta).  You can compute estimates
for posterior means of f(theta), posterior medians, posterior intervals, etc.
It builds in the uncertainty in f(theta) due to the uncertainty for theta,
which is modeled in Bayesian stats using the posterior p(theta | y).

- Bob

messages.subject: Analytic form of joint distribution of two correlations in LKJ matrix
messages.subject_clean: Analytic form of joint distribution of two correlations in LKJ matrix
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I have been trying to work out an analytic form for the joint density of two correlations in the LKJ matrix (e.g. rho(12) and rho(23)). From the Lewandowski et al. (2009) paper, I think I'm right (please correct me if I am wrong) in saying that the marginal distribution of a given correlation is given by a Beta(eta - 1 + d/2, eta -1 + d/2) - where d is the order of the matrix, and eta is a shape parameter - but I can't seem to find if there is an analytic form for the joint of two correlations.

Does anyone know if a joint distribution for two correlations exists, and if so, can you point me in its direction?

Best,

Ben

messages.body_plain:
On Monday, August 10, 2015 at 6:19:47 PM UTC-4, Ben Lambert wrote:
> Does anyone know if a joint distribution for two correlations exists, and if so, can you point me in its direction?

It depends on which two correlations you are referring to. Any two in the first column / row of the correlation matrix are independent, so the bivariate density is just the product of the marginal Beta densities over the (-1,1) interval. And each correlation in the second column / row depends on two correlations in the first column / row, so deriving a bivariate distribution would be difficult. It gets worse from there.

Ben

- Make your Stan program a separate stand-alone .stan file, don’t put it as a character string in your R script.  This won’t speed up your model but it should help your workflow.

- normal(,100) priors on beta don’t look good to me.  Try something more stable such as normal(,1), assuming x and y have been roughly put on unit scale

- change to a ~ normal(0,1); and then in the expression for y_hat, replace “a[streetlist[n]]” by “sigma_a*a[streetlist[n]]”.  This is the so-called non-centered parameterization.

Good luck!

messages.subject_clean: Analytic form of joint distribution of two correlations in LKJ matrix
messages.body_plain:
On Monday, August 10, 2015 at 8:59:18 PM UTC-4, Ben Lambert wrote:
> Sorry for not being clear. Analytic expressions for the joint density of rho(23) with for example rho(34)? Alternatively, is there a paper on the uniform distribution over correlation matrices that you would recommend?

There is the LKJ paper, but that doesn't necessarily help. In general, it is true that if the Omega_{ij} is the partial correlation between variables i < j conditional on all variables prior to i and Sigma_{ij} is the usual Pearson correlation between i and j, then

So, according to the second line

Sigma_{23} = Omega_{12} * Omega_{13} +
                     Omega_{23} * sqrt( (1 - Omega_{12}^2) * (1 - Omega_{13}^2) )

and according to the third line

Sigma_{34} = Omega_{13} * Omega_{14} +
                     Omega_{23} * Omega_{24} * sqrt( (1 - Omega_{13}^2) * (1 - Omega_{14}^2) ) +
                     Omega_{34} * sqrt( (1 - Omega_{13}^2) * (1 - Omega_{14}^2) * (1 - Omega_{23}^2) * (1 - Omega_{24}^2) )

Although the Omegas are independently distributed and have a symmetric beta distribution on the (-1,1) interval with shape alpha_i = eta + (K - i) / 2, it is not easy to figure out the bivariate distribution of Sigma_{23} and Sigma_{34}, even if eta = 1 and K is large. There has to be a copula representation of their dependence, but I don't know what it is. And I'm not sure what the relevance to Stan would be. You could describe / plot it pretty well just by drawing the whole correlation matrix repeatedly from an LKJ distribution.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
> On Aug 10, 2015, at 4:56 PM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:
>
> On Mon, Aug 10, 2015 at 4:46 PM, Avraham Adler <avraha...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Just to make sure I understand you Daniel, the first version is demanding that every datum is a blend of the two models with the set proportion,
>
> yes.
>
> whereas the second is treating the data as a whole as a blend of two models with said proportion,
>
> yes.
>
> but any one datum's contribution can be of a different "proportonal mix" as it were?
>
> umm. I think it can be viewed as each datum's contribution is equal. I think?

Since this is confusing a lot of people, I'll add a compare-and-contrast
section to the manual:

  https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1526#issuecomment-129711045

A mixture model assumes each observation comes from one of the mixture
components.  In the binary mixture of normal case, that's

  z[n] ~ bernoulli(lambda);
  y[n] ~ normal(mu[z[n] + 1], sigma[z[n] + 1]);

But when you marginalize out the discrete "responsibility"
parameter z, you get something that looks like what you call
a "proportional mix",

  p(y[n]|lambda, mu, sigma) = lambda * normal(y[n] | mu[2], sigma[2])
                              + (1 - lambda) * normal(y[n] | mu[1], sigma[1])

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] numerical stability tips
messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] numerical stability tips
messages.body_plain:
[move to stan-users; bcc-ing Sharad]

In general, the best thing to do is work on the log scale and
always use CCDFs where available.  Unfortunately, in Stan,
our log CDFs and log CCDFs are implemented naively, so that's
not going to help.

The problem is that you can represent numbers very close to 0
using IEEE floating point, but not numbers very close to 1.  That's
why we get both erf() and erfc() and log() and log1p().

Aside from underflow/overflow, which the erfc() and log1p()s of the world
try to mitigate, another big problem for arithmetic is subtraction of numbers
that are close to each other or on different scales.  For instance, if beta_cdf
is near 1, then (1 - beta_cdf(...)) is going to cause what's known
as "catastrophic cancellation" --- you lose precision equal to the
shared leading digits.

The only course of action for a complex expression is to rearrange
terms so it's more stable and work on the log scale for as long as
possible, only converting back at the very end.  You might find
that everything cancels nicely given the  a and a+1 in the beta.

You can test overflow and underflow over input ranges of interest.
Accuracy requires a higher-precision package (e.g., Boost uses
something like 1000 decimal place accuracy arithmetic in some of
their tess).

You might find this form more stable:

  exp(log(1 - beta_cdf(x, a+1, b))
      - log(1 - beta_cdf(x, a, b))
      + log(a)
      - log(a + b))

=

  exp(beta_ccdf_log(x, a+1, b)
      beta_ccdf_log(x, a, b)
      + log(a)
      - log(a + b))

What we could really use is someone to implement high-precision
log CDFs and CCDFs.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Need help with improving speed performance
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Need help with improving speed performance
messages.body_plain:
You should replace the long-form arithmetic expression with a dot
product.  Otherwise, besides tightening up the priors to be more
informative, I don't see much else to do.  You could do some more
vectorization, but it's unlikely to help.

Are your predictors standardized?

You also have a model that's only weakly identified by priors:
because of this term

a[streetlist[n]] + beta[streetlist[n]][1] + ...

You could move to a centered parameterization if you have lots of
data, removing the a[streetlist[n]] term from y_hat sum and
instead putting it into the prior for beta[j].

beta[j] ~ normal(a[j] + u[j] * gamma, 100);

That 100 may be bad news if you don't expect beta to be on that
scale.

- Bob

> shared leading digits.
>
> The only course of action for a complex expression is to rearrange
> terms so it's more stable and work on the log scale for as long as
> possible, only converting back at the very end.  You might find
> that everything cancels nicely given the  a and a+1 in the beta.
>
> You can test overflow and underflow over input ranges of interest.
> Accuracy requires a higher-precision package (e.g., Boost uses
> something like 1000 decimal place accuracy arithmetic in some of
> their tess).
>
> You might find this form more stable:
>
>  exp(log(1 - beta_cdf(x, a+1, b))
>      - log(1 - beta_cdf(x, a, b))
>      + log(a)
>      - log(a + b))
>
> =
>
>  exp(beta_ccdf_log(x, a+1, b)
>      beta_ccdf_log(x, a, b)
>      + log(a)
>      - log(a + b))
>
> What we could really use is someone to implement high-precision
> log CDFs and CCDFs.
>
> - Bob
>
>> On Aug 11, 2015, at 11:14 AM, Alp Kucukelbir <akucu...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>
>> hi folks,
>>
>> i've been communicating with sharad goel, who wants to use the function below in a Stan program.
>>
>> functions {
>> 	// mean of beta(a,b) conditioned on being larger than x
>> 	real beta_conditional_mean(real x, real a, real b) {
>> 		return (1 - beta_cdf(x, a+1, b)) / (1 - beta_cdf(x, a, b)) * a / (a+b);
>> 	}
>> }
>>
>> any tips to make this more numerically stable? i think i'm mainly worried about when a and b are small, but i may be missing something here.
>>
>> cheers
>> alp

messages.body_plain:
Hi Mike,

First, the book link [1] is dead.

More below.

On Monday, July 27, 2015 at 10:36:31 AM UTC-4, Mike Lawrence wrote:
> In neuroscience, we often collect EEG data to measure the activity of the brain. However, EEG voltage is a relative measure, and the specific choice of reference point can change the observed voltage topology quite dramatically. Apparently ([1]) there is a known-but-rarely-applied "solution" to this issue whereby you compute the 2nd derivative of the voltage topology using an arbitrary reference, resulting in a current density topology that provides an absolute measure of brain activity, and one that will be the same regardless of the reference chosen to generate the original voltage topology.
>
> Ignoring for the moment the issue of the topology being on the surface of a sphere (which is being discussed elsewhere, [2]), is there a recommended way to model this scenario in stan?

Not sure. Do you have a way to calculate the 2nd derivative?

> I know that one method would be to simply model the voltage as a function of a spatiotemporal GP, then put computation of the 2nd derivative of the GP in the transformed parameters section, but possibly there's a more direct approach whereby the voltage is modelled as a transformation of a current density GP?

If you've got a form of the voltage as a function of that estimated GP, then I don't see why not.

>
>
> [1] https://books.google.ca/books?id=SzavAwAAQBAJ&lpg=PA165&ots=I9lMzlss5L&dq=Luck%20current%20density&pg=PA165#v=onepage&q&f=false

Does anyone have any advice / examples of having done this? Or is there some reason it's not possible?

Thanks,
David Manheim

Hi Folks,

I want to apologize for my naivety as I'm new to Stan and relatively new to Bayesian modeling.  With that said, I've been struggling with implementing the 'Matt Trick' in a simple 2-level logistic regression and cannot seem to replicate what is posted in the Q&A and manual.  Normally, I wouldn't worry too much about computation time, but I'm dealing with 1 to 3 million records in what will eventually be a more complex model structure...so I hope to tweak performance as much as possible as I work towards the final model.  I've attached data simulation code and two .stan files (one with and one without MT implemented).  Both produce accurate output, but file with MT implemented is considerably slower than without...any ideas as to what I'm doing wrong or suggestions for improvement?  Does it have anything to do with the fact that I'm performing these code adjustments on alpha rather than betas?

Thanks for the help!

messages.body_plain: The draws are tucked away in the sim slot of a stanfit object (along with some other stuff). So you could make a copy of your stanfit and then change the sim slot in the copy. All of the metadata and whatnot would still describe the original stanfit with all the draws, but the relevance of that depends on what you need for your post-processing. That can be changed to if need be. A different approach would be to create an empty stanfit object and fill it in with what you need.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Simple multi-level logistic regression with considerable data
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Simple multi-level logistic regression with considerable data
messages.body_plain:
See the Betancourt and Girolami arXiv paper.

  http://arxiv.org/abs/1312.0906

The exec summary is that with a lot of data per group, the centered parameterization
is more efficient than the non-centered ("Matt trick") version.

It probably won't make much difference, but this

  for (n in 1:N)
      y_hat[n] <- alpha[groups[n]] + x[n]*beta;

would probably be more efficient as

  for (n in 1:N)
      y_hat[n] <- alpha[groups[n]];
  y_hat <- y_hat + x * beta;

The reason is that the x * beta is more efficient for derivatives
than the repeated x[n] * beta.

For efficiency, you may also want to standardize your outcome and
predictors and tighten the priors.

You might also find that giving beta a hierarchical prior is more
efficient than the fixed normal(0, 5), especially if normal(0, 5)
isn't a good description of the fitted parameters.

- Bob

messages.subject: lower=0 constrain needed for scale parameters?
messages.subject_clean: lower=0 constrain needed for scale parameters?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

It's a bit of a dump question.

Re Manual v 2.7.0:

Under the "Regression Models" of the manual (Ch 5),

the scale parameters of fitted normal processes are typically specified with <lower=0> constrain (e.g. pg 42)

But, under "Time-Series Models"->"Autoregressive Models" of the manual (Ch 6.1)

<lower=0> is not used for specifying sigma (e.g. pg 77)

Is there any rationale to this?

Many thanks,

Andy

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have a set of time series values (positive) of y:

vector<lower=0>[N] y

I want to estimate the relative likelihood of the following 3 scenarios:

a. diverging AR(1):     y_n ~ normal (alpha + y_(n-1), sigma), alpha > 0
b. converging AR(1):  y_n ~ normal (alpha + y_(n-1), sigma), alpha < 0
c. stationary:             y_n ~ normal (mu, sigma)

What would be the best way to do this in STAN?

Many thanks,
Andy

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Differential equations and forcing functions using data?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Differential equations and forcing functions using data?
messages.body_plain:
More details would be better, but I can confirm you that forcings work in Stan. I.e. I have run an analysis where I model the response to a drug while using the drug concentration over time as (fixed) input function. The difficult part is to code this in Stan, but what it takes is to make use of the x_r and x_i (fixed data) portion of the integrate_ode function. You have to figure out what data you have to pass into the function in order to be able to calculate at any time-point t the values of the forcing function entering your differential.

Sebastian

Welcome to Stan. Yes, use whatever prior you'd like. We aren't limited to conjugacy here.

The only catch is that we don't have discrete parameters. Discrete data is fine. This isn't usually a problem because on most cases you can marginalize out the discrete parameter and estimate a continuous one instead. (Details in the manual.)

sub_sample <- function(stanfit, n, keep_warmup = TRUE) {
  sim <- stanfit@sim
  samp <- sim$samples
  W <- sim$warmup
  I <- sim$iter
  sel <- c(if (keep_warmup) 1:W, sample((W + 1):I, size = n))
  subsamp <- lapply(samp, function(chain_samp) {
    lapply(chain_samp, function(x) x[sel])
  })
  stanfit@sim$samples <- subsamp
  stanfit
}

This doesn't change any of the metadata and probably needs to be adjusted if you did any thinning, but it's along the right lines.

>   http://arxiv.org/abs/1312.0906
>
> The exec summary is that with a lot of data per group, the centered parameterization
> is more efficient than the non-centered ("Matt trick") version.
>
> It probably won't make much difference, but this
>
>   for (n in 1:N)
>       y_hat[n] <- alpha[groups[n]] + x[n]*beta;

>

> than the repeated x[n] * beta.

> For efficiency, you may also want to standardize your outcome and

> You might also find that giving beta a hierarchical prior is more

> isn't a good description of the fitted parameters.

That amount of data's totally manageable.  It looks like you're not
doing anything with the missingness yet --- that's a separate issue.

When you say "very little progress", what happens when you run it?

I'm not that familiar with the ideal-point model applications;
in standard IRT models, we can usually safely assume alpha[k] > 0.
My understanding is that they can be hard to identify in terms
of sign of alpha.

What is the mean of y?  If it's not close to 0, you may want to
add a prior mean for beta (centered parameterization) or an
intercept for the model as a whole (same model, non-centered
parameterization) --- it's a single scalar unconstrained parameter
either way.

One thing that might be a little more efficient is to define

  eta[n] <- alpha[kk[n]]*theta[jj[n]]- beta[kk[n]];

and then use

  y ~ bernoulli_logit(eta);

instead of the loop.  But that'll only give you a small speedup if
it's even noticeable.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
> On Aug 13, 2015, at 6:51 PM, Daniel Lakeland <dlak...@street-artists.org> wrote:
>
> Stan often spits out warnings about jacobian corrections, and I can't figure out logically whether they're needed for my purposes. Let me give some kind of simple example.

The short answer is that if you need it to define the density,
you need to code it in Stan.  We aren't doing anything differently
than all the stats textbooks out there.

The key is that Stan's density is defined in the model block over
the constrained variables defined in the parameters block.  We handle
all the Jacobians from the unconstrained space, so you only need to
worry about defining a density on the variables defined in the
parameters block.

Each

  a ~ foo(theta)

is equivalent to adding a term foo_log(a, theta) to the log density.

> Suppose I have some data x, and some data y.

>
> i know that if I shift and re-scale x by some unknown amounts, that I can transform the result through some nonlinear transformation, and get y to within some amount of error. For example:
>
> y = exp( (x-a)/b) + error
>
> Suppose I have some other information about a, and b. Either prior, or some kind of measurements that I can relate to a and b.
>
> a ~ normal(a_prior,10);
> b ~ normal(b_prior,10);
> a_data ~ normal(a,1);
> b_data ~ normal(b,1);
>
>
> now I'd like to specify the information I have about the relationship between y and x, i could do.
>
> exp(-(x-a)/b) ~ normal(y,ysigma);
>

This last statement is equivalent to

  y ~ normal(exp((a - x) / b), ysigma);

which is the usual way to write the non-linear regression you provided above.  Written
this way, you shouldn't need a Jacobian.  It depends on what density you want to define.
(I've also eliminated a negation for efficiency.)

The key thing is to understand the density you're defining and make sure
it's the one you want.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Or a way that the original example model could arise:

You have a very fast clock circuit which drives some kind of measurement device. Because the clock is so fast it's hard to know precisely how fast, but you have measurements of brightness at a bunch of time values x given in clock ticks, and for a while after some event (time a) the brightness increases exponentially. Unfortunately it's a noisy brightness measurement and you have gaps in your data.

You know that there exists some time-scale on which you can measure x such that an exponential curve goes right through the data. What you want to know is how bright was it during some gap in your data? You want samples of z=exp((x-a)/b) during the gap and also filtered y values (z samples) for the x values you have y values for.

You don't care about a, or b only samples of z, and that the z samples come in the form exp(-(x-a)/b) for some a,b about which you have only diffuse prior information, and maybe some independent measures, and that the a,b should make z have approximately normal distribution relative to y.

Both, kind of. Stan is automatically doing the needed Jacobians to transform any constrained parameters (declared in parameters block) to the unconstrained space for sampling. It's a matter of which density you're trying to define.

Stan doesn't automatically include any Jacobians other than ones
implied by the constraints on parameters.

> The key thing is to understand the density you're defining and make sure
> it's the one you want.
>
> If I knew that, I wouldn't have to ask!!! :-) Partly, the issue is I'm not entirely sure what Stan does and doesn't do under the hood, so your answer to the above would bring me closer to that understanding.

The manual describes exactly what Stan does under the hood.

In short, it transforms the constrained parameters to be unconstrained
as described in the chapter on transforms near the end of the manual,
and applies the appropriate Jacobian correction so that the priors
are by default all uniform on the *constrained* space.

After that, it's up to you to define the right density on the
constrained parameters.

- Bob

It's not a matter of what you care or don't care about.

If you have a random variable X and some non-linear function
f and say f(X) ~ foo(theta), then you need to account for
the change of variables implied by f.

If you instead have a change of parameterization, and have
a variable Y and a parameter phi and a non-linear function g,
you don't need a Jacobian adjustment to set Y ~ bar(g(phi)).

- Bob

On Thursday, August 13, 2015 at 6:51:26 PM UTC-4, Daniel Lakeland wrote:
> Stan often spits out warnings about jacobian corrections, and I can't figure out logically whether they're needed for my purposes.

The short answer is "If you get a parser warning about a Jacobian correction, you need to do the Jacobian correction unless you are sure that the (logarithm of the absolute value of the) Jacobian determinant in question is a constant". Conversely, if you don't get a parser warning about a Jacobian correction or you are sure that the (logarithm of the absolute value of the) Jacobian determinant in question is a constant, then you don't need to do a Jacobian correction unless you need a normalized log-density for some reason.

Ben

No, they are the same model.  I’m not going to get into a big
diatribe about measures vs densities here, but you’re confusing
some fundamental concepts in probability theory.  Perhaps it
will help you get started if you recognize that the fundamental
object is a measure,

p(x) dx

where p(x) is the density.  If you change parameters then you
get a new density and a new volume, but the measure has to
stay the same,

p(x) dx = p(y) dy

or

p(x) = p(y) | dy / dx | = p(y(x)) | dy/dx (x) |

where | dy/dx (x) | is exactly the Jacobian.

On Thursday, August 13, 2015 at 9:56:24 PM UTC-7, Michael Betancourt wrote:

>  Perhaps it
> will help you get started if you recognize that the fundamental
> object is a measure,
>
> p(x) dx
>
> where p(x) is the density.  If you change parameters then you
> get a new density and a new volume, but the measure has to
> stay the same,
>
> p(x) dx = p(y) dy
>
> or
>
> p(x) = p(y) | dy / dx | = p(y(x)) | dy/dx (x) |
>
> where | dy/dx (x) | is exactly the Jacobian.

If you have a precise mathematical model, and you do a change of parameters, then yes you keep the measure the same this way.

But, I'm not starting with a precise model FOO and doing a change of parameters to model BAR and wanting BAR to have the same mathematical properties as FOO!

I'm starting with a model BAR and expressing it by interchanging the order of arguments in normal_log and wondering why both Bob and Stan think that this means I need to give it a jacobian whereas I don't if I change the order of arguments back!

So, there's two questions I guess. first off, is why does Bob say that

exp((x[i]-a)/b) ~ normal(y,sigmay);

"requires a jacobian correction" but

y[i] ~ normal(exp((x[i]-a)/b),sigmay)

"does not require a jacobian" even though normal_log is symmetric in the first two arguments

Second, when my parameters are invented fictions anyway, let's say rather than a,b we have something like the 2D gaussian process, and I'm going to transform them through some nonlinear transform that's complicated, and I'm going to want to know what the data says about this transformed parameter can't I look at this as if the presence or lack of the jacobian really alters what my prior is over the parameters, but by the way I don't have a "true" prior over the parameters. So the lack of the jacobian doesn't make my model "wrong" per-se it makes it "something that isn't explicit there in the code".

in other words, Stan's message seems to insist that there is a model FOO with which I need to maintain equivalence when such a thing isn't necessarily the case.

As Bob says: it all depends on which density you're trying to compute!

messages.body_plain:
> On Aug 14, 2015, at 2:45 PM, Daniel Lakeland <dlak...@street-artists.org> wrote:

...

> So, there's two questions I guess. first off, is why does Bob say that
>
> exp((x[i]-a)/b) ~ normal(y,sigmay);
>
> "requires a jacobian correction" but
>
> y[i] ~ normal(exp((x[i]-a)/b),sigmay)
>
> "does not require a jacobian" even though normal_log is symmetric in the first two arguments

The sampling notation, as used in Bayesian stats papers, implies
different models, because the ~ is read as describing a generative
process where the right-hand side parameters are known and the left
is generated.

But that is NOT how Stan works.   In Stan, these two expressions produce
identical  results up to names of parameters in error messages.

I'll reiterate that the thing to do is understand how Stan
statements get translated to log densities.

The key here is that

  y ~ foo(theta);

is translated as

  increment_log_prob(foo_log(y, theta));

This is just syntactic sugar other than for the fact that the sampling
notation with ~ drops constant terms.

After that, it's up to you to apply whatever Jacobians you need.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: IRT model help
messages.subject_clean: IRT model help
messages.body_plain:
As I understand it, reflection invariance can be solved by constraining the sign of one of the betas, alphas, or thetas (see Bafumi, Gelman, Park, and Kaplan 2005, 176-179). Probably the most practical solution here is to constrain the sign on an alpha for a bill that you know to be conservative (or liberal). This takes a tiny bit of work in Stan, but it's straightforward enough.

I've simulated a binary item-response model (hopefully this was done correctly), and then coded up the item-response model where the sign on one of the alphas is constrained. Because this is simulated data, I took as the "known" conservative bill the one with the minimum alpha from the simulation. This would have to be set manually in the real-data case, and would be the bill that is most clearly a conservative vote in the data.

One of the problems I see after running this, however, is that some chains get stuck sampling around the "wrong" mode (which has a lower log posterior due to constraining the sign of alpha as it should), but I'm not sure how this can be prevented.

Bob, do you have any suggestions on this?

library(rstan)
library(reshape2) # install.packages("reshape2")
library(shinystan)

n_items <- 30 # Items
n_respondents <- 1000 # Respondents
n_obs <- n_items * n_respondents # Total number of observations

theta  <- rnorm(n_respondents, 0, 1) # Abilities
alpha <- rnorm(n_items, 0, 1) # Discrimination
beta <- rnorm(n_items, 0, 1) # Difficulty

slope.ability <- outer(theta, alpha) # Multiply slope vector by ability vector
intercept <- matrix(rep(beta, n_respondents), nrow = n_respondents, byrow = TRUE)
prob <- plogis(slope.ability - intercept)

D <- data.frame(t(apply(prob, 1, function(x) rbinom(length(x), 1, x))))
names(D) <- 1:ncol(D)
D <- data.frame(respondent = 1:nrow(D), D)

D <- melt(D, id = "respondent", value.name <http://value.name> = "y")
D$issue <- as.numeric(gsub("X", "", D$variable))

# SET CONSTRAINT ON ALPHA
constraint <- rep(0, n_items)
# Here I just use the minimum alpha as the one I constrain,
# but any, say, clear conservative roll call could be used here.
constraint[alpha == min(alpha)] <- 1
constraint[(which(constraint == 1) + 1):length(constraint)] <- 2
# This constraint vector will read something like 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2 ... 2,
# where 1 indicates the constrained alpha, and the 2s are for bookkeeping in the
# transformed parameters block as you can see below

model_data <- list(n_items = length(unique(D$issue)),
                   n_respondents = length(unique(D$respondent)),
                   n_obs = length(D$y),

                   issue = D$issue,
                   respondent = D$respondent,
                   y = D$y,
                   constraint = constraint)

model_code <- "data {
                    int n_items;       // number of items
                    int n_respondents; // number of persons
                    int n_obs;         // number of responses

                    int respondent[n_obs];   // respondent ID
                    int issue[n_obs];        // issue ID
                    int y[n_obs];            // respondent response
                    int constraint[n_items]; // constraint on difficulty
                }

               parameters {
                    vector[n_respondents] theta; // ability

                    vector[n_items-1] alpha_raw;           // discrimination (-1 because excludes constrained alpha)
                    real<upper = 0> alpha_raw_constrained; // constrain sign of the assigned alpha
                    real<lower = 0> mu_alpha;              // discrimination mean
                    real<lower = 0> sigma_alpha;           // discrimination scale

                    vector[n_items] beta;       // difficulty
                    real mu_beta;               // difficulty mean
                    real<lower = 0> sigma_beta; // difficulty scale
                }

                transformed parameters {
                    vector[n_items] alpha;

                    for(i in 1:n_items) {
                        if(constraint[i] == 0) alpha[i] <- alpha_raw[i];
                        if(constraint[i] == 1) alpha[i] <- alpha_raw_constrained;
                        if(constraint[i] == 2) alpha[i] <- alpha_raw[i-1];
                    }
                }

                model {

                    // Hyperparameters
                    mu_alpha ~ cauchy(0, 3);
                    sigma_alpha ~ cauchy(0, 3);

                    mu_beta ~ cauchy(0, 3);
                    sigma_beta ~ cauchy(0, 3);

                    // Priors
                    alpha_raw ~ normal(mu_alpha, sigma_alpha);
                    beta ~ normal(mu_beta, sigma_beta);
                    theta ~ normal(0, 1);

                    // Likelihood
                    for(i in 1:n_obs) {
                       y[i] ~ bernoulli_logit(alpha[issue[i]] * theta[respondent[i]] - beta[issue[i]]);
                    }
                }
                "

# Compile to C
model_irt <- stan_model(model_code = model_code)

# Sample from posterior
options(mc.cores = 6)

# Sample from posterior
posterior_irt <- sampling(model_irt, data = model_data, warmup = 500, iter = 1000,
                          open_progress = FALSE, chains = 6)

launch_shinystan(posterior_irt)

# Plot estimates versus true values of theta (ability)
cor(sapply(extract(posterior_irt, paste0("theta[", 1:n_respondents, "]")), mean), theta)
plot(sapply(extract(posterior_irt, paste0("theta[", 1:n_respondents, "]")), mean), theta)

# Plot estimates versus true values of alpha (discrimination)
cor(sapply(extract(posterior_irt, paste0("alpha[", 1:n_items, "]")), mean), alpha)
plot(sapply(extract(posterior_irt, paste0("alpha[", 1:n_items, "]")), mean), alpha)

# Plot estimates versus true values of beta (difficulty)
cor(sapply(extract(posterior_irt, paste0("beta[", 1:n_items, "]")), mean), beta)
plot(sapply(extract(posterior_irt, paste0("beta[", 1:n_items, "]")), mean), beta)

messages.body_plain:
Multimodality is still an open research issue for both optimization
and MCMC.  So no, I don't have a general solution.  In fact, to have
a proper sample from the posterior, you need to be able to visit all
the modes.  Of course, if one is much lower mass than the others (note
this is not lower density at its local optimum, but lower mass in measure
theoretic terms), then there's usually not too much bias in estimation from
ignoring it.  IF that's the case, then you can initialize around the good
mode or just toss out the chains that are from the very-low-mass mode.
But overall, you need to proceed with extreme caution if the posterior
is multimodal.

Also, this is why we don't believe the people who don't want to run
multiple chains to diagnose convergence because they think one long chain
is enough, because in theory it will explore all the modes.  Another case
where something works in theory, but not in practice.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Jacobian needed?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Jacobian needed?
messages.body_plain:
Bob, thanks for your help here. I coded up my example in R with rstan, and ran the model, I use z as a transformed parameter, a vector. and tried both:

z ~ normal(y,2)

and

y ~ normal(z,2)

and the same random seed, and verified empirically that I get exactly the same samples (once i sort them in order, since rstan seems to randomize the order when it extracts them).

This is as it should be.

Then I sat down and tried to figure out what the stan error message even means. Remember, z is a vector z[i] = exp((x[i]-a)/b).

when I write

y ~ normal(z,2)

Stan is perfectly happy, but

z ~ normal(y,2)

stan spits out the error message:

"Left-hand side of sampling statement (~) may contain a non-linear transform of a parameter or local variable.
If so, you need to call increment_log_prob() with the log absolute determinant of the Jacobian of the transform."

So I sat down to blindly carry out this task just to see what happened... and immediately came up against the fact that the transform takes a,b to a scalar. So the jacobian of the transform is a vector, and the determinant of a vector is not defined.

So, what possible mathematical meaning can this Stan warning message have in this specific context?

I think this topic is important enough that I'd like to offer to write some couple of paragraphs on this topic for the manual, if we can come up with a consensus about what to say for this type of case.

In particular, in my mind I was thinking of this as defining

p(y | a,b,x)

which as Michael Betancourt points out, should be thought of as a measure p(y|a,b,x) dy, but y is an observed value!
However, I wrote it in Stan as if it were:

p(z | y,a,b,x)

in which case it's actually meaningless mathematically, since p(z|a,b,x) = delta_function(z-exp((x-a)/b)) in my model, not what I told stan.

So... should we put something in the manual about it being bad coding practice to write data likelihoods with the unknowns on the left side and the knowns on the right side? And that it will trigger warnings about jacobians, but that they are actually spurious in that case?

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Jacobian needed?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Jacobian needed?
messages.body_plain:
Jacobians are always square matrices when you do changes of variables
because you map N variables to N different variables.  This is just
basic calculus.  See, for example:

  http://mathworld.wolfram.com/ChangeofVariablesTheorem.html

  https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobian_matrix_and_determinant

In the Wikipedia article, look at the change of variables examples 5.2 and 5.3.
I'd point to the change of variables page, but it's all stated in
terms of differentiable manifolds!  The manifold perspective does tell
you why it's always a square matrix, but that's a little further than
we need to go in our manual.

It's too hard (technically impossible given Stan's Turing
completeness) to figure out if a Jacobian adjustment is required.  So
Stan spits out warnings whenever it can't easily deduce that the variable
transform is linear.

Statistics is about treating observations as random!  When we write
a linear regression y[i] = a + b * x[i] + epsilon[i], we're treating
y as if it might have been otherwise given x.  The randomness here is
in the epsilon[i] ~ normal(0, sigma) term.  So it's not about what goes
on the left-hand or right-hand side of a sampling statement.

The key to understanding Stan is this:

  *** the sampling statement in Stan is syntactic shorthand for
      incrementing the log probability ***

That's why a ~ normal(b, c) and b ~ normal(a, c) are synonymous.
We just don't want to flag every increment_log_prob() statement as
needing a Jacobian.

And it's not about data vs. parameters, it's about which density you're
trying to define.  The lognormal is still
the lognormal (which includes a Jacobian adjustment to the normal),
even if all the values are known (outcome, location, and scale).
Same with inverse gamma compared to gamma.

The reason we treat a ~ normal(b, c) differently than b ~ normal(a, c)
even though they compile to the same code is that the interpretation
in conventional Bayesian modeling is different.  We think of the the
variable on the left of the ~ as being generated from the parameters
on the right of the ~.  But this is just convention for writing models
in papers using vague notation.  Or writing models in BUGS, where the
two are actually different in graphical modeling terms because of
the direction of the arrows.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Jacobian needed?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Jacobian needed?
messages.body_plain:
Let me be very, very blunt.  If it’s not obvious why you can
ignore the Jacobian here then you shouldn’t risk it.  Densities
are subtle and vulnerable to abuse — so don’t abuse them!

In general we are trying to construct a probability distribution
which assigns probability to neighborhoods of the target space,
\Omega,

p(A) \in [0, 1] for all A \subset \Omega.

This is a pretty abstract idea, so what we typically do is define a
parameterization of \Omega, i.e we say that \Omega looks like
R^{n} and we select n coordinate functions, x, to specify any point
in \Omega.  Then we can decompose our probability distribution
into a probability density and a Lebesgue measure,

p = p(x) d^{n} x

which can be read as “probability mass equals probability density
times volume”.  The probability of a neighborhood is then given
by

p(A) = \int_{A} p(x) d^{n} x.

Okay, now one of the biggest confusions with densities is that
they’re not unique.  We can choose any other parameterization,
y, to give a different decomposition

p = p(y) d^{n} y
p(A) = \int_{A} p(y) d^{n} y.

Now even though p(x) and p(y) might be very different they
have to be related to each other — in particular the integrals
have to be the same for any neighborhood,

\int_{A} p(x) d^{n} x =  \int_{A} p(y) d^{n} y

which implies that

p(x) d^{n} x = p(y) d^{n} y

or

p(x) = p(y(x)) | d^{n}y / d^{n} x |

where | d^{n}y / d^{n} x | is the Jacobian.  So if you’re given
a distribution for y and you want to know the distribution for
x then you sub in y(x) and add the corresponding Jacobian.

In Stan this manifests whenever we are specifying a prior.

theta ~ distribution_name(hyperparameters)

is fine, but

f(theta) ~ distribution_name(hyperparameters)

is assigning a distribution to f(theta) and requires the Jacobian.

But that would be too easy in of itself.  Because in Bayes Theorem
we specify a posterior with two terms — the prior and the likelihood.
The prior behaves is a density and so behaves as above, but the
likelihood is a different object.  The likelihood is a conditional
probability distribution over data and when we plug in a particular
measurement it’s just a function with respect to the parameters.
That means likelihood terms _don’t_ get Jacobians.

trigger Jacobian warnings

symmetry of the Gaussian density to write

meaning of the ~ notation (which ultimately is allowed only because
the ~ notation is somewhat ill-defined in the first place).  For any
other distribution this switch wouldn’t make sense and not needing
the Jacobian would be obvious.

2)  When specifying priors keep the parameters on the left-hand side.

messages.body_plain:
Thanks, Michael.  I still remember the first time
you explained this to me and the whole Jacobian thing
finally clicked.

For everyone else's benefit:

The data-generating process is complicated a bit
by transforms.  For example, I can generate a lognormal
distributed variable y by generating a normal
variable x ~ normal(0, 1) and defining y = exp(x).   The
other way around is a bit trickier.

In Stan, if y is some positive-constrained data, I can write

  log(y) ~ normal(0, 1)

and that will ensure y gets a lognormal distribution.  But
it might not be for reasons people expect.

If I want to know what the density of y is, as opposed
to log(y), then I need the Jacobian correction to the normal
density.  That is, I want to write

  y ~ lognormal(0, 1),

where

  lognormal(y | 0, 1) = normal(log(y) | 0, 1) * |d/dx log(y)|.

Even if y is "data".  But, when I actually look at the Jacobian,

  |d/dx log(y)| = | 1 / y |,

and recall that y is data, then I can drop the Jacobian because
for MCMC and optimization, we only need to definine the density up
to a proportion.  At least that's my understanding of why we can get
away with writing just

  log(y) ~ normal(0, 1)

instead of

  y ~ lognormal(0, 1).

In Stan, if I write y ~ lognormal(0, 1), what will happen under
the hood is that the constant term will get dropped because we
don't need it for optimization or MCMC.

- Bob

P.S.  Could you teach a probability theory class I can attend?
And maybe use that awesome math writing style from Baez's intro
to manifolds in his knots and gauge theory book?  I've never taken a
probability or stats class, but the problem I find with books I've
perused on the topic is that they lose the forest for the trees.
Or maybe I'll just take the Gelman approach and draft such a book
myself, put your name on it, and let you correct all my misconceptions.

> 3)  When specifying likelihoods keep the data on the left-hand side
>     and parameters on the right-hand side.

> But that would be too easy in of itself.  Because in Bayes Theorem
> we specify a posterior with two terms — the prior and the likelihood.
> The prior behaves is a density and so behaves as above, but the
> likelihood is a different object.  The likelihood is a conditional
> probability distribution over data and when we plug in a particular
> measurement it’s just a function with respect to the parameters.
> That means likelihood terms _don’t_ get Jacobians.
>

Right, the data is fixed, there are no neighborhoods involved. Likelihoods are actually weird objects, because we talk about them like they're probabilities, but before you see the data, the probability that you'll get that exact data is 0 (assuming continuous distributions).

> Usually this is pretty clear, because by definition likelihoods define
> how the data are sampled and we’d always write
>
> data ~ distribution_name(theta, hyperparameters).
>
> Because theta is on the right-hand side writing
>
> data ~ distribution_name(f(theta), hyperparameters)
>
> wouldn’t throw a Jacobian warning.  Similarly, because data don’t
> trigger Jacobian warnings
>
> f(data) ~ distribution_name(theta, hyperparameters)
>
> would also be fine.
>
> What’s happening here is that Daniel Lakeland is abusing the
> symmetry of the Gaussian density to write
>
> data ~ normal(f(theta), hyperparameters)
>
> as
>
> f(theta) ~ normal(data, hyperparameters)
>
> The latter doesn’t really make sense and abuses the intended
> meaning of the ~ notation (which ultimately is allowed only because
> the ~ notation is somewhat ill-defined in the first place).  For any
> other distribution this switch wouldn’t make sense and not needing
> the Jacobian would be obvious.
>

Note, I wasn't TRYING to abuse the notation, I simply had a different view of what that notation means than you guys and that's not too surprising given that ~ is a pretty vague concept in the literature.

My thought was: "if I correct this data in a certain way, it will be equal to the expression for the error term, and then I want that corrected data to be a normal(0,sigma) random variable"

That is, I was doing a nonlinear regression by saying in my head:  y - myfunction(x,a,b) = epsilon

and was shocked that Stan would be telling me to change my model, and then when I thought about it, the request for a jacobian wasn't even a well defined request.

Also note, I got the idea that this was a reasonable way to write Stan code (with regression predictions on the left side of the ~) from some examples that Andrew Gelman wrote on his blog!!!

> On Aug 16, 2015, at 11:19 PM, Daniel Lakeland <dlak...@street-artists.org> wrote:

> Right, the data is fixed, there are no neighborhoods involved. Likelihoods are actually weird objects, because we talk about them like they're probabilities,

It's a common misconception, but nobody should be talking about densities as
if they're probabilities --- they're not even constrained to be less than 1!
Probability theory and math stats books are very careful to distinguish
event probabilities from densities.  There's even a different notation with a
capital "P" (or "Pr") for event probabilities.

> but before you see the data, the probability that you'll get that exact data is 0 (assuming continuous distributions).

The trick to doing stats is that even after we see the data, we treat it
as if it might have been different.

...

> I simply had a different view of what that notation means than you guys and that's not too surprising given that ~ is a pretty vague concept in the literature.

It's very precisely defined in Stan.  When you write

  y ~ foo(theta);

what happens is that it's equivalent to writing

  increment_log_prob(foo_log(y, theta));

with the exception that the ~ notation drops constant terms.

Writing

  y ~ normal(mu, sigma);

where y is data and mu and sigma are parameters produces the exact
same effect as:

  increment_log_prob(-0.5 * ((y - mu) / sigma)^2 - log(sigma))

where we drop that pesky sqrt(2 * pi) term.  If I write

  beta ~ normal(0, 1 / sqrt(2));

then I get the exact same behavior as writing

  increment_log_prob(-y^2);

Stan only cares about the density defined on the parameters up to
a proportion.  Everything else follows from that.

> My thought was: "if I correct this data in a certain way, it will be equal to the expression for the error term, and then I want that corrected data to be a normal(0,sigma) random variable"
>
> That is, I was doing a nonlinear regression by saying in my head:  y - myfunction(x,a,b) = epsilon
>
> and was shocked that Stan would be telling me to change my model, and then when I thought about it, the request for a jacobian wasn't even a well defined request.
>
> Also note, I got the idea that this was a reasonable way to write Stan code (with regression predictions on the left side of the ~) from some examples that Andrew Gelman wrote on his blog!!!

I'll insert an editorial note into the blog post if you remember where
it is.

I do love Andrew and Jennifer's book in part because they provide great
translation keys.

- Bob

1) generate truth, myfunction(x,a,b)
2) generate noise, epsilon ~ normal(0, sigma)
3) generate measurement, y = myfunction(x,a,b) + epsilon

Hence

y = myfunction(x,a,b) + epsilon
y ~ normal(myfunction(x,a,b), sigma)

On the other hand,

myfunction(x,a,b) ~ normal(y, sigma)

is not generative!  You can write it down, but it’s certainly
not a likelihood contribution in general and potentially
dangerous, hence the warning.

messages.subject: Re: estimating the variability of the Colorado growth model
messages.subject_clean: estimating the variability of the Colorado growth model
messages.body_plain:
Just a quick followup:

After realizing how difficult the prediction problem is, I decided to retreat a simpler problem.  Given the ability parameter theta in the IRT model, the conditional distribution of scores for the student should be determined independently of any previous test results.  "Growth" can be calculated from this conditional distribution as 100*F(x-1) where F is the conditional CDF.  The Colorado model attempts to determine this approximately with quantile regression.

So I did two simulations with STAN,
1)  Use a betabinomial model and compute the "growth" from the (analytic) posteriors
2)  Construct a STAN model corresponding to the MCAS, which is a mixture of 2PL, 3PL, and polytomous items, using informative normal priors for the IRT parameters (the standardization process produces estimates of the mean and standard deviation of each parameter).  Generate scaled scores and use their sampling distribution to estimate 100*F(x-1) for each possible score.

I used the samples generated from the betabinomial as input to the SGP package, and found that the SGP results generally match  the theoretical value of 100*F(x-1).  I was also able to compute expected values, standard deviations, and credible intervals for "growth".

On Sunday, August 2, 2015 at 10:05:56 AM UTC-4, Eugene Quinn wrote:
> Hello,
>
> I'm working on a project to estimate the variability of "growth" measures in education, specifically the Colorado model, which uses quantile regression to estimate the conditional distribution of the most current test results for a student given between 1 and 4 years of prior test scores.  The growth score is presented as a point estimate with no indication of its variability.
>
> I want to use a Bayesian model with an IRT model with known parameters as the data generating process to estimate the conditional distribution of the most recent score given the scores from previous years, and using it to compute the "growth" score and its variability, where the "growth" score is defined as 100 times the sum of the conditional probabilities of all possible scores that are lower than the student's actual score.
>
> I have a STAN model that seems to work pretty well with two years of data and I'm interested in any suggestions on how to go about incorporating more than two years of data.  Each year will have a different IRT model, and I'd like to tie them together to get a single posterior predictive distribution for the most current year.
>
> In the two year case, I did this by providing only a single ability parameter value for each student that applies to both years (I'm using a 1PL model and the difficulty values vary from year to year).  I'm wondering if there is a better way to do this.
>
> Best regards,
>
> Gene Quinn
>
> code is on github https://github.com/equinn1/STAN.   growth.pdf contains background information on the project.

Hello again,

Thanks! I have resolved my issue. The problem lied within my templated pointer declaration.
Just for the future reference, here is a full example of the code that allows to reproduce the correct
solution. I have tested it on a 'clean' version of CmdStan-2.7.0 after performing the following steps.

1) Replace the file cmdstan-2.7.0/stan/src/stan/lang/function_signatures.h with the provided file.
(The file was changed as follows: the lines
"""
// MWE_DIR__MY_SQUARE_HPP functions
add("my_square", DOUBLE_T, DOUBLE_T);
add("my_square_ptr_wrapper", DOUBLE_T, DOUBLE_T);

"""
were added in the beginning of the file.)

2) Replace the file cmdstan-2.7.0/stan/lib/stan_math_2.7.0/stan/math.hpp with the provided file.
(The file was changed as follows: the lines
"""

//      lib stan cmdstan-2.7.0
#include <../../../mwe_dir/my_square.hpp>
"""
were added to the end of the file.)

3) Create the folder called 'mwe_dir' in the CmdStan-2.7.0 directory.
Copy the files 'my_square.hpp' and '*.stan' to this directory. The
'*.stan' files can be compiled and seem to sample correctly
(tested with clang-3.4, c++11).

Best regards,
Arseniy.

Can I ask why the code has function pointers and global variables?
Was this just a proof-of-concept for something trickier?

If all you need to do is define this

  https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relativistic_Breit–Wigner_distribution

any performance gains from doing it in C++ unless you define
analytic gradients (and you'd get another performance gain from
vectorization).  It shouldn't require any pointers at all in
the definition other than the vari instance inside the returned var.

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

when trying to change the target acceptance probability/statistic/rate in rstan I first had to look up that the name of the acceptance rate parameter "delta" in the cmdstan manual.
Maybe it is possible to add a brief description of sampler parameters with non-selfexplanatory names also to rstan?
E.g.
...
2. adapt_gamma, the regularization scale during adaptation (double, positive, defaults to 0.05)
3. adapt_delta, the target acceptance statistic during adaptation (double, between 0 and 1, defaults to 0.8)
4. adapt_kappa, the relaxation exponent during adaptation (double, positive, defaults to 0.75)
...

In the same vein one could give the name of the control parameter in shiny stan.
E.g:
...  By setting the target acceptance parameter to a value closer to [e.g. with rstan stan(...,control = list(adapt_delta = .9))] ....

Alternatively one could add a warning like "Read sections 7.4 in the cmdstan manual and  section 54 of the stan reference before changing sampler parameters ..." to the rstan manual and shinystan ... :-)

I also found that the default delta is said to be .8 on page 40 of the cmdstan manual but .65 on page 54 of the same manual.
It probably should also be .8 on page 54.

Guido

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob,

thanks, but this is merely a proof-of-concept for more generic class of
functions suited to partial wave analysis (PWA) of heavy meson decay.
It requires complex variables and various other components.
(See, e.g., http://arxiv.org/abs/1406.6311, Chapter 13. Among others, multiple
formulas similar to 13.2.2 and factors therein are necessary.)

Initially, I started with Stan implementation of the aforementioned functions,
however, the *.stan files quickly outgrew several hundred lines and became
completely unreadable. Rather than writing in Stan, it seemed simpler to implement
all the low-level pieces of the analysis in C++. Another reason to instantiate
partial waves in C++ is versatility: it becomes easier to cross-check the results
with existing PWA modules such as ComPWA, RootPWA, and others.

Returning back to the motivation of my question. Pointers seem to be quite
useful to gather various functions with the same input/output (complex-valued
functions describing partial wave amplitudes) to one vector-valued function.
(Just as a point of interest: the same linker problem I have encountered arises
when invoking virtual functions for some templated base class.)

Current version of the code and some documentation may be found at
https://github.com/atsipenyuk/mdeca and partly on
https://github.com/atsipenyuk/stan_pwa (migration to the latter is in progress).
Right now I am performing many changes in order to improve the overall
quality and readability of the project. I will be glad to provide a link to the
stable version when I get so far.

Best regards,
Arseniy.
