messages.body_plain:
On Sunday, August 16, 2015 at 8:58:26 PM UTC-7, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
> > On Aug 16, 2015, at 11:19 PM, Daniel Lakeland <dlak...@street-artists.org> wrote:
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > But that would be too easy in of itself.  Because in Bayes Theorem
> > we specify a posterior with two terms — the prior and the likelihood.
> > The prior behaves is a density and so behaves as above, but the
> > likelihood is a different object.  The likelihood is a conditional
> > probability distribution over data and when we plug in a particular
> > measurement it’s just a function with respect to the parameters.
> > That means likelihood terms _don’t_ get Jacobians.
> >
> >
> > Right, the data is fixed, there are no neighborhoods involved. Likelihoods are actually weird objects, because we talk about them like they're probabilities,
>
> It's a common misconception, but nobody should be talking about densities as
> if they're probabilities --- they're not even constrained to be less than 1!
> Probability theory and math stats books are very careful to distinguish
> event probabilities from densities.  There's even a different notation with a
> capital "P" (or "Pr") for event probabilities.

I wasn't referring to the difference between a density and a probability so much, more that even if you multiply by a fixed differential of the outcome space to get a probability, you evaluate this AT the points where the data fell, these points never change. After plugging in the data, the whole thing becomes a function only of the parameters!

Now that we've been through this discussion, I see the thing that was so confusing to me about Stan's warning was that I was thinking of my line of code as providing likelihood information, but Stan was telling me to alter my likelihood, in other words, alter my model of the world! But I realize now that it was because I was using the Stan notation in a way Stan doesn't really expect.

Before plugging in the data values, you can think of the function as a probability distribution over the data, but it doesn't represent the probability of the actual data obviously, it represents your knowledge of what the data would be conditional only on the parameter values and the structure of your model. Thinking of this as the data "could have been different" is sort of a fundamentally frequentist way of thinking about the data. The sort of philosophically Bayesian viewpoint is that before seeing the data the likelihood can be thought of as a probability distribution describing your information about where the data will lie, conditional on the parameter value. After seeing the data, it's a sort of anchor or tilt on the probability of the parameters since it's purely a function of the parameters.

> I simply had a different view of what that notation means than you guys and that's not too surprising given that ~ is a pretty vague concept in the literature.

It's very precisely defined in Stan.  When you write

  y ~ foo(theta);

what happens is that it's equivalent to writing

  increment_log_prob(foo_log(y, theta));

with the exception that the ~ notation drops constant terms.

Yes, so this makes my model mathematically correct (I would get the mathematical results I wanted). But it seems clear from Michael's posts and the warning messages, that the ~ notation is intended to be thought of in a "generative modeling" manner, and that if you use this notation in another way you may get warnings which don't make sense, and you may confuse other people when they go to read your stan code. So from now on, I'll put my data on the left and functions of parameters and data on the right. Note that when the density isn't symmetric in the first two arguments you HAVE to do that anyway, otherwise you probably won't get the results you want.

My comments above about nonlinear transforms of the parameters should be taken in that light, it's perfectly fine to take some parameters, put them through some nonlinear function, and use that as predictions of the data, without somehow "correcting for" the nonlinearity in the transform, because in that process you're constructing a likelihood, you're describing what you think the "truth" is in Michaels terminology. But if you write that as:

foofunction(data,params) ~ distribution(data,other,parameters)

even if this is mathematically equivalent to:

data ~ distribution(foofunction(data,params),other,params)

you will get Stan warnings about the nonlinear foofunction because Stan doesn't expect you to use ~ in that way. Best to just use the software in the way it was intended I think.

> Also note, I got the idea that this was a reasonable way to write Stan code (with regression predictions on the left side of the ~) from some examples that Andrew Gelman wrote on his blog!!!

I'll insert an editorial note into the blog post if you remember where it is.

I don't remember, but I think it was one of those "how tall is...." posts. You may have even had some editorial remarks already now that I think about it.

That's what I figured --- thanks for confirming.

> Initially, I started with Stan implementation of the aforementioned functions,
> however, the *.stan files quickly outgrew several hundred lines and became

> with existing PWA modules such as ComPWA, RootPWA, and others.

Stan's not really set up for easy testing, which for me is a dealbreaker
for anything other than simple code.  There's a way to unit test functions
in Stan through R, but not through any of the other interfaces I know of.

> Returning back to the motivation of my question. Pointers seem to be quite
> useful to gather various functions with the same input/output (complex-valued
> functions describing partial wave amplitudes) to one vector-valued function.
> (Just as a point of interest: the same linker problem I have encountered arises

a very good description of this in both the Vandevoorde and Josuttis
book and the Alexandrescu C++ books.  It's also the way to interface with
the standard <algorithm> library built into C++ and there's even more support
in C++11 for binding and more general lambda abstracts (allowing functional programming
idioms), but we haven't gotten there yet with Stan because Python and R support
is lagging.

messages.body_plain:
Here are examples for "good" and "bad" initialisation values, where "bad" means that lots of RAM is consumed when using these values.
I replicated the issue on a mac now, so it is  not windows specific.

For the example below I found that fitting with bad initialisation values lead to a consumption of around 3800mb, whereas good initialisation values used around 900mb. At first I thought that the problem could be caused by inits close to the boundaries of constrained parameters. but I am not sure.

To replicate my results on a mac you can do the following in R (session info at the end of the email):

load("wiener_test_data.Rdata") # data attached to the first mail in this thread
m = stan_model(file = "stan_wiener_test2.stan") # stan file attached to the first mail in this thread

bad_inits = list(delta = c(-0.7987087, 1.302651, 0.420765, 0.2789249),
                 alpha = c(1.271243, 7.667402, 1.437398, 2.138264),
                 beta  = c(0.4081320, 0.5393007, 0.7897648, 0.8449466),
                 tau   = c(0.1105052, 0.1264254, 0.1413274, 0.1196919))

get_mem = function() {as.numeric(sub("M","",strsplit(system("top -l 1 | head -n 10 | grep PhysMem",intern = T)," ")[[1]][2]))}

mem_before_fit = get_mem()
fit_inits = sampling(m,data = stan_data,iter = 400,seed = 1234,
                     chains = 1, init = list(bad_inits))
consumed_memory = get_mem()-mem_before_fit
consumed_memory

then close the R session, open a new session (or simply Session-> Restart R in RStudio)
and repeat the code above with good initialisation inits:

good_inits = list(delta = c(0, 0, 0, 0),
                  beta  = c(.5, .5, .5, .5),
                  alpha = c(1, 1, 1, 1),
                  tau   = c(.11, .11, .11, .11))

Guido

Thanks for following up.

That's not unexpected --- there's an underlying iterative algorithm
and we're autodiffing through it, which means the memory is going to
be proportional to the number of iterations run.  You might be able
to mitigate some of that problem by starting with a smaller initial
step size.  Now if we could get analytic gradients, the memory wouldn't
be so bad.  So if anyone knows how to do that (even if the gradients
themselves are an iterative algorithm), it'd really help.

We've been doing that gradually with matrix operations and distributions.
The next release is going to hugely reduce the memory required to do
a Cholesky factorization, for example.

- Bob

Thanks for following up. I wasn't sure how much detail to give about the other pieces of the model that weren't directly related to my question.

RTCWT is a 0/1 indicator for the type of program. The outcome measure is a scale that is forced to be between -256 and 256. The coed variable is also a 0/1 indicator. (0 = not coed, 1 = coed)

I tried using int declarations for these, but then I could't use them in the model. It's been a few weeks, but as I recall, multiplying things together threw errors when some of the pieces were real and some were integer.

The key problem is that I want the b parameter to be modeled for the coed programs (when coed = 1) and not for programs that are single-sex (coed = 0). This makes sense because you can't compute a slope between males and females for programs that don't have both males and females.

But these are parameter declarations with names like slope and intercept.
That won't force the outcome to be between -256 and 256 --- the way to
do that is push it through a scaled tanh (or scaled and translated inverse
logit) link function.

> The coed variable is also a 0/1 indicator. (0 = not coed, 1 = coed)
>
> I tried using int declarations for these, but then I could't use them in the model. It's been a few weeks, but as I recall, multiplying things together threw errors when some of the pieces were real and some were integer.

That shouldn't happen.  If you run across a reproducible case
of this, please let us know because it'd be a bug.  All int
values should be promoted to real anywhere in Stan.   The exception
to this general rule is arrays of ints won't get promoted to arrays
of reals, and you can't multiply arrays, only vectors and matrices.

Now where you have RWCT, you need to make that a vector to allow
multiplication, but it's not being used as a conditional indicator.
It's more efficient to do this:

if (coed[j] && RTWCT[j])
  b[j] ~ normal(g_b_int + gb_slope, sigma_b);
else if (coed[j])
  b[j] ~ normal(gb_int, sigma_b);
else
  b[j] <- 0;

But you have to code it be careful because you can't literally do that
assignment.

> if (coed[j] == 1) {
> >       b[j] ~ normal(g_b_int + g_b_slope * RTCWT[j], sigma_b);
> >     } else {
> >       b = 0;  ??????????????
>     }

  if (RTWCT[j]))
    b[j] ~ normal(g_b_int + g_b_slope, sigma_b);
  else

> The key problem is that I want the b parameter to be modeled for the coed programs (when coed = 1) and not for programs that are single-sex (coed = 0). This makes sense because you can't compute a slope between males and females for programs that don't have both males and females.

If you really want to do this (I still don't understand what's going
on in the model), then you need to set b[j] = 0, not b = 0 (which shouldn't
even compile).  But you can't assign to a parameter, so it won't work.

Instead, you need to do the more efficient thing and preprocess the
data (you can do this in transformed data) to create a vector of coefficients
just for the coed programs.

And given what you're doing, you don't want to do this b[prog[i]] * coed[prog[i]]
because you know coed[j] = 0 implies b[j] = 0, so it's just a wasted
expression evaluation and derivative calculation.

messages.subject: RStan freezes for scenario with extremely narrow parameter distributions
messages.subject_clean: RStan freezes for scenario with extremely narrow parameter distributions
messages.body_plain:
Dear Stan users,

as part of my research, I am comparing the results of a Bayesian ODE-based model implemented in RStan to the results of a Bayesian Markov model. I am investigating different scenarios with varying levels of parameter uncertainty. For a scenario including "realistic" parameter ranges, I could run my model without any problems. However, if I include extremely narrow distributions of the model parameters, RStan first compiles the code to C++, but freezes afterwards. The distributions are so narrow that the parameters are almost deterministic. The idea behind this unrealistic scenario is to make it comparable to a deterministic ODE-based model since ODE-based models in the literature are mainly deterministic. Do you think these narrow parameter distributions could influence the performance of Stan? Also, my model includes an ODE system consisting of 20 equations including dynamic interactions, could this be a problem? If I reduce the number of equations to 5, the performance of RStan is ok.

I am attaching the model code.

I would appreciate your help very much.

All the best,

Katrin

messages.subject_clean: Logistic regression: fitting many individual regressions in a single model
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

We are trying to fit a lot of individual logistic regression models in one go using Stan (the idea is to later add some hierarchical structure to avoid multiple testing artefacts). We are, however, running into a very serious problem, a small subset of the data (<5%, ~250k points) is taking up 19GB of RAM, regardless of using the mcmc or variational approach in cmdstan. We are not really sure why the model takes up so much memory, especially because the subset of data on disk only takes up 193MB. We are not really concerned with speed (yet), but have tried to optimise to use the least amount of memory. If we can ever get the full model with all the data to fit into memory, we will worry about speed.

The idea behind the study is there are a number of events, D, and a number of datapoints, N (in the subsetted data I am using D=255 and N= ~280k). At each data point, there is an event y (the predicted value), which takes on a discrete value from 1-255. The same event may happen at multiple data points. The idea is to model each event individually. I.e. loop over the set of unique events, setting y=1 and y=0 accordingly for each data point.

Any pointers or tips on why it is using so much memory would be much appreciated!

I have attached a Stan script of the model. The models were built and run using the latest version of cmdstan-2.7.0.

Thanks in advance,
David

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Logistic regression: fitting many individual regressions in a single model
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Logistic regression: fitting many individual regressions in a single model
messages.body_plain:
It's the loop in your model.

You have a D x N loop, so that's 255 * 280K = 71 million iterations, each of which
then creates an expression for theta_hat and for the bernoulli_logit that's going
to suck up lots of memory.  It's basically 40 bytes or so per binary subexpression in
the model and you get around 5 per iteration, for another 200 bytes * 71 million
= 14 GB.  The 19GB is almost certainly because we allocate in blocks, rather than
a byte at a time in order to ensure it only takes logarithmic time.

You could save a bit of space by turning (beta_age * age) into a dot-product and
by defining a vector of theta_hat[n] and then vectorizing bernoulli_logit, but it's
still going to take a lot of memory.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] how could I possibly hierarchically code 'ordered logistic' regression with Matt Trick?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] how could I possibly hierarchically code 'ordered logistic' regression with Matt Trick?
messages.body_plain:
I mean rather than coding the cut points as independent regressions,
code the increment past the previous cut point by exp()-transforming it.

  cut[1] <- 0;
  for (c in 2:C)
    cut[c] <- cut[c-1] + exp(...some predictor...);

Or you can have the first cutpoint be unconstrained.  You can use
the non-centered parameterization for the coefficients in the predictor
if you want.

Then you know the sequence cut is increasing.  It's a different model
that's been discussed on the list before --- I can't recall what it's
called in the literature.  I was surprised that pieces of the literature
try to do what you're doing as it makes the model ill-posed.  That is,
the support is restricted to where all the constraints are satisfied,
which itself is data-dependent and can't be easily normalized (not that
we need normalized densities for optimization or MCMC).

- Bob

Just because there are no boys in girl programs or girls in boy programs doesn't mean there isn't some kind of theoretical reason to consider b_boy and b_girl for each program. You'll just get the prior as the posterior when there's no data, but if you include any other prediction model for b_boy and b_girl based on other aspects of the programs for example, you could actually figure out some small amount of evidence for a kind of hypothetical "what if we put girls in this boy only program" etc.

anyway, you could do:

y[i] ~ normal(a[prog[i]] + if_else(coed[i]==0,0,if_else(sex[i] == 1, b_boy[prog[i]], b_girl[prog[i]])), sigma_y);

or something similar.

another alternative:

randomly select 20 event types and 1 million relevant data points or something like that, get the posterior distribution of the parameters from this reduced set of observations. Then fit a parametric prior for the parameters, and use it repeatedly in 1200 regressions on the remaining 79 million data points?

The point being to reduce the chance of over-fitting by gleaning some information from a subset of the data which is then used as an informed prior to regularize the individual fits to some extent. It's not as clean as the full heirarchical bayes, but it's actually do-able, so there's that going for it.

messages.body_plain:
You don't define any actual priors over the sigmas, I assume that'd go a long way towards preventing the blow-up. Can't you at least get an order-of-magnitude guess of what sigma should be?

Also, you could break out the sigmas into sigma_b_boy, sigma_b_girl, sigma_b_coed.

or just take the empirical sigma of the posterior samples for b values for coed programs only?

All the blowup is telling you is that when you pool together the coed and the non-identifiable b values, you have a lot of variation, but the variation in the identifiable b values should be a lot smaller, hence the sigma of posterior samples for those b values should be empirically smaller.

I recommend moderately informative priors all around.

If the point is to compare how well the full uncertain model fits compared to how the ODE system behaves when the parameters are close to particular values, instead of running two stan models one with realistic priors, and one with extremely tight priors, you might just be able to give realistic priors for your coefficients, and then subset the posterior samples by the ones that are close to your values of interest and see how well they fit compared to the full set.

If you want to ensure you sample in those regions, you could always just use the generated quantities block to sample from those narrow priors and generate the y values you need. (assuming integrate_ode works in generated quantities, which I haven't checked).

messages.body_plain:
Stan assumes support on the constrained parameter space.  That
is, everywhere the parameter meets its constraints, it should
have density > 0.

If that is violated, then multiple things might happen.  In the
best case, you'll init near the solution and the sampler won't
move near the boundaries.  If you had a big vector of y ~ uniform(-1,1)
and used our random inits, you're very unlikely to be able to move.

Michael will have to weigh in on what happens with bias in cases
where things run without crashing or getting stuck.

- Bob

On Friday, August 21, 2015 at 2:45:55 PM UTC-7, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Bob:  No, I don’t think your model is correct.  Rounding to 2 decimal places is not the same as adding independent uniform(-.005,.005) errors.  In practice, the two approaches might give similar results—and I’m pretty sure Bob’s will run faster, as it doesn’t require normal cdfs—but it’s not the same model.  I guess if anyone wanted, they could run a simulation study to see if the two approaches are the same in practice.
> A
>

It's not (necessarily, obviously) the same model, but I wouldn't say it "isn't correct".

we have p, the unknown proportion, and y, the observed, rounded value. Given that y is rounded, we know that it can't be more than 0.005 away from y_true, which is unobserved.

so:

ydelta ~ uniform(-0.005, 0.005); // specifies prior information for an unobserved parameter, the distance from the rounded data to the actual value

y_true <- y + ydelta;

y_true ~ normal(foo,bar); // the jacobian warning will show up here, since y_true is a transformed parameter

however, because of the normal distribution's symmetry, this can be rewritten:

y ~ normal(foo - ydelta,bar); // this doesn't trigger the jacobian warning and looks more like a likelihood

this whole thing works really because the normal density is determined by the difference between two values, or looked at another way because it's symmetric between the first and second argument. We had a big discussion on this that I started recently (see post about jacobian errors).

so, another way to look at this model is where we assume a prior for the rounding error to be uniform, and do inference on the posterior of the true value under that assumption. You could actually work with other priors, but if you know only that the rounding error is inside an interval, the uniform prior is the maximum entropy one.

Bob:

Hi, see the solution to exercise 3.5b here:
http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/book/solutions3.pdf

The point is that, in rounded data, the “generative model” is to start with the underying quantity (the “true measurment”) and then round it.  Your model is different.

One way to see this is to imagine running your model in a “forward simulation”:  It just doesn’t work.  Where does y_obs get created?  Another way to put it is that your model is what’s called a quasi-likelihood: it’s a frunction that looks like a likelihood and can be used in a posterior-like caculation but does not come from a generative model.

> I'm pretty sure we don't want to put a truncation on the y sampling statement
> here.  Or are you saying we should use something other than a uniform rounding
> error for your z (my y_err)?
>
> Or are you talking about adding some measurement error model on top of the
> rounding error and on top of the regression error sigma_y?   In that case,
> don't you want to allow z to range further?
>
> Of course, I'm probably just missing something fundamental in either the problem
> or your proposed answer.
>
> Could you write out a longer example of what you intend with the full model
> including truncation?    I can put it in the manual as an example when I understand
> it.  I don't see what kind of error model would make sense for y_err given that there
> is a range of measurments.
>
> - Bob
>

Bob, I'm pretty sure Andrew is saying that the rounding means that whatever your model is for the "true" measurement error, the fact that it's rounded means that conditional on the observed value, you have to use a truncated form of your measurement error distribution, truncated to the region that makes sense given the rounding.

if y is observed, and y_err is a measurement error, and you have a model for your measurement error

y_err ~ foodistrib(a,b,c,d,e)

then consistent with the information we have, we have to truncate this prior to the region y-0.005 to y+0.005

in pseudocode, since I am not sure how stan does truncation:

y_err ~ foodistrib(a,b,c,d,e) Truncated_to(y-0.005,y+0.005)

This, more or less, provides a mixture of likelihood and prior information, and I think it more or less is equivalent to Michael Betancourt's model. I think it's a bit ... awkward. and the justification for my model above, using maximum entropy priors on an unobserved rounding error seems more, at least understandable.

messages.body_plain:
I take it back. It looks like what Andrew and Michael are proposing is to actually discretize the likelihood model on the grid of possible rounded outcomes, and then calculate a likelihood as a probability to get the actual discrete y_obs value. Is that fair to say?

I don't think this discrete model is a problem for Stan to sample since it's in the likelihood, and it's still a continuous function of the parameters.

Still, I think the motivation for my model involving a uniform prior on the rounding portion of the error also logically holds, it doesn't ONLY hold when the data were sampled uniformly, since the posterior for the y_err values need not be uniform!

In my/bob's case, you're writing the likelihood:

y ~ normal(y_true + y_roundoff_error, sigma) where y_true and y_roundoff_error are BOTH parameters, only ONE of which has a uniform prior.

in other words, the rounding part is an additional, unobserved quantity, with a maximum entropy prior.

if your model for y_true happens to predict y to within much smaller variation than the uniform on y_roundoff_error, then the posterior on y_roundoff_error will be sharply peaked around 0, more sharply than the uniform prior.

messages.body_plain:
OK, here's the result of coding Andrew's approach and my approach
(which I believe is the same as Daniel Lakeland's modulo the Stan
coding), for the BDA3 exercise 3.5.  I have some questions below
about fitting the measurement error as a parameter and the relation to cut.

For those without BDA3, the problem Andrew's referring to is this,
without the extra bits:

Question
--------
  3.5 ... Suppose we weigh an object five times and
  measure weights, rounded to the nearest pound, of 10, 10, 12,
  11, 9.  Assume the unrounded measurements are normally distributed
  with a noninformative prior distribution on mu and sigma^2.

  b) Give the correct posterior distribution for (mu, sigma^2)
     treating the measurements as rounded.

Answer
------
Andrew's answer from his answer key corresponds to the following Stan model:

transformed data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  vector[5] y;
  N <- 5;
  y[1] <- 10;
  y[2] <- 10;
  y[3] <- 12;
  y[4] <- 11;
  y[5] <- 9;
}
parameters {
  real mu;
  real<lower=0> sigma_sq;
}
transformed parameters {
  real<lower=0> sigma;
  sigma <- sqrt(sigma_sq);
}
model {
  increment_log_prob(-2 * log(sigma));
  for (n in 1:N)
    increment_log_prob(log(Phi((y[n] + 0.5 - mu) / sigma)
                           - Phi((y[n] - 0.5 - mu) / sigma)));
}

What I was proposing corresponds to this model:

transformed data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  vector[5] y;
  N <- 5;
  y[1] <- 10;
  y[2] <- 10;
  y[3] <- 12;
  y[4] <- 11;
  y[5] <- 9;
}
parameters {
  real mu;
  real<lower=0> sigma_sq;
  vector<lower=-0.5, upper=0.5>[5] y_err;
}
transformed parameters {
  real<lower=0> sigma;
  sigma <- sqrt(sigma_sq);
}
model {
  increment_log_prob(-2 * log(sigma));
  for (n in 1:N)
    (y + y_err) ~ normal(mu, sigma);
}

Here's what Stan says.

Andrew's model:

          mean se_mean   sd   2.5%   25%   50%   75% 97.5% n_eff Rhat
mu       10.35    0.02 0.65   8.87 10.00 10.37 10.75 11.56  1086 1.00
sigma_sq  2.35    0.17 4.47   0.39  0.84  1.38  2.47  9.37   657 1.00
sigma     1.35    0.03 0.72   0.63  0.92  1.17  1.57  3.06   739 1.01
lp__     -8.36    0.04 1.16 -11.55 -8.78 -8.01 -7.54 -7.22   685 1.00

My model:

           mean se_mean   sd   2.5%    25%    50%    75%  97.5% n_eff Rhat
mu        10.42    0.00 0.19  10.06  10.30  10.42  10.55  10.79  2324    1
sigma_sq   0.63    0.01 0.23   0.32   0.47   0.59   0.75   1.20  2099    1
y_err[1]   0.19    0.00 0.23  -0.35   0.05   0.24   0.38   0.49  2740    1
y_err[2]   0.19    0.00 0.23  -0.36   0.06   0.23   0.37   0.49  2755    1
y_err[3]  -0.40    0.00 0.11  -0.50  -0.47  -0.43  -0.36  -0.09  2694    1
y_err[4]  -0.24    0.00 0.21  -0.49  -0.41  -0.29  -0.13   0.27  2874    1
y_err[5]   0.39    0.00 0.12   0.07   0.34   0.42   0.47   0.50  2593    1
sigma      0.79    0.00 0.14   0.57   0.69   0.77   0.87   1.09  2110    1
lp__     -18.36    0.07 2.23 -23.66 -19.61 -18.02 -16.74 -15.12  1096    1

So yes, definitely different answers, which is clear from the posterior
interval on mu and for sigma.

You can see what's going on in my model --- the observations 10, 10, 12, 11, 9
have error estimates that push it toward mu.

I was attempting to model the same generative process:

  y ~ normal(mu, sigma)
  y_obs <- round(y)
  y_err <- y_obs - round(y)

But clearly my model's not doing that, because I see how Andrew's model fits
that generative story.

So what'd I do wrong?  Or asked another way, is there a way to create a model
like this treating the measurement error as an unknown parameter?  I believe
this is related to the suggested use of cut in the BUGS Book, but given that
I only have a print version, I don't have it with me on the road (it's around
page 202 from the Amazon search, but most of the analysis isn't part of
the preview).

- Bob

P.S.  At least Andrew's correct version is going in the manual soon.

Hi—you just have to forget the idea of an independent measurement error.  Instead you have to model the rounding process directly.  In Stan, this can be done in two ways:  either use the truncated likelihood or treat the unmeasured “true” value as a latent variable.

>
>

> transformed data {

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] What's a good way to incorporate rounding in measurement in STAN?
messages.body_plain:
The two models are different because they have different goals and different parameters. I personally don't think yours is "wrong" it just isn't doing what you think it is.

Andrew's model is asking: "what's the underlying mean and standard deviation of the normal that generated the pre-rounded data?"

Your model is asking: "What is the underyling weight of the object, and what is the vector of actual roundoff errors in the particular cases of each measurement?"

>>>>>>>
>>>>>>> Hi, we have a hwk problem in chapter 3 of BDA on this.  If the underying value is z and the rounded value is y, then the observation constrains z.  For example, if y=2.34, and things are rounded to 2 decimal places, then z ~ uniform(2.335, 2.345).

>>>>>>>>> stan_data <- list(

>>>>>>>>> sample_size=c(300,300,300)
>>>>>>>>> )
>>>>>>>>> stan_code <- '
>>>>>>>>> data {
>>>>>>>>> int num_obs;
>>>>>>>>> real y[num_obs]; // Observed residuals
>>>>>>>>> int sample_size[num_obs];
>>>>>>>>> }
>>>>>>>>> parameters {
>>>>>>>>> real<lower=0,upper=1> p;
>>>>>>>>> }
>>>>>>>>> model {
>>>>>>>>> real y_sigma[num_obs];
>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>> for(j in 1:num_obs)

>>>>>>>>> }
>>>>>>>>>

>>>>>>>> That won't work as written, because yact is unconstrained, but
>>>>>>>> has support only on y +/- 0.005.
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>> If you want to treat the true value as missing data and assume
>>>>>>>> the measurement error is uniform, you could do this so that
>>>>>>>> the support matches the constraints (the uniform on y_err is
>>>>>>>> implicit):

>>>>>>>> data {
>>>>>>>> ...
>>>>>>>> vector[N] y_obs;

>>>>>>>> parameters {
>>>>>>>> ...

>>>>>>>> transformed parameters {

>>>>>>>> vector[N] y;
>>>>>>>> ...

>>>>>>>> ...
>>>>>>>> y ~ normal(mu_y, sigma_y);

>>>>>>>> where y_meas is the measurement of y.

>>>>>>>> a Jacobian warning that you don't need to worry about.

>>>>>>>> it might make sense to just roll the rounding error in with the rest of

Nope, if it’s rounded data, my model is right and Bob’s is wrong.  And my model can be expressed using latent data to also give inference for the underlying weights  and the actual roundoff errors.

Rounded data is a famously tricky problem in statistics, which is why I put a hwk problem on it in BDA.

>
> Your model is asking: "What is the underyling weight of the object, and what is the vector of actual roundoff errors in the particular cases of each measurement?"

Of the latent models, I prefer rounding_latent_2, as it makes it more clear where the data are coming in, and where the model for the latent z is coming in.  The only difficulty is that we’re putting a hard constraint on unconstrained parameters z, so one could imagine it slowing HMC down.  I did not, however, want to put the data in as constraints, for two reasons:
(1) To me, it makes the model less transparent when data are entered as constraints.  I like the clarity of the uniform dist in the model block.
(2) I’m a bit worried about the logit transformation since in this case the underlying parameters have essentially a uniform dist.  So here I’m thinking HMC might move faster in the unconstrained space (except for the fall-off-the-edge-of the-earth thing).
On the downside, the model roiunding_latent_2 is awkward because we need to specify inits for the latent z’s in the call to Stan.

messages.body_plain:
D'oh!  I can answer my own question from first principles.  All I
had to do was step away from the computer.

Punchline:  Marginalizing the latent error parameters out of my model
gives you Andrew's model.

Posterior for Andrew's model:

  p_a(mu, sigma | y)

    propto (1 / sigma^2) PROD_n normal_cdf(y + 0.5 | mu, sigma) - normal_cdf(y - 0.5 | mu, sigma)

    = (1 /sigma^2) PROD_n INT_{z in (y - 0.5, y + 0.5)} normal(z | mu, sigma)

Posterior for my model:

  p_b(mu, sigma, y_err | y)

    propto p(mu, sigma) p(y_err) p(y_err + y | mu, sigma)

    propto (1 / sigma^2) PROD_n normal(y + y_err | mu, sigma)

The trick is thinking of the generative model as producing
a "true" measurement z by

  z ~ normal(mu, sigma)

and then defining two (deterministic) functions of z by

  y <- round(z)

  y_err <- z - y

Then we observe y and estimate z as (y + y_err).  Then we
get

  p(y_err) = uniform(-0.5, 0.5)

Note that this is not generating y_err --- it's just providing the
density of the random variable y_err, which is derived as a function
of z, where z does does have a generative story.  Whew --- that was a
challenge for me to write out and I'm still not sure I've convinced
myself of that last bit other than that the math works out in the next step.

Now if you marginalize the y_err out of my model, you get Andrew's model:

  p_b(mu, sigma | y)

    = p(mu, sigma) * p(y | mu, sigma)

    = p(mu, sigma) * PROD_n p(y[n] | mu, sigma)

    propto (1 / sigma^2) PROD_n INT_{y_err in (-0.5, 0.5)} p(y_err) p(y[n] + y_err | mu, sigma)

    = (1 / sigma^2) PROD_n INT_{z in (y - 0.5, y + 0.5)} p(z | mu, sigma)

This assumes the distribution of y_err to be uniform(-0.5, 0.5).

Andrew basically followed up with the same examples.

- Bob

On Saturday, August 22, 2015 at 12:31:58 AM UTC-7, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> D'oh!  I can answer my own question from first principles.  All I
> had to do was step away from the computer.
>

I know that feeling. Thanks for giving the analysis. I think your analysis confirms my story that

A) your model isn't wrong, it's just a model for both the underlying "true" measurement error, and the individual roundoffs

B) generative models aren't the only way to think about writing Stan programs (this goes back to my post on Jacobians and the meaning of ~ in Stan), as you point out, p(y_err) isn't generating y_err because y_err is a deterministic function of y and z, the underlying normal. I consider p(y_err) to be a maxent prior on y_err, but in your math the uniform is necessary to that you can get a correspondence between the marginalization, and the model that Andrew used with the normal_cdf. There are different perspectives here, but they lead to the same conclusion.

> Punchline:  Marginalizing the latent error parameters out of my model
> gives you Andrew's model.
>

As a general perspective, my intuition is that it should always work out to write something of the form:

an_expression_involving_something_you_know_or_want_to_know ~ a_distribution_describing_your_state_of_knowledge(parameters, describing, knowledge)

Rarely are we in the situation where the frequency distribution assumed is actually "true". So for example in Andrew's example you have a scale, and you assume if you put a weight on it, it generates say a voltage that is normally distributed, and then rounds off the measurement of the voltage.

But, why normally distributed? In reality, it's probably not, it's gotta be much lighter-tailed than that (ie. it has to have finite bounds based on the voltage available in the battery or whatnot) yet within those bounds it could be normal, or t, or even some kind of skewed distribution, or it could vary from time to time based on the temperature of the transistors... etc

So, it's not necessary to get too attached to the idea that "generative" models are the one-true-path for modeling. For example, it leads to intuitions like that uniform distributions will only work if the distribution of the actual roundoffs is uniform.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] What's a good way to incorporate rounding in measurement in STAN?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] What's a good way to incorporate rounding in measurement in STAN?
messages.body_plain:
What the math showed is that Andrew's model produces the same
result as marginalizing out the latent parameters from my model.

The story with the latent variables is generative.  Generate
a measurement, then round it off.  That measurement model
doesn't need to be normal, but that's a good generic assumption
for effects that are additive combinations of other effects.

The uniform "prior" on p(y_err) is just derived from working
backward from the measurement model (normal error plus rounding).
That was the whole point of Andrew's exercise in BDA.

- Bob

> On Aug 22, 2015, at 12:23 PM, Daniel Lakeland <dlak...@street-artists.org> wrote:
>
>
>
> On Saturday, August 22, 2015 at 12:31:58 AM UTC-7, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> D'oh!  I can answer my own question from first principles.  All I
> had to do was step away from the computer.
>
>
> I know that feeling. Thanks for giving the analysis. I think your analysis confirms my story that
>
> A) your model isn't wrong, it's just a model for both the underlying "true" measurement error, and the individual roundoffs
>
> B) generative models aren't the only way to think about writing Stan programs (this goes back to my post on Jacobians and the meaning of ~ in Stan), as you point out, p(y_err) isn't generating y_err because y_err is a deterministic function of y and z, the underlying normal. I consider p(y_err) to be a maxent prior on y_err, but in your math the uniform is necessary to that you can get a correspondence between the marginalization, and the model that Andrew used with the normal_cdf. There are different perspectives here, but they lead to the same conclusion.
>
>
> Punchline:  Marginalizing the latent error parameters out of my model
> gives you Andrew's model.
>
>
> As a general perspective, my intuition is that it should always work out to write something of the form:
>
> an_expression_involving_something_you_know_or_want_to_know ~ a_distribution_describing_your_state_of_knowledge(parameters, describing, knowledge)
>
> Rarely are we in the situation where the frequency distribution assumed is actually "true". So for example in Andrew's example you have a scale, and you assume if you put a weight on it, it generates say a voltage that is normally distributed, and then rounds off the measurement of the voltage.
>
> But, why normally distributed? In reality, it's probably not, it's gotta be much lighter-tailed than that (ie. it has to have finite bounds based on the voltage available in the battery or whatnot) yet within those bounds it could be normal, or t, or even some kind of skewed distribution, or it could vary from time to time based on the temperature of the transistors... etc
>
> So, it's not necessary to get too attached to the idea that "generative" models are the one-true-path for modeling. For example, it leads to intuitions like that uniform distributions will only work if the distribution of the actual roundoffs is uniform.
>
>
>
>

Yes, it is written to a file.  If the :file argument ends with ".stan"
or if org-babel-stan-cmdstan-directory is not set, the block content is
written to the file.  :var in the R block specifies to use the file name
that has the results from Stan code block.

not end in ".stan", then the contents are written to another file (file

> shell code block through a :var or from a file.

Yep, the result of the block is just a file name for the Stan file that
it created, so it can be pulled through any interface with Babel support
(and the Stan file can be used outside of Org).  In cases where you'd
rather not have the Stan block in the Org file (e.g., if the Stan code
is really long), you could just use the name of an external Stan file
directly in the interface block and (optionally, for reference or easy
access) have a link to the Stan file.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] What's a good way to incorporate rounding in measurement in STAN?
messages.body_plain:
On Saturday, August 22, 2015 at 11:50:15 AM UTC-7, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> What the math showed is that Andrew's model produces the same
> result as marginalizing out the latent parameters from my model.
>
> The story with the latent variables is generative.  Generate
> a measurement, then round it off.  That measurement model
> doesn't need to be normal, but that's a good generic assumption
> for effects that are additive combinations of other effects.
>
> The uniform "prior" on p(y_err) is just derived from working
> backward from the measurement model (normal error plus rounding).
> That was the whole point of Andrew's exercise in BDA.
>

The exercise of course has a particular "generative" model from the start. But the original question was "how to include roundoff in a binomial proportion reported as rounded to the nearest percent" and the thought process that brought me to my model for that was: "we know the rounding means that the underlying value was within a particular interval, so put a maxent prior on that difference value and then subtract it from the measurement and tell Stan that you know the distribution of this new quantity which is a function of data and parameter"

I feel like that's a different route to the model than thinking the other way around, and the math showed that it was marginally, the same in your case. One question is, is this model building methodology valid in general? Can you put distributions over f(data,parameters) by claiming from your scientific knowledge that such a distribution is justified, and always produce a model which is mathematically well posed (not necessarily maximally efficient, or maximally informative mind you, but at least which produces a normalizable posterior pdf for example)?

I don't think we'll get a solution to that question, except that most likely there are some counterexamples where the method produces bad results because of pathologies in the function f, or whatnot.

messages.body_plain:
> The exercise of course has a particular "generative" model from the start. But the original question was "how to include roundoff in a binomial proportion reported as rounded to the nearest percent" and the thought process that brought me to my model for that was: "we know the rounding means that the underlying value was within a particular interval, so put a maxent prior on that difference value and then subtract it from the measurement and tell Stan that you know the distribution of this new quantity which is a function of data and parameter"

No, no, no, no.  Unless the distribution of the latent measurement is
uniform, this “maxent” distribution will be inconsistent with the rest
of the measurement model and define only a weird target distribution.
In particular, the rounding is a censoring process which belongs in

messages.body_plain:
On Saturday, August 22, 2015 at 2:25:10 PM UTC-7, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> > The exercise of course has a particular "generative" model from the start. But the original question was "how to include roundoff in a binomial proportion reported as rounded to the nearest percent" and the thought process that brought me to my model for that was: "we know the rounding means that the underlying value was within a particular interval, so put a maxent prior on that difference value and then subtract it from the measurement and tell Stan that you know the distribution of this new quantity which is a function of data and parameter"
>
> No, no, no, no.  Unless the distribution of the latent measurement is
> uniform, this “maxent” distribution will be inconsistent with the rest
> of the measurement model and define only a weird target distribution.
> In particular, the rounding is a censoring process which belongs in
> the _likelihood_ and has nothing to do with _priors_.

Bob has just shown (above) that the maxent prior distribution on the latent rounding error produces the same exact model (when marginalized) as shifting it all into the likelihood. In other words, from the point of view of the underlying measurement error, the models produce the same exact inference! It doesn't matter what the actual frequency distributions of the roundoff errors is. In particular, they dont' have to be uniform, and their posterior distributions are NOT uniform.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] What's a good way to incorporate rounding in measurement in STAN?
messages.body_plain:
I'm particularly interested in this topic because I think it's frequently the case that a model is more naturally expressed (for me) in this way.

For example, suppose you have an A/D converter looking at a signal which is composed of f(t) whose form you know, plus a bunch of high frequency noise which has MSE sigma which you know approximately and this high frequency noise can be considered gaussian like, plus some low frequency noise which has total amplitude less than epsilon, and of course, roundoff error in the A/D... (let's pretend this is to nearest 0.001)

You have NO idea what the frequency distribution of the values caused by the low frequency signal will be, but you know the error they induce is always between -epsilon and epsilon.

To me, a very natural model for this is:

y_round ~ uniform(-0.001,0.001);
y_err ~ uniform(-epsilon,epsilon);
sigma ~ exponential(1/my_guess_for_sigma); // or maybe some other prior expressing what I know about sigma
Data - y_err -y_round ~ normal(f(t), sigma)

especially if I want to know something about the low frequency signal y_err which is polluting my measurements...

Very often, it's latent things like measurement errors or diffusion coefficients, or the size of the effect of some temperature change... or whatever that I'd like to know. It makes sense to write models that directly do inference via a parameter on the thing I'm interested in.

messages.body_plain:
I don’t have the energy for any more discussion of this, but let me just echo Betancourt:  It does not make sense to think of there being a “prior” on the errors.  What we have is a data model, giving the data as a function of the unobserved continuous measurement.  In one of the models I posted yesterday, I did express things in terms of a prior for the roundoff error, but that is truly a hack and not a good way to write this sort of model.  In general, and as usual, it is best to write the model directly as I did in my model rounding_latent_2.stan.  Here I speak, not of Stan efficiency, but of general statistical principles.
A

> On Aug 22, 2015, at 8:59 PM, Daniel Lakeland <dlak...@street-artists.org> wrote:
>

>
> Another example, suppose it's just like Andrew's example, but someone designing the microcontroller code for the scale had a bug, so 50 % of the time the display rounds to the nearest 1 lb, 40% of the time it rounds UP, and 10% of the time it rounds DOWN.
>
> Now, you could put a maxent prior on the roundoff errors that's a mixture model of the 3 possibilities, and that would be a step-function, but of course HMC isn't going to like that. So you could graph this step function and design a sort of smoothish approximation to that step function, and then write
>
> for(i in 1:N)
>   increment_log_prob(my_smooth_approximation(roundoff_parameter[i]));
>
> Or you could write a weird likelihood, and try to back-out the rounding errors with weird generated quantities...
>
> Generally, it makes sense to me to write your model so you have parameters that describe the unknown quantities of interest, and priors on those parameters that describe the information you have about them going into the analysis.
>
>

The diagnostic_file is not intended to be used for progress checking. If it is a Linux server, you could just use screen or whatever and periodically log back in to see what iteration it has completed. I fear you are talking about a Windows server, in which case I guess you could just leave Internet Explorer open and refresh it periodically. It is not possible to specify a file to write the progress to but it is a randomly named file in tempdir() so you could call tempdir() before calling Stan to see what that directory is and open the resulting progress file some other way.

Ben

I guess this might be one of those cases where Gibbs sampling works better, though there might be problems with convergence.

David

In theory we could run 1,200 individual scripts no problem, but we really want to avoid doing that. Without any hierarchical structure we fear we might run into a lot of false positives, plus we also want to make use of shrinkage to pull the coefficients from similar events to the same scale.

>

>
> randomly select 20 event types and 1 million relevant data points or something like that, get the posterior distribution of the parameters from this reduced set of observations. Then fit a parametric prior for the parameters, and use it repeatedly in 1200 regressions on the remaining 79 million data points?
>
> The point being to reduce the chance of over-fitting by gleaning some information from a subset of the data which is then used as an informed prior to regularize the individual fits to some extent. It's not as clean as the full heirarchical bayes, but it's actually do-able, so there's that going for it.

messages.subject: Linear regression with uncertainty in x and y
messages.subject_clean: Linear regression with uncertainty in x and y
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

in small examples I'm trying to understand how to use Bayesian inference to take measurement uncertainty into account. I made this toy example for normally distributed measurements, where x and y both include a noise term: http://rpubs.com/biocs/uncertainty

For each (x,y) point with associated sigma_x and sigma_y, I derive virtual points (xx, yy) on the regression line -- see code in the linked example -- which maximise the likelihood. This is possible because the PDF for the multivariate normal distribution can be analysed analytically. So when the sampling algorithm changes the slope or intercept, each measurement's uncertainty is taken into account using the maximum likelihood that can be associated with the measurement.

To account for outliers, I'd like to use a Student's t distribution as suggested in "Doing Bayesian Data Analysis". However, it looks like the PDF cannot be treated that easily. I was therefore wondering if there's another approach to this problem with STAN.

For example, could I call an external function to compute the virtual points with maximum likelihood numerically?

thanks, Michael

If you can't combine observations with same probability of
success a priori, then the Bernoulli to binomial data aggregation
won't help.

I doubt Gibbs is going to work better --- it has a hard time in
high dimensions, especially with hierarchical models inducing high
posterior correlations.  You can easily get fooled with Gibbs or
Metropolis into thinking you've converged if you aren't careful to
start from diffuse initializations and make sure you converge to the
same posterior means.

- Bob

messages.subject: Idea, Interfacing "frequentist statistic package" code from STAN
messages.subject_clean: Idea, Interfacing "frequentist statistic package" code from STAN
messages.body_plain:
Dear STAN team,

I see a lot of STAN users re-implementing solved problems in Bayesian way with STAN,
including myself.

Would it be impossible in each iteration step to call a function from R or any other interface
using the input from the sampled values, take the output and use it for further processing
in STAN?

Benefits would be:

- not re-implementing the wheel.
- speed gain
- more focus of STAN users on the problem domain and do the standard "things" with
statistic package code.

Just some thoughts,
Andre

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Using a continuous distribution to model a time series
messages.body_plain:
You are simulating y on the linear scale and then
using the log in Stan.  To match your simulation,
you need to do this:

  y_hat[n] <- exp(gamma_log(x[n], alpha, beta));

I'll let others comment on the wisdom of this kind of model,
which is going to depend on how your data's generated.
And then you're going to fit

We also don't recommend the uniform(0, 100) priors --- see
the manual for current recommendations and Andrew's to-appear
Wiki.  And then you want to vectorize this for efficiency:

>  for(n in 1:N)
>     y[n] ~ normal(y_hat[n], sigma);

- Bob

> On Aug 25, 2015, at 10:26 AM, Jan <aaka...@googlemail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi,
>
> I was wondering if one could use the distributions included in Stan to model a time series. E.g. a process that starts at zero then rises quickly and returns to baseline more slowly could be approximated by a gamma density (or mixture of gamma densities).
>
> Similar to linear models (y_hat <- a + b*x) one would declare this relationship in the transformed parameters block, I assume. I couldn't find a good example, except for  example-models/bugs_examples/vol2/pines/pines-2.stan which uses the normal_log function in the transformed block.
>
> As described in the attached files, I simulate a gamma density-based time series
>
> x <- 1:10
> y <- dgamma(x, shape=alpha, scale=1/beta)
> y <- y + rnorm(length(x), 0, sigma_y)
>
>
> and then try to recover the gamma parameters with stan
>
> data {
>   int<lower=0> N;  // nr samples
>   real y[N];       // y values
>   real x[N];       // x values
> }
> parameters {
>   real<lower=0> alpha;
>   real<lower=0> beta;
>   real<lower=0,upper=100> sigma;
> }
> transformed parameters {
>   real y_hat[N];
>   for(n in 1:N)
>     y_hat[n] <- gamma_log(x[n], alpha, beta);
> }
> model {
>   for(n in 1:N)
>     y[n] ~ normal(y_hat[n], sigma);
> }
>
>
> This sort-of works, but estimated parameters become non-sensical when adding more terms to the data and model, e.g.
>
> y <- a + b * y + rnorm(length(x), 0, sigma_y)
>
>
> I was wondering if I should abandon this approach in favour of a better way to parameterize smooth time series?
>
> Cheers.

messages.subject: Re: Beta model and Poisson prior on one Beta parameter
messages.subject_clean: Beta model and Poisson prior on one Beta parameter
messages.body_plain: You cannot have discrete parameters in your model as Stan uses HMC, which requires a continuous parameter space. For some models that do have discrete parameters, you can marginalize over the possible values for the discrete parameter, provided that they constitute a limited set (or can be assumed to be). See Stan manual chapter on mixture models. Manual in general is a good place to start reading up on HMC.

I would appreciate any help that anyone can provide on addressing this warning. I have included the model as an attachment to this message.

Thanks,
Daniel Chamberlain

Absolutely --- could you let us know exactly what the error message
was and what you'd like it to say?  We want to make these interpretable
to our users.

> Either way, I would share my own experience with this error message.
>
> EX1. beta(a,b) does not allow a (or/and b) = 0

Correct --- it's undefined.

> EX2. x[i]/sum(x) when sum(x)=0, in this case, you could try x[i]/ (sum(x) + machine_precision() )

Divide by zero creates NaN.  But you probably do not want to do
x[i] / machine_precision() as that will just produce
roughly 1e15 * x[i], which is probably not what you want.

> EX3. the dimension of your parameters is ill specified

Not sure what you mean here.  Our vectorization requires all args to
be either scalars or the same size container.

- Bob

messages.subject: Priors for the regression coefficients of an ordinal input variable
messages.subject_clean: Priors for the regression coefficients of an ordinal input variable
messages.body_plain:
Does anyone know of any literature on priors for the regression coefficients of an ordinal input variable? Here's what I have in mind:
You have an ordinal input variable x[N] with K levels.
You have K (or K-1) corresponding effects betax[K].
You must have betax[k+1] > betax[k].
The linear predictor for observation i includes a term betax[x[i]].
I don't want to have to assume that the betax values are equally spaced, but it would be good if the prior could penalize very small differences between beta[k] and beta[k+1].

messages.subject: Re: 2D interpolation and splines
messages.subject_clean: 2D interpolation and splines
messages.body_plain:
> Hello
>
> Is there a easy way to use 2D interpolation in a stan-model? If not is that on the agenda?
>
> Same with splines. I did not find examples in the manual. But I was wondering is someone had any examples before I would dig into it myself.
>
> Cheers
> Jóhannes

Hi Jóhannes,

I did some experimenting with splines in Stan -- specifically with Ramsay's M-splines (non-negative basis splines that integrate to 1) and I-splines (integrated M-splines, useful for fitting a monotone spline). The idea is the same if you use B-splines though. I found this to work very well with Stan.

As Krzysztof said, you can precompute the values of the basis splines outside of Stan and pass them through as data, and then the only model parameters are the weights of these basis splines. You probably want to use a prior for the spline weights that induces a smooth spline though, like the Bayesian P-spline specification described by Lang & Brezger (http://dx.doi.org/10.1198/1061860043010). That is, in the github example posted here you may replace
beta ~ normal(0,10)
by something like
tail(beta, d-1) ~ normal(head(beta, d-1), sigma_beta)
with some prior for sigma_beta.

If there is interest I can share some of my stuff and help construct an illustrative example -- I do think that Stan excels in this kind of thing.

Regards,

Michael

is there a specific reason you don't simply specify a prior for a (and v and t)?*
it looks as if your statistical model is more complex than the true generative model.
i.e. when you generate the data
a <- 3.25
but in your stan model
a <- a_mu + a_sd * a_raw.

so  I think
a ~ normal(0,2);
after specifying real<lower=0,upper=10> a;
in the parameters block and removing a_mu, a_raw, and a_sd should work better.
(same for v and t).

maybe you can try this simpler model first
(I had no issues to recover the correct wiener parameter values
when testing such a simple model a few weeks ago).

personally, I would try this simpler model first and see if I can recover parameters,
before trying the more complex model. but if you do this and you use

a <- a_mu + a_sd * a_raw;

in stan, then you might also want to generate the data in R accordingly

I also would use more informative priors than the (implicit) flat priors you used for
a_mu, a_sd, ... you have in your model.

guido

*(maybe this is a preparation to run the full DDM with between trial variability for v,a,t?)

messages.body_plain:
I had the priors on the wiener parameters setup for a hierarchical model later down the line, which is why you might see the mu, sd, raw, etc..

However, even when setting normal priors constrained on some range as suggested, I still get weird estimates, in this case alpha=5.27, tau=0.12, v=0.92, b=0.58. Next I tried just using uniform priors on a, t, v, b and I get 7.27, 0.11, 1.04, 0.66 respectively (see code below).

I guess I'm not sure what the proper constraints should be, but I've seen normal priors used before but with the JAGS version of the wiener distribution.

library(rstan)
library(loo)
library(RWiener)

# if running chains in parallel
rstan_options(auto_write = TRUE)
options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())

# wiener parameters
a <- 3.25
t <- 0.25
b <- 0.4
v <- 0.65
n <- 150

# random RT values from RWiener using parameters above
rt <- rwiener(
    n = n,
    alpha = a,
    tau = t,
    beta = b,
    delta = v
)

# make stan data list
stan_data <- list(rt = rt$q,
                  acc = ifelse(rt[, "resp"] == "upper", 1, 0),
                  n = nrow(rt))

# number of chains to run
n_chains <- 5

# use inits from above dist. parameters
stan_inits <- lapply(1:n_chains, function(i) {
    list(

        a = a,
        t = t,
        v = v,

        b = b
    )
})

# STAN code
stan_model <-
"
data {
    int<lower=1>                n;
    vector[n]                   rt;
    vector<lower=0,upper=1>[n]  acc;
}
parameters {

    real<lower=0,upper=10> a;
    real<lower=0,upper=5>  t;
    real<lower=0,upper=5>  v;
    real<lower=0,upper=1>  b;
}
model {
    //a ~ normal(0, 2);
    //t ~ normal(0, 2);
    //v ~ normal(0, 2);
    //b ~ beta(2, 2);

    // likelihood
    for (i in 1:n) {
        if (acc[n] == 1) {
            rt[i] ~ wiener(a, t, b, v);    // upper bound
        } else {
            rt[i] ~ wiener(a, t, 1-b, -v); // lower bound
        }
    }
}
generated quantities {
    vector[n] log_lik;

    for (i in 1:n) {
        if (acc[n] == 1) { // upper
            log_lik[i] <- wiener_log(rt[i], a, t, b, v);
        } else { // lower
            log_lik[i] <- wiener_log(rt[i], a, t, 1-b, -v);
        }
    }
}
"

# run model
stan_fit <-
    stan(
        model_name = "diffusion_test",
        model_code = stan_model,
        data = stan_data,
        init = stan_inits,
        chains = n_chains
    )

# print stan model parameters
print(stan_fit)

# print elpd_loo
print(loo(extract_log_lik(stan_fit)), digits = 3)

# print RWiener likelihood
print(wiener_likelihood(c(a,t,b,v), rt))

On Wednesday, August 26, 2015 at 1:07:24 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> There are a lot of problems with that model.
>
> But multiple assignment isn't one of them.  To start,
>
> > theta[j] ~ normal(mu,sigma);
>
> isn't an assignment in Stan, it's equivalent to
>
>   increment_log_prob(normal_log(theta[j], mu, sigma));
>
> modulo constant terms.
>
> The problem is that you want to do this the other way around.
> Declare the parameter thetato be unconstrained,
>
>   parameters {
>     vector[J] theta;
>     ...
>
> and then you can do this:
>
>   transformed parameters {
>     vector<lower=0,upper=1>[J] p;
>     for (j in 1:J)
>       p[j] <- inv_logit(theta[j]);
>
> Note the loop.  You can't just have a dangling p[j] or theta[j] without
> defining j.
>
> But you can vectorize the model, writing
>
>    theta ~ normal(mu, sigma);
>
> instead of
>
>   for (n in 1:N)
>     theta[j] ~ normal(mu, sigma);
>
> Finally, what you really want to do is just use the logit-scaled
> parameter version of binomial directly
>
>   y ~ binomial_logit(n, theta);
>
> Again, this is vectorized. You can't just have dangling j.
>
> Then if you really need the p values and don't want to compute them on the
> outside, define them as generated quantities,
>
>   generated quantities {
>     vector<lower=0, upper=1>[N] p;
>     for (n in 1:N)
>       p[n] <- inv_logit(theta[n]);
>   }
>
> - Bob
>
>
>
>
> > On Aug 26, 2015, at 9:48 AM, Jan <aaka...@googlemail.com> wrote:
> >
> > I don't think you can assign the same variable twice:
> >
> > transformed parameters {
> >
> >   theta[j] <- logit(p[j]); // conversion to log odds. This line throws the warning.
> >
> >  and here
> >
> > model{
> >   theta[j] ~ normal(mu,sigma);
> >
> > I'm not familiar with odds models. But usually you estimate the mean y_hat in the transformed block and then the 'error' in the model block, e.g. y ~ normal(y_hat, sigma). Following this 'design pattern' should solve your problem.
> >
> > Cheers,
> > J

messages.body_plain:
You could extract the samples

fit <- stan(..)
samples <- extract(fit)

and then look at correlations between them to troubleshoot the problem.

plot(samples$muG, samples$muR)

One can also plot all variables at once using a scatter plot matrix <http://www.statmethods.net/graphs/scatterplot.html>, e.g. pairs(). But it is probably advisable to get a slightly simpler model to work first, before troubleshooting a complex multilevel model.

J

messages.subject: Using STAN for deterministic problems
messages.subject_clean: Using STAN for deterministic problems
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I'm new to this list , so please excuse any possible faux-pas I may commit.

I am trying to estimate the parameters of a deterministic data generating process that closely resembles a probabilistic (multinomial) one. In particular, for data X and unknown parameters theta, f(X, theta) is a N x 5 matrix where each row is a 5-simplex i.e. sums to 1. In a normal multinomial model, each Y_i would be drawn from a multinomial distribution with probability parameters equal to each row of f(X, theta). However, in this case, instead of a random multinomial draw, Y_i is simply the category with the highest probability.

The parameters in this problem may be calculated analytically, but I'm wondering if there is anyway to get at them through Monte Carlo methods. Also, generally, in problems where there might also be similar deterministic data generating processes and where there might not be unique solutions for the parameters, would Monte Carlo methods be useful at all? And if MC can be useful, how do I do it in STAN? I am thinking of using distributions with variability close to zero to mimic the deterministic process, but I'm not sure if this is theoretically justified.

Thanks so much,
Minh

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Thanks for providing me with your model to look at. The main differences I noticed was setting the max of tau to the minimum response time from the data, and using a half-cauchy prior with small scale. You also allowed delta to be negative. I made all these changes and still the parameters don't match up with the original I used to sample the data. The chains are mixing well, so that doesn't seem to be the issue. I then tried sampling 1000 trials instead of 150, still no luck. Below is my final attempt.

library(rstan)
library(loo)
library(RWiener)

# if running chains in parallel
rstan_options(auto_write = TRUE)
options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())

# wiener parameters
a <- 3.25
t <- 0.25
b <- 0.4
v <- 0.65

n <- 1000

# random RT values from RWiener using parameters above
rt <- rwiener(
    n = n,
    alpha = a,
    tau = t,
    beta = b,
    delta = v
)

# make stan data list
stan_data <- list(rt = rt$q,
                  acc = ifelse(rt[, "resp"] == "upper", 1, 0),

                  n = nrow(rt),
                  min_t = min(rt$q))

# number of chains to run
n_chains <- 5

# use inits from above dist. parameters
stan_inits <- lapply(1:n_chains, function(i) {
    list(
        a = a,
        t = t,
        v = v,
        b = b
    )
})

# STAN code
stan_model <-
"
data {
    int<lower=1>                n;
    vector[n]                   rt;
    vector<lower=0,upper=1>[n]  acc;

    real<lower=0>               min_t;
}
parameters {
    real<lower=0,upper=6>  a;
    real<lower=.1,upper=min_t>  t;
    real<lower=-2,upper=2> v;
    real<lower=0,upper=1>  b;
}
model {
    a ~ normal(0, 2);
    t ~ cauchy(0, 0.1);
    v ~ normal(0, 2);
    b ~ beta(1.25, 1.25);

    // likelihood
    for (i in 1:n) {
        if (acc[n] == 1) {
            rt[i] ~ wiener(a, t, b, v);    // upper bound
        } else {
            rt[i] ~ wiener(a, t, 1-b, -v); // lower bound
        }
    }
}
generated quantities {
    vector[n] log_lik;

    for (i in 1:n) {
        if (acc[n] == 1) { // upper
            log_lik[i] <- wiener_log(rt[i], a, t, b, v);
        } else { // lower
            log_lik[i] <- wiener_log(rt[i], a, t, 1-b, -v);
        }
    }
}
"

# run model
stan_fit <-
    stan(
        model_name = "diffusion_test",
        model_code = stan_model,
        data = stan_data,
        init = stan_inits,
        chains = n_chains
    )

# print stan model parameters
print(stan_fit)

# print elpd_loo
print(loo(extract_log_lik(stan_fit)), digits = 3)

# print RWiener likelihood
print(wiener_likelihood(c(a,t,b,v), rt))

print(lapply(extract(stan_fit), mean))

# Plots -------------------------------------------------------------------

# stan traceplot

#traceplot(stan_fit)

# plot distributions from RWiener
plot_rwiener <- function(rt) {
    rt_u <- rt$q[rt$resp == "upper"]
    rt_l <- rt$q[rt$resp == "lower"]

    xlim <- max(c(rt_u, rt_l))
    rt_seq <- seq(0, xlim, .005)

    d_rt_u <-
        dwiener(rt_seq, a, t, b, v, resp = rep("upper", length(rt_seq)))
    d_rt_l <-
        dwiener(rt_seq, a, t, b, v, resp = rep("lower", length(rt_seq)))

    ylim <- max(c(d_rt_u, d_rt_l))

    par(mfrow = c(3, 1))

    plot(
        x = rt_seq,
        y = d_rt_u,
        type = "l",
        xlim = c(0, xlim),
        ylim = c(-ylim, ylim),
        main = "Density of upper/lower responses",
        ylab = "density",
        xlab = "quantile",
        col = "green"
    )

    lines(x = rt_seq, y = -d_rt_l, col = "red")

    xbrks <- seq(0, xlim, length.out = 30)

    hist(
        rt_u,
        freq = FALSE,
        breaks = xbrks,
        xlim = c(0, xlim),
        ylim = c(0, ylim * 2),
        main = "upper",
        xlab = paste("N =", length(rt_u))
    )

    hist(
        rt_l,
        freq = FALSE,
        breaks = xbrks,
        xlim = c(0, xlim),
        ylim = c(0, ylim * 2),
        main = "lower",
        xlab = paste("N =", length(rt_l))
    )
}

#plot_rwiener(rt)

> a "proportional mix",
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Using STAN for deterministic problems
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Using STAN for deterministic problems
messages.body_plain:
If you want to use Bayesian methods, you need to write down
a joint model, typically defined in terms of a
probabilistic data-generating process.  It isn't clear to me
what the shape of X and Y_i would be or what theta is.  It
helps if you can write down the dimensions and a short description
of what the values mean.

Stan's not ideally suited to this kind of deterministic data-generating
problem, because it amounts to a constraint solving
problem for the parameters (assuming X is some matrix of predictors for
individuals and there is a latent coefficient vector).

You don't want to try to write down a low-variance approximation to
something deterministic --- you want to write down the data generating
process.

- Bob

The place to look is the manual --- there's a chapter on
user-defined functions that shows you how to write a new
density and there's a reference chapter on all the densities.
Assuming you want to do this all on the log scale, it'd
look something like:

functions {
  real erlb(...) {

  }
  real erlc(...) {
    ...
  }
  real SL_log(real rho, int M, real ts, real t) {
     return log1m(erlc(M, rho * M) *  exp(-M * (1 - rho) * t / ts));
  }
}

I removed the "fun" suffix and added the required "_log" for densities
and returned on the log scale.  And I just chose the log scale --- it's
all you need for Stan, so I wouldn't add all the flags you have in the R
code.

Then you just need to define the other functions pretty much the same
way as in R.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Ah, but it does influence a parameter.  If the transformed parameter
constraints are violated, the whole sample is rejected.

These assignments are not consistent in their constraints:

parameters {
   real gamma[Ncon];

transformed parameters {

   real<lower=0,upper=1> beta[N];                                 //alpha sampled well when truncation is removed

      beta[i]    <- gamma[consumer[i]];

The problem is that gamma can be outside of [0, 1].  Whenver that
happens, you reject.

Either constrain gamma or unconstrain beta.  Or, do an inverse-logit
transform to turn the unconstrained gamma into a probability in [0, 1].

- Bob

> I did some experimenting with splines in Stan -- specifically with Ramsay's M-splines (non-negative basis splines that integrate to 1) and I-splines (integrated M-splines, useful for fitting a monotone spline). messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Priors for the regression coefficients of an ordinal input variable
messages.body_plain:
This has been discussed before, albeit inconclusively.

Yes, that's one way to do it.  I've been asking Andrew about this
for a while and he didn't have a recommendation (or if he did, maybe
he can remind us all).

To construct a sequence of cutpoints, you can fix the first
at 0 and then define

  c[1] <- 0;
  c[n+1] = c[n] + delta[n]

where delta[n] has to be positive.  You can define

 delta_raw ~ normal(0, 2);

or another unconstrained prior and then take

 delta <- exp(delta_raw);

or you can constrain the delta to be positive and put any prior
on them.  Like a lognormal or gamma.

Or you can just model all the cutpoints as having independent
priors, which gives you the same result as generating them
independently and sorting given the constraint (I've verified this
all computationally but haven't quite got my head around why it's
true theoretically --- there are lots of moving boundaries to adjust
for).

- Bob

Thank you very much for your reply. I hesitated at first to give more specific description of X and Y since I was worried it might come off as asking for help on specific homework questions. In any case, X_1, X_2, X_3 are three N x 4 matrices of 0's and 1's where each row has one 1 and three 0s (e.g. answers to multiple choice questions). Theta_1, Theta_2, Theta_3 are 4 x 5 matrix to "score" the answers. Then, p = f(X, Theta) is (X_1 x Theta_1) .* (X_2 x Theta_2) .* (X_3 x Theta_3) where .* is elementwise multiplication. After rescaling, p is a N x 5 matrix where each row is the probability of each observation falling into one of five "types." Y is then a N x 1 matrix where each Y_i \in {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} corresponding to each "type."

An example maybe personality tests, where you answer a couple of multiple choice questions and are told what kind of personality type you belong to. The tricky bit here is that I know that each Y_i is not randomly drawn from a multinomial distribution with probability p_i, but simply obtained by referencing the category in p with the highest probability. For example, if p_i = [0.2, 0.2, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1] then Y_i = 3.

So my understanding is that what I have here is a working data generating process, except for that it is deterministic instead of probabilistic. Since Stan only allows probabilistic models for the final step, the low-variance approximation approach was the first thing that popped in my head, but it seems that it's not well justified. I would love to hear your thoughts and suggestions on whether there's any alternatives.

On Saturday, August 29, 2015 at 5:35:08 PM UTC-4, Asim Ansari wrote:
> Page 414 of the manual documents the pdf of the LkjCholesky(L|eta). I am wondering whether the exponent of L_{kk} in the product be (K-k+2\eta-1), instead of (K-k+2\eta-2) as reported.

I think the manual is right. You've got a density proportional to |J| |LL'|^(eta - 1), which we can simplify using the fact that |LL'| = |L|^2 and |L| is the product of the diagonal elements of L. So the density is proportional to |J| |L|^(2eta - 2) and then the |J| contributes the K - k piece in the exponent.

Ben

messages.subject: Convergence considerations with a shifted lognormal hierarchical model
messages.subject_clean: Convergence considerations with a shifted lognormal hierarchical model
messages.body_plain:
Hi, I'm back with my shifted-lognormal hierarchical model (this is my previous post <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/nicenboim/stan-users/xv-Yjpb7faw/vx2YHXagvZgJ>), I
started to increase the complexity of the model, and I started to notice
problems in convergence. So I simplified everything again to check it.
Basically I'm trying to fit a model where reading times (rt) are assumed to be
produced by a shifted lognormal distribution. I'm assuming a general shift, a
by-subject adjustment coming from a normal distribution centered in 0, an
intercept for the lognormal part (alpha), a fixed effect (beta), and
by-subjects random intercept and slopes centered in 0 that they are somewhat
correlated: (the complete code is in shifted_log_simple.stan)

 transformed parameters{
 (...)
 for (i in 1:N_obs){
    mu[i] <- alpha  + x_betas[i] * beta +
          x_u[i] * u[subj[i]];
    psi[i] <-  shift + shift_u[subj[i]]; //
  }
}

model {
 (...)
     (rt - psi) ~ lognormal(mu, sigma);
}

So the same parameters that don't get an Rhat of 1 in the complex mode, here
they are around 1.01-1.02 (while the other params are more in the
1.00something).

These parameters are the ones that are in a different scale than the rest:
alpha (the intercept of fixed effects) has an estimate around 5 (I simulate
this but that's also the case in "real life"), the intercept for shift is
around 200, while the adjustment for shift for participants is between 0-200.
(The other parameters are below 1). I checked the get_sampler_params, and I
noticed that Max treedepth reaches 11 and n_divergent has a Max of 1, which I
understand from the manual is something bad.

So from reading previous answers in the forum, I understand that there are two
possibilities: either to decrease the stepsize and increase the treedepth; or
to normalize the parameters to be near 1. I'm trying to avoid the first
possibility just because it's extremely slow.

Regarding the second option, one problem that I face is that the
initialization fails unless I set init=0.

I'm normalizing the intercept alpha with alpha_k= mean(log(rt)), which is
always a bit bigger than the intercept, and the shifts with shift_k which is
mean(rt) also bigger than the shift. I'm doing this (in shifted_log_simple_norm.stan):

 for (i in 1:N_obs){
    mu[i] <- alpha * alpha_k + x_betas[i] * beta +
          x_u[i] * u[subj[i]];
    psi[i] <-  shift_k * (shift + shift_u[subj[i]]); //
  }

First of all, it doesn't improve the Rhats (in fact all Rhats are
even bigger). So does it even make sense? (And I guess that constraining the
init to 0 is not ideal, but maybe a side effect of the problems I'm having).
And I still have the same problems with treedepth n_divergent. So my question
is: Is there a solution besides changing step size and the maximum tree depth?

I'm attaching my models to generate the data, to fit it in two different ways, r code and output.
Thanks
Bruno

That's an excellent question. It often happens that the null model can be approximated by the alternative model when coefficients go toward zero, for example. However, if you compare models you should also take their complexity into account. If the null model fits just as well it should be preferred by your choice of model comparison, because it has less parameters.

J
