messages.subject: Re: change point detection
messages.subject_clean: change point detection
messages.body_plain:
If the changepoint exists, do you know when it occurs?  It's going to be really hard to tell the difference between a one-change-point system with a small change-point effect from a zero-change-point system unless you know where the change-point is.  Even then you would need a lot of data around the change-point time.

I'm only bringing this up because it's not clear that your specific question matters.  I agree with Jan that a simpler model is often preferable for various reasons but in this case I don't think one parameter is going to make a big difference unless you have special requirements (e.g., someone has declared that there must be a hypothesis test).

Krzysztof

messages.subject: about a hierarhical logistic regression model
messages.subject_clean: about a hierarhical logistic regression model
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am new to Stan. And I have a question regarding a hierarchical logistic regression model.

Suppose there are J individuals. For the response of each individual y_j, it follows a logistic regression. And the regression coefficient beta is a vector with random effect. That is, for each individual j we have:
logit(y_j) = x_j * beta_j;
beta_j ~normal(mu_j,Sigma_j)
(mu_j|Sigma_j) ~ normal(mu0_j,Sigma_j)
Sigma_j ~ invwish(nu,I)

The main part of the code is:
tau_j ~ Cauchy(0,2.5);
z ~ Normal(0,1);
L_Omega ~ lkj_corr_chlesky(2);
mu0_j ~ Normal(0,5);
mu_j <- mu0_j+diag_pre_multiply(tau,L_omega) * z;
beta_j <-  mu_j+diag_pre_multiply(tau,L_omega) * z;
h_j <- x_j * beta_j;
y_j <- exp(h_j) ./ (1.0 + exp(h_j));
where it optimizes the inverse wishart prior through Cholesky factorization.

The problem is that response y_j will sometimes become negative.
I am not sure how this comes.
Any ideas or suggestions for solving this issue would be greatly appreciated!

Thanks,
Sophia

messages.body_plain:
The change-point model is an expansion of the non-change-point model.
Without a prior on where the changepoint is or a prior on there being
a changepoint, a predictive comparison should favor the change-point model.

You could also fit a changepoint and compare the posterior of the
two components to see if they are much different and how they compare
to the non-changepoint model.  That is, do some posterior predictive
comparisons.

- Bob

what you think you're getting.  Then fit with simulated data to
make sure the model's right.

The problem is here:

  vector[] U2SL_log(vector[] rho, int M, real ts) {

That defines rho as a 1-dimensional array of vectors so that rho[i] is
a vector.  And returns the result type as a 1-D array of vectors.

So you probably wanted

  vector U2SL_log(vector rho, int M, real ts) {

There's a description of the language of types for functions in
the functions chapter of the manual.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Problem with mixture model and prior
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Problem with mixture model and prior
messages.body_plain:
Unless variables are marginally independent given data,
putting a prior on one will affect the other.    And all
your variables appear related.

That is, a mixture model isn't equivalent to fitting all the
data with component one, fitting all the data with component two,
then mixing them.  Everything's fit jointly.

You can see how this works in a simple mixture of two normal
cases.  Compare the effect of the prior on one of the two
means (assume equal variance to keep it really simple).

- Bob

Theta_1, Theta_2, Theta_3 are 4 x 5 matrix to "score" the answers. Then, p = f(X, Theta) is (X_1 x Theta_1) .* (X_2 x Theta_2) .* (X_3 x Theta_3) where .* is elementwise multiplication. After rescaling, p is a N x 5 matrix where each row is the probability of each observation falling into one of five "types." Y is then a N x 1 matrix where each Y_i \in {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} corresponding to each "type."
>
> An example maybe personality tests, where you answer a couple of multiple choice questions and are told what kind of personality type you belong to. The tricky bit here is that I know that each Y_i is not randomly drawn from a multinomial distribution with probability p_i, but simply obtained by referencing the category in p with the highest probability. For example, if p_i = [0.2, 0.2, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1] then Y_i = 3.
>
> So my understanding is that what I have here is a working data generating process, except for that it is deterministic instead of probabilistic. Since Stan only allows probabilistic models for the final step, the low-variance approximation approach was the first thing that popped in my head, but it seems that it's not well justified. I would love to hear your thoughts and suggestions on whether there's any alternatives.
>
> On Friday, August 28, 2015 at 2:27:48 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> If you want to use Bayesian methods, you need to write down
> a joint model, typically defined in terms of a
> probabilistic data-generating process.  It isn't clear to me
> what the shape of X and Y_i would be or what theta is.  It
> helps if you can write down the dimensions and a short description
> of what the values mean.
>
> Stan's not ideally suited to this kind of deterministic data-generating
> problem, because it amounts to a constraint solving
> problem for the parameters (assuming X is some matrix of predictors for
> individuals and there is a latent coefficient vector).
>
> You don't want to try to write down a low-variance approximation to
> something deterministic --- you want to write down the data generating
> process.
>
> - Bob
>
> > On Aug 28, 2015, at 3:17 AM, Minh Trinh <minhtr...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi everyone,
> >
> > I'm new to this list , so please excuse any possible faux-pas I may commit.
> >
> > I am trying to estimate the parameters of a deterministic data generating process that closely resembles a probabilistic (multinomial) one. In particular, for data X and unknown parameters theta, f(X, theta) is a N x 5 matrix where each row is a 5-simplex i.e. sums to 1. In a normal multinomial model, each Y_i would be drawn from a multinomial distribution with probability parameters equal to each row of f(X, theta). However, in this case, instead of a random multinomial draw, Y_i is simply the category with the highest probability.
> >
> > The parameters in this problem may be calculated analytically, but I'm wondering if there is anyway to get at them through Monte Carlo methods. Also, generally, in problems where there might also be similar deterministic data generating processes and where there might not be unique solutions for the parameters, would Monte Carlo methods be useful at all? And if MC can be useful, how do I do it in STAN? I am thinking of using distributions with variability close to zero to mimic the deterministic process, but I'm not sure if this is theoretically justified.
> >
> > Thanks so much,
> > Minh

> On Aug 31, 2015, at 8:51 AM, Bruno Nicenboim <bruno.n...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>
> Hi, I'm back with my shifted-lognormal hierarchical model (this is my previous post), I
> started to increase the complexity of the model, and I started to notice
> problems in convergence. So I simplified everything again to check it.
> Basically I'm trying to fit a model where reading times (rt) are assumed to be
> produced by a shifted lognormal distribution. I'm assuming a general shift, a
> by-subject adjustment coming from a normal distribution centered in 0, an
> intercept for the lognormal part (alpha), a fixed effect (beta), and
> by-subjects random intercept and slopes centered in 0 that they are somewhat
> correlated: (the complete code is in shifted_log_simple.stan)
>
>
>  transformed parameters{
>  (...)
>  for (i in 1:N_obs){
>     mu[i] <- alpha  + x_betas[i] * beta +
>           x_u[i] * u[subj[i]];
>     psi[i] <-  shift + shift_u[subj[i]]; //
>   }
> }
>
>
> model {
>  (...)
>      (rt - psi) ~ lognormal(mu, sigma);
> }
>
>
>
> So the same parameters that don't get an Rhat of 1 in the complex mode, here
> they are around 1.01-1.02 (while the other params are more in the
> 1.00something).
>
> These parameters are the ones that are in a different scale than the rest:
> alpha (the intercept of fixed effects) has an estimate around 5 (I simulate
> this but that's also the case in "real life"), the intercept for shift is
> around 200, while the adjustment for shift for participants is between 0-200.
> (The other parameters are below 1). I checked the get_sampler_params, and I
> noticed that Max treedepth reaches 11 and n_divergent has a Max of 1, which I
> understand from the manual is something bad.
>
> So from reading previous answers in the forum, I understand that there are two
> possibilities: either to decrease the stepsize and increase the treedepth; or
> to normalize the parameters to be near 1. I'm trying to avoid the first
> possibility just because it's extremely slow.
>
> Regarding the second option, one problem that I face is that the
> initialization fails unless I set init=0.

Do you mean throws exceptions then quits?  This is usually a sign that your
constraints don't match the support of your model, which can also cause
all sorts of problems downstream with divergent iterations (going out of support
is a kind of divergence).

Which of these models has this problem?  I'm afraid I don't have time to
read three models and diff them in my head, but I can check over one
for constraints matching support.

> I'm normalizing the intercept alpha with alpha_k= mean(log(rt)), which is
> always a bit bigger than the intercept, and the shifts with shift_k which is
> mean(rt) also bigger than the shift. I'm doing this (in shifted_log_simple_norm.stan):
>
>  for (i in 1:N_obs){
>     mu[i] <- alpha * alpha_k + x_betas[i] * beta +
>           x_u[i] * u[subj[i]];
>     psi[i] <-  shift_k * (shift + shift_u[subj[i]]); //
>   }
>
>
>
> First of all, it doesn't improve the Rhats (in fact all Rhats are
> even bigger). So does it even make sense? (And I guess that constraining the
> init to 0 is not ideal, but maybe a side effect of the problems I'm having).
> And I still have the same problems with treedepth n_divergent. So my question
> is: Is there a solution besides changing step size and the maximum tree depth?

It's an issue of parameterizing the model in a more friendly way.  The
problem with all these hierarchical models is only a week identifiability
in play, especially if the hierarchical variance is high.  You can check out
the pairs plot of the posterior to see if any correlations jump out at you (just
be warned it won't work for more than 10 or so input variables at a time).

- Bob

With a bit further manipulation, I can get service level--the probability that an incoming service request will have to wait longer than t seconds to be served.
> > > >
> > > > If I did that right (I seem to get the same answers using the queueing package and this), the R code looks like
> > > >
> > > >       erlb <- function(nsrv, nerl, log=FALSE)
> > > >       {
> > > >         # Returns Erlang-B blockage for nsrv servers and nerl erlangs of traffic.
> > > >         # If log=TRUE, then logarithm of the blockage is returned.  Works for all
> > > >         # nsrv>=0 and all nerl>=0.  Both nsrv and nerl can be non-integers.
> > > >
> > > >         # Same as queueing::B_erlang
> > > >         # From https://stat.ethz.ch/pipermail/r-help/2001-September/014986.html
> > > >         # See, too, https://ia601606.us.archive.org/26/items/bstj53-3-525/bstj53-3-525_text.pdf
> > > >
> > > >         lnerlb<-
> > > >           dgamma(nerl, shape=nsrv+1, scale=1, log=TRUE) -
> > > >           pgamma(nerl, shape=nsrv+1, scale=1, log.p=TRUE, lower.tail=FALSE) ;
> > > >           if (log) lnerlb else exp(lnerlb)
> > > >       }
> > > >
> > > >       erlc <- function (c = 1, r = 0)
> > > >       {
> > > >           # Same as queueing::C_erlang but with erlb instead of B_erlang
> > > >           ## if (is.anomalous(c))
> > > >           ##     stop("The parameter c is anomalous. Check it!")
> > > >           ## if (is.anomalous(r))
> > > >           ##     stop("The parameter r is anomalous. Check it!")
> > > >           ## if (c < 1)
> > > >           ##     stop(ALL_c_warning)
> > > >           ## if (!is.wholenumber(c))
> > > >           ##     stop(ALL_c_integer)
> > > >           b_result <- erlb(c - 1, r)
> > > >           (r * b_result)/(c - (r * (1 - b_result)))
> > > >       }
> > > >
> > > >       SLfun <- function(rho, M, ts, t) {
> > > >         # M = number of servers
> > > >         # rho = utilization (fraction of available time servers are busy)
> > > >         # ts = expected value of service time in seconds
> > > >         # t = SL time in seconds
> > > >           SL  <- (erlc(M, rho * M) *
> > > >                   exp(-M * (1 - rho) * t / ts))
> > > >           1 - SL
> > > >       }
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Because I don't know capacity well, I'd like to do a Stan model that looks something like
> > > >
> > > > data {
> > > >   int<lower=0> N;                      // no. of days of data
> > > >   vector<lower=0,upper=1>[N] sl;       // daily recorded service level
> > > >   int<lower=1> M;                      // no. of servers
> > > >   vector<lower=0>[N] load;             // load in units of time
> > > >   vector<lower=0>[N] recordedcapacity; // capacity in the same units of time
> > > >   real<lower=1> t;                     // Time threshold for calculating SL
> > > >   real<lower=1> ts;                    // average service time
> > > > }
> > > >
> > > > transformed data {
> > > >   vector<lower=0,upper=1>[N] recordedrho;
> > > >   recordedrho <- load / recordedcapacity;
> > > > }
> > > >
> > > > parameters {
> > > >   real<lower=0> sigma;
> > > >   vector<lower=0>[N] capacity;
> > > >   vector<lower=0,upper=1>[N] rho;
> > > >   rho <- load / capacity;
> > > > }
> > > >
> > > > model {
> > > >   rho ~ normal(recordedrho, sigma) T[0.0, 1.0];  // there's probably a better distribution for this
> > > >   sl ~ SLfun(rho, M, ts, t);
> > > > }
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > It's probably simple algebra, but I'm missing how to convert SLfun into Stan functions, presumably built into a functions {} block with Stan's gamma distribution functions.  Pointers?
